parole.significato: Connective infix encountered in loanwords and phrases, generally no longer carrying a distinct meaning.
parole.testo: From French à (“various prepositions”) and related prepositions in other Romance languages. Also from related misunderstandings, as all-a-mort from French à la morte.

parole.significato: One affected with.
parole.testo: From French -acque, from New Latin -acus, from Ancient Greek -ακός (-akós, “-ic”). Related to -ic and -y.

parole.significato: One whose wealth exceeds a specific number of units in the local currency.
parole.testo: Rebracketing of millionaire, which was, in turn, borrowed from French millionnaire.

parole.significato: head
parole.testo: From French -céphalie, German -zephalie, or Latin -cephalia, from Ancient Greek κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”) and a suffix: French -ie, German -ie, or Latin -ia.

parole.significato: bacteriocin
parole.testo: From English colicin, from French colicine, from coli- + -cine, with ending formed by analogy from antibiotics like auréomycine, streptomycine, with second element from myc- + -ine.

parole.significato: Forms nouns (and occasionally adjectives) relating to organisms that inhabit a particular habitat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -cole, from Latin -cola (“cultivator”).

parole.significato: digits
parole.testo: From French -dactyle, from Latin -dactylus, ultimately from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “finger”).

parole.significato: Diminutive suffix in words of French origin.
parole.testo: Variant of French -eille, from Middle French -eille, from Old French -eille, -eil, -ele, -eyle, from Latin -icula, from rebracketing of -i- + -culus.

parole.significato: Used to form feminine proper names
parole.testo: From French -elle.

parole.significato: Indicates the presence of a carbon-carbon double bond.
parole.testo: From French -ène.

parole.significato: An unsaturated hydrocarbon having at least one double bond; an alkene.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -ène, chosen by French chemist Jean-Baptiste Dumas to avoid confusion with chemicals in -ine.

parole.significato: In the style or manner of; appended to nouns, especially proper nouns, and forming adjectives.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -esque (“-ish, -ic, -esque”), from Italian -esco, from Latin -iscus, of Germanic origin, from Lombardic -isc (“-ish”), from Proto-West Germanic *-isk, from Proto-Germanic *-iskaz (“-ish”), from Proto-Indo-European *-iskos. Cognate with Old High German -isc (German -isch), Old En

parole.significato: Forming nouns denoting female people, usually from terms ending in French -eur.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -euse.

parole.significato: The act of creating something, or (more broadly) any process involving the specified thing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -faction, from Latin -factiō. This is the ending that arises when forming action nouns using -tiō (equivalent to English -tion) from compound verbs ending in -faciō (“to make, to do”), which carry a causative meaning. For example, liqueō (“to be liquid”) + faciō > liquefaciō (“t

parole.significato: A producer of something, or an agent in the production of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -gène, from the Ancient Greek -γενής (-genḗs).

parole.significato: describes something which is formed in a certain way or produces something
parole.testo: From French -gène and German -gen, from Latin -genus and Ancient Greek -γενής (-genḗs).

parole.significato: Something written or otherwise represented in the specified manner, or about a specified subject.
parole.testo: From French -graphie, inherited from Latin -graphia, borrowed from Ancient Greek -γραφία (-graphía), from γραφή (graphḗ, “writing, drawing, description”). By surface analysis, -graph + -y.

parole.significato: forming nouns denoting occupations
parole.testo: From French -icien, from -ique f sg + -ien. By surface analysis, -ic + -ian.

parole.significato: indicates a female variant of a noun ending in -ian
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -ienne, feminine of -ien (“-ian”).

parole.significato: Forming nouns denoting the quality or condition of being what is indicated by the first element of the word.
parole.testo: From French -ieté or its source, Latin -ietas.

parole.significato: Combined with Latin prefixes for names of integers in order to form names of large numbers as 10⁶ⁿ⁺³.
parole.testo: From French -illiard.

parole.significato: Combined with Latin prefixes for names of integers in order to form names of powers of a million.
parole.testo: Back-formation from million, then used in billion, trillion, quadrillion, each from French, ultimately from Italian mille (“thousand”) and the augmentative suffix -one. -illion was segmented from million as if mi- was a prefix, and -illion the stem.

parole.significato: Suffix denoting ordinal number.
parole.testo: From French -ime, from decime, ultimately from Latin -ima.

parole.significato: Used to form nouns denoting followers or adherents of a specified person, idea, doctrine, movement, etc.
parole.testo: From French -ite, from Old French, from Latin -ītēs, from Ancient Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs).

parole.significato: -logical
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -logique. By surface analysis, -logy + -ic.

parole.significato: A branch of learning; a study of a particular subject.
parole.testo: The English -logy suffix originates with loanwords from the Greek, usually via Latin and French, where the suffix -λογία (-logía) is an integral part of the word loaned. E.g. astrology from astrologia, since the 16th century. The French -logie is a continuation of Latin -logia, ultimately from Ancie

parole.significato: Forming compound nouns with the sense of person who has a mania for.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -mane, from Ancient Greek -μανής (-manḗs).

parole.significato: Having parts of the specified quality.
parole.testo: From French -mère and its etymon Ancient Greek -μερής (-merḗs, “having (the specified number of) parts”, “sharing”): the combining form of μέρος (méros, “part”)) with the English suffix -ous; compare the English -mer and -mere, as well as the French -mère and the German -mer.

parole.significato: Used to form the names of measuring devices.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -mètre, a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron).

parole.significato: Forming adjectives corresponding to nouns in -meter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -métrique, from Latin metricus.

parole.significato: Forming a placename or a surname derived therefrom and denoting or connoting a hill or mountain; sometimes (as in estat…
parole.testo: From French -mont, from French mont (“hill, mountain”).

parole.significato: Indicating a life-form, often microscopic
parole.testo: Abstracted from aerobe and microbe, both formed in French using the Ancient Greek word βίος (bíos, “life”).

parole.significato: Forming nouns, mainly in borrowed words.
parole.testo: From French -on.

parole.significato: Having disease or abnormal condition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -otique, from Latin -ōticus, from Ancient Greek -ωτικός (-ōtikós), from -όω (-óō)-stem verbs + -τικός (-tikós). Equivalent to -όω (-óō) + -σις (-sis) + -ικός (-ikós).

parole.significato: Suffix indicating an organism or person with a specified number or type of feet.
parole.testo: Partly from French ‑pède and partly from Latin pedis (genitive of pēs (“foot”)).

parole.significato: Used to form nouns denoting a person having a fear of a specific thing.
parole.testo: From French -phobe, from Latin -phobus, from Attic Greek -φόβος (-phóbos), combining form of φόβος (phóbos), ablaut variant of φέβεσθαι (phébesthai), middle infinitive of φέβομαι (phébomai), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰegʷ-. Cognates include Russian бегать (begatʹ, “run, flee”), Slovak bežať (“run”)

parole.significato: Forms nouns related to:
parole.testo: From French -phonie, from Old French -phonie, and its etymon Classical Latin -phōnia, from Ancient Greek -φωνία (-phōnía). By surface analysis, -phone + -y. Doublet of -phonia.

parole.significato: exhibiting a behavior.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -tropie, from Ancient Greek -τροπίᾱ (-tropíā), from τρόπος (trópos, “a turn”).

parole.significato: Used to form a name of an inhabited place, a town or city.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ville (“town, city”).

parole.significato: Having a certain number of broods or generations in a year.
parole.testo: From French -voltin, from Italian volta (“time, instance, occasion”) + -in.

parole.significato: A univalent radical or functional group formed from a given molecule. Thus propyl from propane, benzyl from benzene, an…
parole.testo: Via French méthylène from Ancient Greek ὕλη (húlē, “wood, material”).

parole.significato: In the style or manner of.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French à la.

parole.significato: Prepared to order, not prepared in advance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French à la minute.

parole.significato: Fashionable; in the current style or fashion.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French à la mode (“in fashion”). The US sense was coined by polyglot restaurant owner John Gieriet in Minnesota in the 1800s though later attributed to Berry Hall and Charles Watson Townsend.

parole.significato: Of a ship, especially a tall square-rigged one: in which all running rigging is hauled taut; having all spars hoisted a…
parole.testo: French autant (“as much (as possible)”).

parole.significato: Synonym of nomogram.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French abaque, from Classical Latin abacus, from Ancient Greek ἄβαξ (ábax). Doublet of abacus and abaque.

parole.significato: A short- or long-sleeved button-up jacket, worn without a shirt, that was promoted in Zaire under the regime of Mobutu…
parole.testo: From French. A contraction of à bas le costume (“down with the western suit”)

parole.significato: A thin undercrust of pastry.
parole.testo: From French abaisser.

parole.significato: Of a charge, especially a fess: borne lower than usual.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abaissé (“to lower”).

parole.significato: The act of abandoning, or the state of being abandoned; total desertion; relinquishment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abandonnement, from abandonner (“to abandon, relinquish”). abandonner was originally equivalent to mettre à bandon (“to leave to the jurisdiction, i.e. of another”), bandon being from Medieval Latin bandum, bannum (“order, decree, ban”). Equivalent to abandon + -ment. (See also

parole.significato: A nomogram.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abaque. Doublet of abacus and abac.

parole.significato: A skylight.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abat-jour.

parole.significato: An architectural device consisting of large louvres with the purpose of directing sound in a specific direction.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abat-son, from abat (“to bring down”) + sons (“sounds”)

parole.significato: Louvres or strips of wood or metal used as windbreaks that allow light and air in, often seen in belfries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abat-vent, from abattre (“to throw down”) + vent (“wind”), from Latin ventus.

parole.significato: A device for reflection of sound, as in a sounding board over a pulpit or rostrum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abat-voix, from French abattre (“to beat down”) + voix (“voice”).

parole.significato: A means of defense formed by felled trees, or sometimes by bent trees, the ends of whose branches are sharpened and dir…
parole.testo: From French abatis, abattis (“mass of things beaten or cut down”), from abattre. See abate.

parole.significato: A device for directing sound downward. Sounding board.
parole.testo: * Borrowed from French abatsons, from abattre (“to throw down”) + sons (“sound”)

parole.significato: The slaughter of animals, especially diseased ones to limit the spread of the disease.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abattage.

parole.significato: A public slaughterhouse for cattle, sheep, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abattoir, from abattre (“to slaughter”) (cognate to abate) + -oir (“-ory”).

parole.significato: A low-ranking member of the Roman Catholic clergy in France who is not a member of a religious order, is not a priest,…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French abbé (“abbot”), from Latin abbās (“abbot”). Doublet of abbot.

parole.significato: Acting to diminish irritation; soothing.
parole.testo: From ab- (prefix from Latin ab (“from”)) + irritant, from French irritant, from Latin irrītō (“to irritate”).

parole.significato: To send abroad.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ablégate, from Latin ablēgātus, perfect passive participle of ablēgō (“to send off or away; banish”), from ab (“from, away from”) + lēgō (“to dispatch, send on a commission”). See legate.

parole.significato: A small fresh-water fish (Alburnus alburnus); the bleak.
parole.testo: From French ablet, ablette, a diminutive from Late Latin abula, for albula, diminutive of albus (“white”). Compare abele.

parole.significato: To abominate.
parole.testo: From French abominer.

parole.significato: A subscription or season ticket in a French-speaking country or another country where abonnement is the local term.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abonnement, from French abonner (“subscribe”).

parole.significato: A subscriber; a season ticket holder.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abonné, from abonner (“subscribe”).

parole.significato: The act of approaching or arriving; approach.
parole.testo: From French abord, from aborder (“to aboard”).

parole.significato: The act of boarding a ship as part of an attack.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abordage.

parole.significato: The point of union of two vessels.
parole.testo: French abouchement

parole.significato: ludicrous, preposterous
parole.testo: From French abracadabrant.

parole.significato: An oil from the tung tree that is used in paints and varnishes; tung oil.
parole.testo: Partial translation from French huile d'abrasin

parole.significato: The act of abrading, wearing, or rubbing off; the wearing away by friction.
parole.testo: First attested in 1656. From French abrasion (attested since 1611), from Medieval Latin abrasio (“a scraping”), from Latin abrādō (“scrape off”). See also abrade.

parole.significato: A cold water drinking fountain (for people) typically found in a public location; more generally, any fountain or water…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abreuvoir (“a watering place”).

parole.significato: a shelter; a cavity in a hillside; a shelter on the side of hill with an overhung rock as its roof
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abri (“shelter”), from Old French abrier (“to shelter”), see below.

parole.significato: Of or belonging to the prehistoric culture between the late Mousterian and Aurignacian.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Abri Audit (literally “Audit shelter”).

parole.significato: Doctrine of preordination; doctrine of absolute decrees; doctrine that God acts in an absolute manner.
parole.testo: First attested in 1753 (in the theological sense); attested in 1830 in the political sense. From absolute + -ism, based after French absolutisme.

parole.significato: One who is in favor of an absolute or autocratic government.
parole.testo: From absolute + -ist after French absolutiste.

parole.significato: The act of restraining oneself.
parole.testo: First attested in 1521. Borrowed from French abstention, from Late Latin abstēntiō from Latin abstinēō (“withhold, to abstain”)

parole.significato: A policy of abstaining or of the desirability of withholding one's vote or other participation with regard to some aspe…
parole.testo: From French abstentionnisme. By surface analysis, abstention + -ism.

parole.significato: Cleansing, detergent.
parole.testo: From French, from Latin abstergens, present participle of abstergeo (“wiping off”).

parole.significato: Prone to treat someone badly by coarse, insulting words or other maltreatment; vituperative; reproachful; scurrilous.
parole.testo: First attested in the 1530s. From French abusif, from Latin abūsīvus, from abusus + -ivus (“-ive”). Equivalent to abuse + -ive.

parole.significato: A member (especially a senior one) of the faculty at a college or university; an academic.
parole.testo: From academic + -ian (“one skilled in”), partly after French académicien.

parole.significato: An academic philosopher.
parole.testo: From French académiste, from académie (“academy”).

parole.significato: The cashew tree.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French acajou (“cashew”), from Old Tupi akaîu. Doublet of cashew.

parole.significato: To overwhelm; to encumber.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French accabler (“to overwhelm”).

parole.significato: Easy of access or approach.
parole.testo: First attested in 1400, from French, from Late Latin accessibilis, from accessus, perfect passive participle of accēdō (“approach”), equivalent to access + -ible.

parole.significato: Acclimatization.
parole.testo: From French acclimatation.

parole.significato: To habituate to a climate not native; to acclimatize.
parole.testo: 1792, from French acclimater.

parole.significato: An expression of approval; praise.
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1591 in the publications of Thomas Lodge, borrowed from French accolade, from Occitan acolada (“an embrace”), from acolar (“to embrace”), from Italian accollato, via Vulgar Latin *accollō (“to hug around the neck”), from Latin ad- + collum (“neck”) (English collar) + -āta.

parole.significato: Crescent-shaped.
parole.testo: From French accolé, past participle of accoler.

parole.significato: Lodging in a dwelling or similar living quarters afforded to travellers in hotels or on cruise ships, or students, etc.
parole.testo: From French accommodation, from Latin accommodātiō (“adjustment, accommodation, compliance”), from accommodō (“adapt, put in order”). Superficially accommodate + -ion. The sense of "lodging" was first attested in 1600.

parole.significato: A part, usually performed by instruments, that gives support or adds to the background in music, or adds for ornamentat…
parole.testo: From French accompagnement; equivalent to accompany + -ment. First attested in 1744.

parole.significato: The act of accomplishing; completion; fulfilment.
parole.testo: * First attested in the early 15th century. * (completes, perfects, equips): First attested around 1600. * accomplish + -ment * Borrowed from French accomplissement, from accomplir

parole.significato: Approachable; affable; willing to be accosted.
parole.testo: Originally from French accostable, in later usage partly recoined from accost + -able.

parole.significato: To aid in an accouchement; to assist (a mother) in the birth (of a child).
parole.testo: A back-formation from accouchement, or else from French accoucher.

parole.significato: Delivery in childbed; parturition
parole.testo: Borrowed from French accouchement, from French accoucher (“to be delivered of a child, to aid in delivery”), from Old French acouchier (“to lay down, put to bed, go to bed”), from Latin ad- + collocare (“to lay, put, place”). See collate.

parole.significato: A person, especially a man, who delivers a baby (in childbirth).
parole.testo: Attested since 1727. Borrowed from French accoucheur, from accoucher (“to go to childbed, be delivered”), from Old French culcher (“to lie”), from Latin collocō (“to place, put, set in order, assign”), from con- + locō (“to put, place, set”). See accouchement.

parole.significato: A midwife.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French accoucheuse, female of accoucheur.

parole.significato: The act of coupling, or the state of being coupled; union
parole.testo: Borrowed from French accouplement.

parole.significato: To ascribe; attribute; credit with.
parole.testo: * First attested in the 1610s. * From French accréditer, from à (“to”) + to credit, from crédit (“credit”). * See credit.

parole.significato: A male accuser.
parole.testo: From literary French accusateur, from Latin accūsātōrem, accusative singular of accūsātor (“accuser”). Doublet of accuser.

parole.significato: Having no head.
parole.testo: From French acéphale, from Ancient Greek ἀκέφαλος (aképhalos, “headless”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”). By surface analysis, a- + -cephalous.

parole.significato: Sourness of taste, with bitterness and astringency, like that of unripe fruit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French acerbité, from Latin acerbitās (“acerbity; harshness”), from acerbus (“bitter”). See acerb.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or producing vinegar.
parole.testo: From French acétique, from Latin acētum (“vinegar”), from acēre (“to be sour”). By surface analysis, acet- + -ic.

parole.significato: The act of making acetous or sour; the process of converting, or of becoming converted, into vinegar.
parole.testo: Circa 1733. Directly or via French acétification, from New Latin acētificātiō, from acētum (“vinegar”) + -ficātiō, from faciō (“to make”).

parole.significato: Any organic compound having one or more carbon–carbon triple bonds; an alkyne.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French acétylène, coined by French chemist Marcellin Berthelot, from acetyl + -ene.

parole.significato: Savage fierceness; ferocity.
parole.testo: From French acharnement.

parole.significato: Relentlessly opposed; irreconcilable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French acharné.

parole.significato: A small, dry, indehiscent fruit, containing a single seed, as in the buttercup.
parole.testo: From French achène and its source, New Latin achena, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “a-”) + χαίνω (khaínō, “to gape”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a lower Paleolithic period characterized by the presence of flaked bifacial hand axes.
parole.testo: From French acheuléen, from Saint-Acheul, a suburb of Amiens where the first tools from this period were found.

parole.significato: Sour, sharp, or biting to the taste; tart; having the taste of vinegar.
parole.testo: From French acide, from Latin acidus (“sour, acid”), from aceō (“to be sour”). Doublet of agita.

parole.significato: The act or process of making something sour (acidifying), or changing into an acid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French acidification, equivalent to acid + -ification.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being acid.
parole.testo: From French acidité, from Latin aciditātem, accusative singular of aciditās (“sourness, acidity”), from acidus (“sour, acid”). Equivalent to acid + -ity.

parole.significato: The process of electroplating a copper engraving with iron or steel.
parole.testo: French aciérage, from acier (“steel”).

parole.significato: To convert (iron) into steel, or to coat with a layer of steel by converting only the surface of the iron.
parole.testo: From French aciérage, from acier (“steel”).

parole.significato: The conversion of iron into steel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French acier (“steel”) + -ation.

parole.significato: The herb wolfsbane, or monkshood; any plant of the genus Aconitum, all the species of which are poisonous.
parole.testo: From French aconit, from Latin aconītum, from Ancient Greek ἀκόνιτον (akóniton).

parole.significato: Any of several rodents of the genus Myoprocta, smaller than agoutis, which inhabit Amazonia.
parole.testo: From French acouchi, probably from the same Old Tupi name akuti as agouti.

parole.significato: Acquiescence (assent, submission).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French acquiescement, equivalent to acquiesce + -ment.

parole.significato: A silent or passive assent or submission, or a submission with apparent consent, distinguished from avowed consent on t…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French acquiescence.

parole.significato: Ellipsis of acquis communautaire.
parole.testo: Shortened from acquis communautaire: French acquis (“that has been acquired or obtained”) + communautaire (“of the community”).

parole.significato: The full body of European Union law.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French acquis communautaire.

parole.significato: To weaken, impair, or enfeeble in mind, body, or estate; craze.
parole.testo: From French acraser (“to break, burst, craze, bruise, crush”), same as écraser (“to squash”), from Middle French ecraser (“to squash”), from Middle English crasen (“to break, shatter”), from Old Norse *krasa (“to shatter”). More at craze.

parole.significato: An athlete who performs acts requiring skill, agility and coordination, often as part of a circus performance.
parole.testo: From French acrobate, from Ancient Greek ἀκροβάτης (akrobátēs, “walking on tiptoe, climbing aloft”), from ἀκροβατέω (akrobatéō, “to walk on tiptoe”), from ἄκρον (ákron, “highest or farthest point, mountain top, peak”) + βαίνω (baínō, “to walk, step”).

parole.significato: A chronic disease marked by enlargement of the bones of the extremities, face, and jaw that is caused by over-activity…
parole.testo: From French acromégalie, from New Latin acromegalia, from Ancient Greek ἄκρον (ákron, “tip, extremity”) and μέγας (mégas, “large”). By surface analysis, acro- + -megaly.

parole.significato: An acroterium.
parole.testo: From French acrotère, from Latin acrōtērium, from Ancient Greek ἀκρωτήριον (akrōtḗrion), from ἄκρος (ákros) + -τήριον (-tḗrion). Doublet of acroterium.

parole.significato: The doctrine, in European law, that cases involving a law with a reasonably obvious interpretation do not need to be re…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French acte clair.

parole.significato: An impulsive act lacking motive.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French acte gratuit.

parole.significato: A radioactive, metallic chemical element (symbol: Ac) with an atomic number of 89; found in uranium ores.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French actinium. actin- + -ium.

parole.significato: The theory of sociologist Alain Touraine that aims to replace sociology's focus from society to actors. Here, they emph…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French actionnalisme.

parole.significato: The state of existing; existence.
parole.testo: From actual + -ity. * (television): Influenced by French actualité.

parole.significato: Present, current, living, active.
parole.testo: From French actuel, from Latin actuālis.

parole.significato: The branch of palynology concerned with the study of modern-day pollens and spores, rather than with fossils.
parole.testo: From actuo- (“present, current, living, active”) + palynology, from French actuel, from Latin actuālis + Ancient Greek παλύνω (palúnō, “to sprinkle, scatter”) (from πάλη (pálē, “fine meal, dust”)) + Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía). By surface analysis, actuo- + palyno- + -log + -y.

parole.significato: The process of adapting something or becoming adapted to a situation; adjustment, modification.
parole.testo: From French adaptation, from Medieval Latin adaptātiō, from Latin adaptō (“to fit, adjust, modify; to adapt, fit or adjust to”); see adapt. Equivalent to adapt + -ation.

parole.significato: A class that is converted to another class using a so-called adapter class.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French adaptée.

parole.significato: A large African antelope (Addax nasomaculatus) with long, corkscrewing horns which lives in the desert.
parole.testo: From French addax, from Arabic أبو عدس (ʔabū ʕadas, literally “father of the lentil”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to lymphatic glands or lymphoid tissue.
parole.testo: Late 19th century borrowing from French adénoïde, from New Latin adenoīdēs, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓δενοειδής (ădenoeidḗs, “glandular”), from ᾰ̓δήν (ădḗn, “gland”) + -ο- (-o-) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-oid, -like”); equivalent to aden- + -oid. The noun is derived from ellipsis of tumeur adénoïde (“glandular

parole.significato: Well skilled; completely versed; thoroughly proficient.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French adepte, from Latin adeptus (“who has achieved”), the past participle of adipisci (“to attain”).

parole.significato: The ability of a substance to stick to an unlike substance.
parole.testo: From French adhésion, from Latin stem of adhaesio, from past participle of adhaerare.

parole.significato: Sticky; tenacious, as glutinous substances.
parole.testo: From French adhésif, from Medieval Latin adhaesivus, from adhaereō (supine adhaesum); see adhere.

parole.testo: From French adjoindre (“to join”), from late 19th C; see also adjoin. Doublet of adjunct. parole.significato: The action of adjusting something.
parole.testo: From French ajustement, or else adjust + -ment.

parole.significato: The office or jurisdiction of an admiral.
parole.testo: From French amirauté, for an older amiralté (“office of admiral”), from Late Latin admīrālitās. See admiral. Analyzable as admiral + -ty.

parole.significato: Characterized by admiration.
parole.testo: Via French admiratif or directly from its etymon, Medieval Latin admirativus.

parole.significato: An adopted son or daughter.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French adoptée, feminine past participle of adopter meaning "to adopt", equivalent to adopt + -ee.

parole.significato: The act of adopting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French adoption, from Latin adoptio, allied to adoptare (“to adopt”). Equivalent to adopt + -ion.

parole.significato: Synonym of adorer.
parole.testo: From French adorateur and its etymon Latin adōrātor. By surface analysis, adore + -ator or adorate + -or.

parole.significato: Gum tragacanth.
parole.testo: From French, a corruption of tragacanth. Doublet of tragacanth.

parole.significato: The sun-facing side of a mountain; in the northern hemisphere, this is typically the south-facing slope.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French adret or Occitan adret, adré, adrech, adreit (“sun-facing side of a mountain”), from Old Occitan adreg, adreit, from a (“to, towards”) (from Latin ad (“to, towards”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“at; to”)) + dreg, dreit (“just; right”) (from Latin dīrēctus (“direc

parole.significato: deft, dexterous, or skillful
parole.testo: Borrowed from French adroit, from French à (“on the; to”) (from Old French a (“to; towards”), from Latin ad (“to; towards”), from Proto-Indo-European *ád (“at; near”)) + French droit (“right”) (from Old French droit, dreit, from Late Latin drictus, syncopated form of Latin dīrēctus (“laid straight;

parole.significato: To accumulate on a surface, by adsorption.
parole.testo: From French adsorber, from Latin ad- (“to”) + sorbeō (“suck in”).

parole.significato: Flattery; fulsome praise.
parole.testo: From French adulation, from Latin adulātio (“flattery”).

parole.significato: An animal that is full-grown.
parole.testo: From French adulte, from Latin adultus (“grown up”), perfect passive participle of adolescō (“to grow up”). Compare adolescent.

parole.significato: A word that modifies a verb, adjective, other adverbs, or various other types of words, phrases, or clauses.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French adverbe, from Latin adverbium, from ad- (“to”) + verb(um) (“word, verb”) + -ium, so called because it is used to supplement other words (not specifically verbs). By surface analysis, ad- + verb.

parole.significato: A steam engine powered by rocket propulsion due to escaping steam, consisting of a pressure vessel mounted on a bearing…
parole.testo: From French éolipyle, from Latin Aeoli pylae (“doorway of Aeolus”).

parole.significato: Of or belonging to the atmosphere or to the air; aerial.
parole.testo: From the French aérien, from the Old French aerïen, from the Classical Latin āerius; compare aerial.

parole.significato: Any organism (but especially a bacterium) that can tolerate the presence of oxygen, or that needs oxygen to survive.
parole.testo: Derived from French aérobie. By surface analysis, aero- + -obe.

parole.significato: Living or occurring only in the presence of oxygen e.g. aerobic bacteria.
parole.testo: From French aérobie, coined in 1863 by Louis Pasteur, from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + βίος (bíos, “life”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A dirigible balloon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aéronat.

parole.significato: A person who travels through the air in an airship or balloon.
parole.testo: From aero- + -naut, from the French aéronaute; compare the Italian aeronauta.

parole.significato: The design, construction, mathematics, and mechanics of aircraft and other flying objects; the study of and control of…
parole.testo: From French aéronautique or New Latin aeronauticus. Equivalent to aero- + -naut + -ics.

parole.significato: airplane; a flying machine, an aircraft.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aéronef.

parole.significato: A thin fabric resembling crape
parole.testo: From aero- + -phane, or from French aérophane.

parole.significato: Synonym of airplane. A powered heavier-than-air aircraft with fixed wings.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aéroplane, from Ancient Greek ἀερόπλανος (aeróplanos, “wandering in air”), from ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + πλάνος (plános, “wandering”), equivalent to aero- + plane. First used by Joseph Pline in an 1855 patent.https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Aircraft_Design/NeHoahlhCGMC?hl=en&gb

parole.significato: An aircraft, such as a dirigible or balloon, that derives its lift from buoyancy rather than from wings or rotors.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aérostat, from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + στατός (statós, “stable”), equivalent to aero- + -stat.

parole.significato: Aerial navigation; the act or science of raising and guiding balloons in the air.
parole.testo: From French aérostation, from aérostat (“aerostat”) + -ion, after navigation. By surface analysis, aerostat + -ion.

parole.significato: Sensory information that cannot be articulated in language.
parole.testo: Calque of French information esthétique, as used by French social psychologist and philosopher Abraham Moles in his Théorie de l’information et perception esthétique (1958).

parole.significato: Receiving others kindly and conversing with them in a free and friendly manner; friendly, courteous, sociable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French affable, from Latin affābilis, from affor (“to address”), from ad + for (“to speak, to talk”). See fable. By surface analysis, af- + fable.

parole.significato: A duel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French affaire d'honneur (“matter of honour”).

parole.significato: To cause (somebody) to die of hunger; to starve.
parole.testo: From French affamer, from Latin ad + fames (“hunger”). Compare famish.

parole.significato: The brain’s reception of signals from the body.
parole.testo: Adjective form of afferent, from French afférent (“which brings inward”), from Latin afferent-, from afferēns, present participle of afferre (“bring to”), from af- (variant of ad-) + ferre (“bear”). Doublet of afferentia.

parole.significato: A written or printed notice to be posted, as on a wall; a poster; a placard.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French affiche.

parole.significato: The relationship resulting from affiliating one thing with another.
parole.testo: From French affiliation, from Latin affiliatiō, noun of action from verb affiliō, from af- (form of ad- (“to”) before an f) + filiō (from filius (“son”)).

parole.significato: The aging of cheese as part of its manufacture.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French affinage.

parole.significato: One who ages cheese and purveys it.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French affineur.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being affined; mental affinity or attraction.
parole.testo: From French affiner, from Medieval Latin affinare, affine + -ition.

parole.significato: A freed (manumitted) black person in one of France's colonies, especially Haiti.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French affranchi.

parole.significato: A group of particularly brutal mercenaries who were active in Africa and Asia during the 1960s.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French affreux.

parole.significato: Face to face, or with the fronts facing each other.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French affronté, past participle of affronter (“to confront, face”).

parole.significato: A nihilistic expression of indifference to whatever happens after one is gone.
parole.testo: Calque of French après moi le déluge.

parole.significato: A nihilistic expression of indifference to whatever happens after one is gone.
parole.testo: Calque of French après nous le déluge.

parole.significato: Coquetry; flirtatiousness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French agacerie.

parole.significato: A South American bird, Psophia crepitans, allied to the cranes, and easily domesticated.
parole.testo: From French agami, from Kari'na akami.

parole.significato: A layout (of e.g., a store) set up for a particular purpose; the structure of an economic market.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French agencement.

parole.significato: Someone acting as the representative of an organisation, country etc.
parole.testo: From agent + general, after French agent général, Italian agente generale.

parole.significato: A person who secretly disrupts a group's activities from within the group, particularly by encouraging or committing il…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French agent provocateur (literally “provocative agent”).

parole.significato: An agente provocatrice.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Gallicism, derived from agente + provocateur + -euse, as the French female equivalent of agent provocateur is agente provocatrice.

parole.significato: A female agent provocateur; a woman who incites someone to do something, especially something incriminating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French agente provocatrice.

parole.significato: To make great; to enlarge; to increase.
parole.testo: From French agrandir. By surface analysis, ag- + grand + -ize.

parole.significato: The act of aggrandizing, or the state of being aggrandized or exalted in power, rank, honor, or wealth; exaltation; enl…
parole.testo: From French agrandissement, from agrandir; equivalent to aggrandize + -ment.

parole.significato: Stock exchange business; especially, stockjobbing, manipulation of securities prices.
parole.testo: From French agiotage, from agioter (“to practice stockjobbing”), from agio.

parole.significato: The act of agitating, or the state of being agitated; the state of being disrupted with violence, or with irregular act…
parole.testo: From French agitation, from Latin agitātiō (“movement, agitation”).

parole.significato: of the male bloodline; patrilineal
parole.testo: From French agnatique, from Latin agnātus (“paternal kinsman”). Equivalent to agnate + -ic.

parole.significato: Synonym of witch of Agnesi.
parole.testo: Derived from French agnésienne.

parole.significato: Characterized by agony.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French agonique (“possessing or filled with agony; agonous”), from agonie (“the moment just before death”) + -ique (suffix forming adjectives from nouns) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-kos (suffix forming adjectives denoting “the characteristic of, typical of, pertaining to”)).

parole.significato: To writhe with agony; to suffer violent anguish.
parole.testo: From French agoniser, from Late Latin agonizare, from Ancient Greek ἀγωνίζομαι (agōnízomai, “to fight, contend”). See agony. By surface analysis, agon + -ize.

parole.significato: A rodent of the genus Dasyprocta, similar in appearance to a guinea pig but having longer legs, mainly native to Centra…

parole.significato: A decorated clasp consisting of a hook which fastens onto a ring, similar to hook and eye, used in armor or in ordinary…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French agrafe (“hook”), from agrafer (“to hook”).

parole.significato: Synonym of sour cherry.
parole.testo: From French aigrette, griotte, formerly Old French agriote (“sour cherry”). Compare aigre (“sour”).

parole.significato: The science of utilizing plants, animals and soils for food, fuel, feed, fiber, etc.
parole.testo: From French agronomie, from agronome (“agriculturist”), from Ancient Greek ἀγρός (agrós, “field”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”). By surface analysis, agro- + -nomy.

parole.significato: Synonym of agrément (“formal approval given by a state government to a foreign diplomat”).
parole.testo: From French agréation.

parole.significato: In France, a civil servant who teaches as a professor.
parole.testo: From French agrégé.

parole.significato: Agreeable qualities or circumstances.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French agrémens.

parole.significato: Pleasant qualities, charms.
parole.testo: From French agrément. Doublet of agreement.

parole.significato: accustomed to war
parole.testo: From French aguerrir (“to make warlike”).

parole.significato: An assistant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aide ("aid; assistant", as in aide-de-camp (“field assistant”)). More at aid.

parole.significato: A military officer who serves as an adjutant to a higher-ranking officer, prince or other high political dignitary.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French aide de camp, from aide + de (“of”) + camp (“[military] camp”).

parole.significato: A memory aid; a reminder or memorandum, especially a book or document serving this purpose.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French aide-mémoire (literally “memory aid”).

parole.significato: A feather or plume, or feather-shaped item, used as an adornment or ornament, typically in hats or hair.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aigrette (“egret”). Doublet of egret.

parole.significato: A needle-shaped peak.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aiguille (“needle”).

parole.significato: Shaped like an aiguille.
parole.testo: From French aiguille (“needle”) + -esque.

parole.significato: The hinged part on the trailing edge of an airplane wing, used to control longitudinal turns.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aileron, diminutive of aile (“wing”), also refers to the extremities of a bird's wings used to control their flight. parole.significato: A small square piece of armour, normally made of boiled leather, worn on the shoulders of knights.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ailette, diminutive of aile (“wing”).

parole.significato: Likeable, amiable.
parole.testo: From French aimable. Doublet of amable.

parole.significato: A type of sauce made from garlic and olive oil, often with egg and lemon juice and similar to mayonnaise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aïoli, from Occitan alhòli, from alh (“garlic”) + òli (“oil”).

parole.significato: A piece of secular vocal music of a kind popular in France in the late Renaissance and early Baroque period, from about…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French air de cour.

parole.significato: Current popular opinion or trends of a very large group of people, a city or a country.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French air du temps (literally “air of the time”).

parole.significato: A technique for creating patterns of open areas in fabric by tying woven threads together.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ajouré (“perforated”).

parole.significato: A tube through which is water is discharged; an efflux tube.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ajutage, from ajoutage, from ajouter (“to add”), from Latin adjuxtare, from ad + juxta (“near to, nigh”). Compare adjutage, adjustage, adjust.

parole.significato: An indigenous Muscogee people of central Alabama.
parole.testo: Probably from French Alibamou or Alibamon, from Spanish Alibamo, from Alabama albaamo, the name for a member of a people native to the area.

parole.significato: The state of being winged.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French, from Latin alatus (“winged”).

parole.significato: A white crystalline resinous substance extracted from gutta-percha by the action of alcohol or ether.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French albane (in the form alban, respelt after the German Alban), from the Latin albus (“white”) + the French -ane (“-an”).

parole.significato: A member of the Albigenses.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French.

parole.significato: Any of a class of monomeric proteins that are soluble in water, and are coagulated by heat; they occur in egg white, mi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French albumine, from Latin albumen. Compare albumen.

parole.significato: grain alcohol, everclear
parole.testo: Borrowed from French alcool (“alcohol”). Doublet of alcohol and kohl.

parole.significato: A small recessed area set off from a larger room.
parole.testo: From French alcôve, from Spanish alcoba or Portuguese alcova, from Arabic القُبَّة (al-qubba, “vault, chamber with vaulted roof”). Doublet of qubba.

parole.significato: vinegar produced from fermented ale.
parole.testo: ale + French aigre (“sour”)

parole.significato: An early chemical apparatus, consisting of two retorts connected by a tube, used to purify substances by distillation.
parole.testo: From French alambic, from Medieval Latin alembīcus, from Arabic الإِنْبِيق (al-ʔinbīq), from Ancient Greek ἄμβιξ (ámbix, “cup, cap of a still”). Doublet of ambix and lambic.

parole.significato: Alençon lace.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Alençon.

parole.significato: Attentive; awake; on guard.
parole.testo: From French alerte (“alert”), from the phrase à l'erte (“on the watch”), from Italian all'erta (“to the height”), from erta (“lookout, tower”).

parole.significato: Newly hatched fish, especially salmon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French alevin.

parole.significato: A migrating North American fish, Alosa pseudoharengus.
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from aloof, the Narragansett name of a fish. See Winthrop on the culture of maize in America, “Phil Trans.” No. 142, p. 1065, and Baddam’s “Memoirs,” vol. ii. p. 131. Possibly from allowes (“a type of shad”), from French alose (“shad”), from Old French [Term?], from Late Latin alau

parole.significato: Any of various umbellifers, often specifically Smyrnium olusatrum or Heracleum maximum, the cow parsnip.
parole.testo: From French alisander, apparently named for Alexander the Great, for one or more species thought to be endemic to Macedonia.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an alexipharmac; also, acting as an alexipharmac by protecting against or warding off the ill effec…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French alexipharmaque (archaic), and from its etymon Late Latin alexipharmacus, from Ancient Greek ἀλεξιφάρμακος (alexiphármakos) (see etymology 1).

parole.significato: A pale white emetic powder formerly used in alchemy, consisting of a compound of trichloride and trioxide of antimony.
parole.testo: From French algaroth, from the name of the inventor, Algarotti.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to, algebra.
parole.testo: Partly from algebra + -ic and partly from French algébraïque.

parole.significato: A descendant of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the fourth caliph and the first Shi'ite Imam.
parole.testo: From Ali + -id, possibly under influence from French Alide.

parole.significato: A type of sighting device used for measuring angles.
parole.testo: From French alidade, from Spanish alidada, from Arabic العِضَادَة (al-ʕiḍāda), perhaps from عَضُد (ʕaḍud, “upper arm”).

parole.significato: The study or treatment of mental disorders; psychiatry.
parole.testo: From French aliénisme, from aliéné in the meaning of "insane".

parole.significato: An expert in mental illness, especially with reference to legal ramifications.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aliéniste, from aliéné (“insane”).

parole.significato: An arrangement of items in a line.
parole.testo: From French alignement, by surface analysis, align + -ment.

parole.significato: A dish traditionally made in the south of Auvergne from melted Tomme cheese blended into mashed potatoes, often with ga…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aligot.

parole.significato: A white grape variety and white wine from Burgundy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French.

parole.significato: Food.
parole.testo: From French aliment, from Latin alimentum (“food”).

parole.significato: Alimony.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French alimentation.

parole.significato: Contained in the whole an integral number of times, a factor or divisor.
parole.testo: From French aliquote, from Latin aliquot.

parole.significato: The madder of the Levant; wild madder (Rubia peregrina).
parole.testo: From French alizari (“madder root (commercial name)”), from Greek αλιζάρι (alizári, “madder”), from Ottoman Turkish آلاجهری (ala cehri).

parole.significato: A red substance, 1,2-dihydroxyanthraquinone, extracted from madder root and used as a dye.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French alizarine, corresponding to alizari + -in.

parole.significato: One of a class of caustic bases, such as soda, soda ash, caustic soda, potash, ammonia, and lithia, whose distinguishin…
parole.testo: From French alcali, from Medieval Latin alcali, ultimately from Arabic اَلْقِلْي (al-qily, “alkali, ashes (in reference to ashes of the saltwort)”), related to قَلَى (qalā, “to roast in a pan, fry”).

parole.significato: A herbaceous plant of the nightshade family (Alkekengi officinarum).
parole.testo: Through French alkékenge, Spanish alquequenje, from Arabic كَاكَنْج (kākanj).

parole.significato: Very attentive.
parole.testo: Calque of French tout yeux, tout oreilles; originally found only in translations of French works. Compare all eyes, all ears.

parole.significato: Having all the standard or expected toppings, dressings, condiments, seasonings, etc.
parole.testo: Calque of French toute garnie. From tout (“all”) + garnir (“garnished”), literally “all the garnishings”

parole.significato: The allantois.
parole.testo: From French allantoïde, and its source, Renaissance Latin allantoides, from Koine Greek ἀλλαντοειδής (allantoeidḗs, “sausage-shaped”), from Ancient Greek ἀλλᾶς (allâs, “sausage”). By surface analysis, allant- + -oid.

parole.significato: A tree-lined avenue, often particularly one that is part of a landscaped garden.
parole.testo: From French allée (“path”).

parole.significato: A popular instrumental dance form in Baroque music, and a standard element of a suite, generally the first or second mo…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French allemande (“German (dance)”).

parole.significato: Move in which two facing dancers take left hands or forearms, turn halfway around to the left, let go, and step forward.
parole.testo: From French allemande (“German”) + left. Contrary to some folk etymologies, this term does not come from the phrase a la main (“by the hand”).

parole.significato: Encouraging or calling attention to a physical performance, especially one involving an upwards lift or leap.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French allez-hop!, the cry of a circus acrobat about to leap. From allez (“go! let's go!”), 2nd-person plural or formal indicative form of aller, and hop, onomatopoeic.

parole.significato: A German, especially during the First World War.
parole.testo: From French Allemand (“a German”), with alteration after alley, man.

parole.significato: Speaking a non-native language.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French alloglote, equivalent to allo- + -glot.

parole.significato: A slip of paper attached to a negotiable instrument to hold endorsements should the document itself be unable to hold a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French allonge (“a lengthening”). Doublet of lunge.

parole.significato: A pseudonym, (particularly) another person's name used as a pseudonym by the author of a work.
parole.testo: From allo- (“other, different”) + -onym (“name”), probably via French allonyme. Compare German allonym, Allonym. First attested in 1725.

parole.significato: The act or art of alloying metals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aloyage.

parole.significato: A matchstick.
parole.testo: From French allumette. By surface analysis, al- + Latin lum- + -ette.

parole.significato: A woman who teases with a promise of sexual intercourse.
parole.testo: From French.

parole.significato: An alley in a formal garden or park, bordered by trees or bushes.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French allée. Doublet of alley.

parole.significato: A canoe made from tree bark, formerly used in Africa.
parole.testo: From French almadie (compare Spanish & Portuguese almadia), from Arabic مَعْدِيَة (maʕdiya, “ferry”).

parole.significato: Like or of the almond or almond tree.
parole.testo: From Middle English almandin; equivalent to almond + -ine. Sense 2 is modelled on French almondin.

parole.significato: A small circle on the celestial sphere, parallel to the horizon, that is used in astronomy and navigation to show altit…
parole.testo: From Middle English almicanteras, French almicantarat, almucantarat, from Medieval Latin almicantarath, almucantarath, from Arabic المقنطرات (almuqanṭarāt, “circles of celestial latitude”), from قَنْطَرَة (qanṭara, “arch”).

parole.significato: Any of certain shad:
parole.testo: Borrowed from French alose, from Latin alausa, from unattested Gaulish *alausa. Cognate with German Alse.

parole.significato: A South American howler monkey (of the genus Alouatta).
parole.testo: From French alouatte, alouate, from a Cariban language; compare Kari'na arawata, Trió arawata, Wayana alawata, Ye'kwana adawa'ta, Apalaí arauta, Akawaio arawta, Pemon arauta, Macushi arauta. Compare araguato.

parole.significato: A very high mountain. Specifically, one of the Alps, the highest chain of mountains in Europe.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, back-formation from alps pl, via French from Latin Alpes (“high mountains, especially those of Switzerland”). Compare Old Saxon elbon (“Alps”), Old High German Alpūn (“Alps”); Old High German alba (“alp, mountain”)).

parole.significato: Of or relating to an alphabet, especially the characters A to Z, both uppercase and lowercase.
parole.testo: Partly from French alphabétique and partly from its etymon Latin alphabēticus. By surface analysis, alphabet + -ic.

parole.significato: White barley sugar
parole.testo: From French alphénic, alfénic, from Spanish alfeñique, from Arabic فَانِيد (fānīd), from Persian پانید (pânid, “sugar candy”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or inhabiting the Alps, a mountain range in Western and Central Europe.
parole.testo: From French alpin, equivalent to Alps + -ine, see also alpine.

parole.significato: A lead ore found in Cornwall, England, and used to give a green glaze to pottery.
parole.testo: Equivalent to arquifoux, from French alquifoux, from the same Arabic word as alcohol.

parole.significato: Denotes a philosophy in opposition to or variation on the suffixed term.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French alter-.

parole.significato: The custom, among diplomats, of rotation in precedence among representatives of equal rank, sometimes determined by lot…
parole.testo: From French.

parole.significato: Highness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French altesse.

parole.significato: Regard for others, both natural and moral without regard for oneself; devotion to the interests of others; brotherly ki…
parole.testo: From French altruisme, which was coined in 1830 by Auguste Comte from autrui (“of or to others”) + -isme, from Old French, from Latin alteri, dative of alter (“other”) (whence also English alter). Apparently inspired by the French Latin legal phrase l'autrui, from le bien, le droit d'autrui (“the go

parole.significato: An aluminium sulfate mineral often found on the walls of mines and quarries.
parole.testo: From French alun (“alum”) + -gen.

parole.significato: mixed wool and silk or mohair and cotton fabric
parole.testo: Borrowed from French alépine.

parole.significato: A spongy, flammable substance prepared from bracket fungi, formerly used as a styptic and as tinder.
parole.testo: From French amadou (“tinder, lure, bait”), from amadouer (“to allure, caress”), perhaps from Icelandic mata (“to feed”), which is akin to English meat.

parole.significato: A cosmetic cream prepared from almonds.
parole.testo: From French amandine, feminine of amandin.

parole.significato: A lover, especially if illicit; a paramour.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amant, from Latin amantem, present participle of amō.

parole.significato: The act of amassing.
parole.testo: Probably from French amassement (“the act of amassing; the result of this action, objects that have been amassed or piled up”); equivalent to amass + -ment.

parole.significato: A lover of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amateur, from Latin amātor (“lover”), from amāre (“to love”).

parole.significato: A female amateur.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Gallicism, from amateur + -euse (the French equivalent is amatrice).

parole.significato: A female amateur.
parole.testo: From French amatrice, female equivalent of amateur.

parole.significato: A member of a particular ethnic group indigenous to northwest Africa.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amazigh, borrowed from a Berber language, from Proto-Berber *a-maziɣ. Compare Central Atlas Tamazight ⴰⵎⴰⵣⵉⵖ (amaziɣ).

parole.significato: A woman's riding habit.
parole.testo: From French amazone.

parole.significato: Evasive or ambiguous language; circumlocution.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English ambages, from French ambage as well as its etymon Latin ambāgēs (“a roundabout or circuitous path”).

parole.significato: The mission of an ambassador.
parole.testo: From French ambassade. Doublet of embassy.

parole.significato: Synonym of ambassadorship.
parole.testo: From French embassadrie.

parole.significato: A particular mood or atmosphere of an environment or surrounding influence.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French ambiance.

parole.significato: An entertainment at which a medley of dishes is set on at the same time; a buffet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ambigu.

parole.significato: The musk mallow plant (Abelmoschus moschatus).
parole.testo: From French ambrette.

parole.significato: An emergency vehicle designed for transporting seriously ill or injured people to a hospital.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ambulance, which replaced hôpital ambulant (“moving hospital”) via the suffix -ance, from Latin ambulō (“to walk; to go about”).

parole.significato: ambulanceman; paramedic
parole.testo: From French ambulancier.

parole.significato: An ambush; a trap laid for an enemy.
parole.testo: From French embuscade, from Italian imboscata from the past participle of imboscare (“to ambush”), from Vulgar Latin *imbosco (“I hide, ambush”) (see there for more), from Frankish *busk (“bush”), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“bush, heavy stick”). Compare ambush. More at bush.

parole.significato: To make better, or improve, something perceived to be in a negative condition.
parole.testo: Alteration of meliorate after French améliorer.

parole.significato: A monetary punishment; a fine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amende.

parole.significato: A public confession and apology.
parole.testo: From French [Term?].

parole.significato: An alteration or change for the better; correction of a fault or of faults; reformation of life by quitting vices.
parole.testo: From French amendement, from Late Latin amendamentum, equivalent to amend + -ment.

parole.significato: Compensation for an injury or loss; recompense; reparation.
parole.testo: From French amendes, plural of amende. Compare with amende.

parole.significato: Starch modified by heat so as to become a transparent mass, like horn. It is soluble in cold water.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amidine, from amido (“starch”), from Latin amylum.

parole.significato: Any of an extinct group of cephalopods of the subclass Ammonoidea; a fossil shell of such an animal.
parole.testo: From French ammonite, from Latin Ammōnis (cornū) (“horn of Ammon”), as it was called by Pliny the Elder in reference to coiling ram horns used to symbolise the Egyptian god Amun. Equivalent to Ammon + -ite.

parole.significato: That lives by a river.
parole.testo: From French amnicole, from Latin amnicola + -ous.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the amnion.
parole.testo: Likely borrowed from French amniotique, from Ancient Greek ἀμνίον (amníon, “vessel for collecting the blood from sacrifices”). Equivalent to amnion + -otic.

parole.significato: A hint about the future; an instance of foreshadowing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amorce.

parole.significato: Self-regard, self-esteem.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amour-propre.

parole.significato: A petty love affair.
parole.testo: From French amourette.

parole.significato: A lover; a romantic partner.
parole.testo: From the French. Doublet of amoroso and amorous.

parole.significato: The discipline within botany concerned with the taxonomy of cultivars in the grapevine genus, Vitis.
parole.testo: From French ampélographie, from ampelo- (“vine”) + -graphy.

parole.significato: Any of a large group of structurally similar hydrated double silicate minerals, containing various combinations of sodi…
parole.testo: From French amphibole, coined by René Just Haüy from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβολος (amphíbolos, “ambiguous”), in reference to its many forms.

parole.significato: Amphiboly.
parole.testo: From French amphibologie, from late Latin amphibologia, earlier amphibolia, from Ancient Greek ἀμφιβολία (amphibolía, “ambiguity”).

parole.significato: A nonsense verse; a rigmarole, which is meaningless despite possibly appearing to have meaning.
parole.testo: From French amphigouri, of uncertain derivation; perhaps from Ancient Greek ἀμφί (amphí) + γῦρος (gûros, “circle”) or -αγορία (-agoría, “speech”).

parole.significato: A type of winged serpent, with two bat-like wings and typically with no other limbs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amphiptère, from Ancient Greek ἀμφί (amphí, “amphi-”) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing”). Compare amphisbaena (French amphisbène).

parole.significato: A small hermetically sealed vial, often used to contain a sterile solution suitable for injection.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ampoule. Etymologically equivalent to amphora + -ule/-le. Doublet of ampulla.

parole.significato: To amputate (a limb).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amputer (“to amputate”) or its etymon Latin amputāre, amputō. Doublet of amputate, which was borrowed through the past participle amputātus.

parole.significato: A person who has had one or more limbs removed.
parole.testo: From French amputée, (past participle of amputer (“to amputate”)), from Latin amputatus, perfect passive participle of amputare (“to amputate”).

parole.significato: A bite-sized hors d'oeuvre or appetizer that is served before a meal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amuse-bouche.

parole.significato: A light field cannon, or stocked gun mounted on a swivel.
parole.testo: From French amusette.

parole.significato: An almond-shaped inclusion in igneous rock or lava.
parole.testo: From French amygdale, from Medieval Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē, “almond”). Doublet of almond, amygdala, and mandorla.

parole.significato: palindromic
parole.testo: From French anacyclique.

parole.significato: An anaerobic organism; one that does not require oxygen to sustain its metabolic processes.
parole.testo: From French anaérobie.

parole.significato: Without oxygen; especially of an environment or organism.
parole.testo: From French anaérobie, from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-, “not”) + ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + βίος (bíos, “life”) + -ic. By surface analysis, an- + aerobic.

parole.significato: anaerobes
parole.testo: From French anaérobie, plural anaérobies.

parole.significato: A creator or finder of anagrams.
parole.testo: From anagrammatism or anagrammatize + -ist, perhaps modelled on French anagrammatiste.

parole.significato: In which the value of a data item (such as time) is represented by a continuous(ly) variable physical quantity that can…
parole.testo: First attested in the early 19th century; from French analogue, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλογος (análogos, “proportionate”), from ἀνά (aná, “up to”) + λόγος (lógos, “ratio”). Equivalent to ana- (“functionally similar”) + -log.

parole.significato: Someone who analyzes.
parole.testo: From French analyste.

parole.significato: The application of calculus to classical mechanics.
parole.testo: Calque from French Mécanique analytique, a 1788–1789 book by Joseph-Louis Lagrange.

parole.significato: Extreme sensitivity to a substance such as a foreign protein or drug.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French anaphylaxie, coined by French physiologist and parapsychologist Charles Richet and French zoologist Paul Portier from the Ancient Greek ᾰ̓νᾰ- (ănă-, “(intensifier) thoroughly”) from ᾰ̓νᾰ́ (ănắ, “to, again, upon”) and φύλαξις (phúlaxis, “protection, watching, guarding”).

parole.significato: A form of spirometer.
parole.testo: From French anapnographe, coined by the device's inventors Léon Bergeon and M. Kastus in the 1860s, from Ancient Greek ἀναπνοή (anapnoḗ, “recovery of breath; respiration”) (from ἀναπνέω (anapnéō, “to draw breath”), from ἀνα- (ana-, “up”) + πνέω (pnéō, “to breathe”)) + French -graphe (see -graph).

parole.significato: One who believes in or advocates the absence of hierarchy and authority in most forms (compare anarchism), especially o…
parole.testo: From French anarchiste, from Ancient Greek ἀναρχία (anarkhía) from the roots ἀν- (an-, “without”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”), equivalent to anarchy + -ist.

parole.significato: A blue or brown mineral, a form of titanium dioxide, used as a pigment.
parole.testo: From French anatase, from Ancient Greek ἀνάτασις (anátasis, “extending, extension”), named for the length of its crystals.

parole.significato: native carbonate of soda; natron
parole.testo: From French anatron, an old variant of natron, from Ancient Greek νίτρον (nítron, “nitre”) by way of Spanish natrón and Arabic نَطْرُون (naṭrūn).

parole.significato: The initial zooid of a bryozoan colony
parole.testo: Scientific Latin, after French ancestrule, corresponding to ancestor + -ula.

parole.significato: A system of government that has been supplanted by another, particularly a state of feudalism with an absolute monarchy…
parole.testo: From French ancien régime (“former rule, former order”); the term first appeared in English print in 1794.

parole.significato: A spiced, heavily smoked Cajun pork sausage, often made from the entire gastrointestinal system of the pig.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French andouille, ultimately from Latin indūcō (“to lead in, to bring in”). Doublet of nduja.

parole.significato: A small andouille (type of sausage).
parole.testo: From French andouillette.

parole.significato: A person who is androgynous.
parole.testo: From French androgyne, from Latin androgynus.

parole.significato: A short account of a real incident or person, often humorous or interesting.
parole.testo: Late 17ᵗʰ c., from French anecdote, from Ancient Greek ἀνέκδοτος (anékdotos, “accounts unpublished”), from ἀν- (an-, “not, un-”) + ἔκδοτος (ékdotos, “published”), from ἐκδίδωμι (ekdídōmi, “I publish”), from ἐκ- (ek-, “out”) + δίδωμι (dídōmi, “I give”). Virtually identical cognates in other European

parole.significato: Building deep vertical burrows and surfacing to feed.
parole.testo: From French anécique, coined by Marcel B. Bouché, French earthworm biologist (1971), from Ancient Greek ἀνέχω (anékhō, “to rise up, emerge”).

parole.significato: Not using or containing fluid
parole.testo: From French anéroïde, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-) + νηρός (nērós, “wet, damp”).

parole.significato: The right of one belligerent (government) in a conflict to seize, use or destroy the property of another belligerent or…
parole.testo: From French angarie, from Late Latin angaria (“forced service”) from Ancient Greek ἀγγαρεία (angareía, “the office of a courier or messenger”), from ἄγγαρος (ángaros, “courier”), from Old Persian *𐎠𐎥𐎼𐎠 (*a-g-r-a /⁠*angarā⁠/, “missive, letter”), from Aramaic *𐡀𐡍‬𐡂𐡓‬𐡀 (*ʾn‬gr‬ʾ /⁠*ʾengarā⁠/), form of

parole.significato: Having the form of an angel; representing a specified person or object in such a manner.
parole.testo: From angel + -o- + -morphic. First attested in the 19th century, but popularised after the 1950s on the basis of French angélomorphique as used in the work of Jean Daniélou.

parole.significato: A French gold coin from the reign of Louis XI, bearing the image of Saint Michael
parole.testo: Borrowed from French angelot (“small angel”).

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Anjou, a former province of France (previously a county, duchy and the associated House of Anjo…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French angevin.

parole.significato: That is thought to stretch the blood vessels
parole.testo: Borrowed from French angioténique, from angio- + Ancient Greek τείνω (teínō, “to stretch”).

parole.significato: A person who loves or admires the country, culture or people of England.
parole.testo: From Anglo- + -phile, probably partly after French anglophile.

parole.significato: A plucked bowl lute with two necks and most often sixteen strings, played in the manner of a harp, and popular in Baroq…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French angélique. Doublet of angelic and angelique (“a plant of the genus Angelica”).

parole.significato: The inability to feel pleasure from activities usually found enjoyable, such as exercise, hobbies, music, sexual activi…
parole.testo: From French anhédonie (coined by Ribot, 1896), from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-) + ἡδονή (hēdonḗ, “pleasure”).

parole.significato: Breathing difficulty, shortness of breath.
parole.testo: From French anhélation, or directly from its etymon Latin anhēlātiō (“shortness of breath, gasping, panting, puffing”) (compare Late Latin anhēlātiō (“desire; eager pursuit”)), from anhēlātus (“exhaled”) + -iō (suffix forming abstract nouns from verbs). Anhēlātus is the perfect passive participle of

parole.significato: Sexual attractiveness; charisma derived from non-intellectual characteristics.
parole.testo: Calque of French magnétisme animal; 18th century. The pseudoscientific sense (sense 2) predates the sense that is now the more common one.

parole.significato: An artist who depicts animals.
parole.testo: Borrowing from French animalier.

parole.significato: The nature of an animal.
parole.testo: From French animalité or its etymon Late Latin animālitās. By surface analysis, animal + -ity.

parole.significato: One who promotes particular activity, especially one of a cultural or artistic nature.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French animateur.

parole.significato: A woman who is trained to teach skills and lead activities for her peers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French animatrice.

parole.significato: Violent hatred leading to active opposition; active enmity; energetic dislike.
parole.testo: From French animosité, from Latin animositas (“courage, spirit, vehemence”), from animosus, from animus (“courage, spirit, mind”); see animose, animate.

parole.significato: The resin of the courbaril (Hymenaea courbaril), used in varnishes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French animé (“animated”), supposedly from the insects entrapped in it. Doublet of animate.

parole.significato: A French alcoholic liqueur flavored with anise
parole.testo: Borrowed from French anisette, from anis + -ette.

parole.significato: A writer of annals; a chronicler; a historian.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French annaliste, equivalent to annal + -ist.

parole.significato: Any of various wormlike animals, of the phylum Annelida, having a segmented body; they include the earthworm and the le…
parole.testo: From French annélidé, coined by French naturalist Lamarck.

parole.significato: An addition, an extension.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French annexe, from Latin annexus. More at Etymology 2. See also an-.

parole.significato: A right to receive amounts of money regularly over a certain fixed period, in perpetuity, or, especially, over the rema…
parole.testo: From French annuité, from Medieval Latin annuitās, from Latin annuus (“annual”). Cf. annuality.

parole.significato: Something anomalous, especially an irregular word in a language.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French anomal.

parole.significato: Alienation or social instability caused by erosion of standards and values.
parole.testo: From French anomie, from Ancient Greek ἀνομία (anomía, “lawlessness”), from ἄνομος (ánomos, “lawless”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”). Popularized by French sociologist Émile Durkheim (1858–1917).

parole.significato: An anonymous person.
parole.testo: Coined or borrowed around 1812, from French anonyme, from Ancient Greek ἀνώνυμος (anṓnumos, “without name”).

parole.significato: Lacking olfactory organs, and so having no sense of smell; anosmic.
parole.testo: From French anosmatique (“anosmatic”), coined by French anthropologist, anatomist and physician Pierre Paul Broca (1824–1880) in Revue d’Anthropologie (2nd Series), volume II, page 398); analysable as an- + osmatic.

parole.significato: A room before, or forming an entrance to, another; a waiting room.
parole.testo: From ante- + room, as a calque of French antichambre or its model Italian anticamera.

parole.significato: The pollen-bearing part of the stamen of a flower.
parole.testo: From French anthère, from Ancient Greek ἀνθηρός (anthērós, “flowery, blooming”), from ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).

parole.significato: A tricyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (an acene containing three fused rings) obtained from coal tar; used in the manufactur…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French anthracène, coined by its co-discoverer Auguste Laurent in 1837, from Ancient Greek ἄνθραξ (ánthrax, “coal”) + -ene. By surface analysis, anthrac- + -ene.

parole.significato: The science of measuring the human body to ascertain the ranges and averages of dimensions of the human form, for vario…
parole.testo: 1839, as anthropo- (“human”) + -metry (“measurement”), from French anthropométrie, from anthropo- + -métrie, from Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “human”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”), influenced by Latin use.

parole.significato: Any substance that can destroy or inhibit the growth of bacteria and similar microorganisms, generally transported by t…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French antibiotique; by surface analysis, anti- + -biotic.

parole.significato: A substance that induces an immune response, usually foreign (nonself) but not always so.
parole.testo: From French antigène, from anti- + gène.

parole.significato: A political opponent of the Jacobins.
parole.testo: From anti- + Jacobin, after the model of earlier French antijacobin.

parole.significato: Characterized by antipathy.
parole.testo: From French antipathique. By surface analysis, anti- + -pathic.

parole.significato: A devotional chant; a piece of music sung responsively.
parole.testo: From French antiphone or Medieval Latin antiphōna, from Ancient Greek ἀντίφωνα (antíphōna, “responses, musical accords”), neuter plural substantive of ἀντίφωνος (antíphōnos, “concordant”) from ἀντί (antí, “in return”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”). Doublet of anthem.

parole.significato: A form of foot juggling where the juggler lies on his or her back, usually on a sort of chair.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French antipodisme.

parole.significato: One who practices antipodism; one who juggles using his or her feet lying down.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French antipodiste.

parole.significato: Having existed in ancient times, descended from antiquity; used especially in reference to Greece and Rome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French antique (“ancient, old”), from Latin antiquus (“former, earlier, ancient, old”), from ante (“before”); see ante-. Doublet of antic.

parole.significato: Synonym of antivenom, (now) particularly for snakebites containing venin.
parole.testo: From French antivenin (“antivenom”), from anti- + venin (“venom”), popularized by Albert Calmette & al.'s 1894 work creating serums to treat snakebites. Equivalent to anti- + venin (“venom; biochemical toxin found in certain snakes”). Doublet of antivenom and antivenene.

parole.significato: A word which has the opposite meaning of another word.
parole.testo: From French antonyme (1840s and 1850s), which was modeled on earlier synonyme and influenced by the etymons of Ancient Greek ἀντωνυμία (antōnumía, “pronoun”); credit for popularization of the French loanword's naturalization into English is given principally to Charles John Smith and his 1867 book S

parole.significato: A vassal or bodyguard of Merovingian kings.
parole.testo: From French, from Latin antrustio; compare Latin trustis.

parole.significato: A label for French wines named after their regions of origin certifying that origin.
parole.testo: From French AOC (“appellation d'origine contrôlée”, literally “controlled designation of origin”).

parole.significato: The Barbary sheep, Ammotragus lervia.
parole.testo: From French aoudad, from Tashelhit awdad.

parole.significato: A 40-day period between the 25th of July and the 2nd of September, characterized by high humidity and high temperatures…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Aoussou, from Tunisian Arabic أوسو (ʔawissu), from Sicilian agustu. Doublet of August.

parole.significato: A grant (especially by a sovereign) of land (or other source of revenue) as a birthright.
parole.testo: From French apanage, from Latin *appanare, adpanare (“to give bread”), from pānis (“bread”).

parole.significato: A complete domicile occupying only part of a building, especially one for rent; a flat.
parole.testo: From French appartement, from Italian appartamento, from Spanish apartamiento (“separation, seclusion”), equivalent to apart + -ment. See apart and -ment.

parole.significato: Lack of emotion or motivation; lack of interest or enthusiasm towards something; disinterest (in something).

parole.significato: In a vertical line, the cable having been sufficiently hove in to bring the ship over it.

parole.significato: A hard, polishable composition of fine sawdust mixed with blood or egg white, formerly used for making household items.…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bois durci (“hardened wood”).

parole.significato: panelling; wood trim
parole.testo: From French boiserie, from bois (“wood”).

parole.significato: The nose.
parole.testo: Circa 1820. Multiple potential origins: * From beak (“nose”) * From French beaucoup (“very much”) * Blend of beak (“nose”) + coconut * From boke (“point; thrust”) * From poke, as in poke one's nose into

parole.significato: An extremely bright meteor.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bolide, from Latin bolis, from Ancient Greek βολίς (bolís, “missile, arrow, javelin”). Doublet of bolis.

parole.significato: To attack using one or more bombs; to bombard.
parole.testo: From French bombe, from Italian bomba, from Latin bombus (“a booming sound”), from Ancient Greek βόμβος (bómbos, “booming, humming, buzzing”), imitative of the sound itself. Doublet of bombe. Compare boom.

parole.significato: To continuously attack something with bombs, artillery shells or other missiles or projectiles.

parole.significato: A brass instrument, the bass version of the tuba.
