parole.significato: A dessert made from ice cream frozen in a (generally spherical or hemispherical) mold.
parole.testo: From French bombe. Doublet of bomb.

parole.significato: Having a rounded or domed surface; convex.
parole.testo: From French bombé (“rounded, convex”) + -ous. First attested in 1878.

parole.significato: Featuring a protruding convex bulge.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bombé.

parole.significato: Used to wish someone enjoyment of the meal they are about to eat.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French bon appétit (literally “good appetite”).

parole.significato: A clever saying, phrase, or witticism; often, a witty riposte in dialogue.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bon mot (literally “good word”).

parole.significato: The height of fashion; fashionable society.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bon ton (literally “good tone”).

parole.significato: A man who enjoys luxurious things in life, especially good food and drink; a man about town.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bon vivant (literally “one who lives well, good ‘liver’ (living person)”), from bon (“good”) + vivant (“person who is living”), agent noun of vivre (“to live”).

parole.significato: Used to wish someone a good journey.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bon voyage (“bon voyage, (have a) good journey”), from bon (“good”) + voyage (“journey”).

parole.significato: goodwill; harmony
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French

parole.significato: A sweet, especially a small chocolate-covered candy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bonbon, reduplication of bon (“good”).

parole.significato: A demijohn or carboy.

parole.significato: A small decorative container (box, dish or pouch) used to hold sweets.
parole.testo: From French bonbonnière, from bonbon + -ière.

parole.significato: Any of several varieties of pear, such as the Williams pear.
parole.testo: French, literally "good Christian".

parole.significato: Any devotional ornament or church object, especially one having little artistic value; a religious knick-knack.

parole.significato: To sight along an object or set of objects to check whether they are level or in line.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bornoyer (“to look at with one eye, to sight”), from borgne (“one-eyed”).

parole.significato: A brim or shade projecting from a bonnet.
parole.testo: French [Term?]

parole.significato: An 18th- and 19th-century lady's portable writing desk with a raised back.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bonheur-du-jour (literally “daytime delight”), conjectured to be from its sudden rise in popularity.

parole.significato: A friendly, good-natured, pleasant manner; an affable and approachable disposition; friendliness.

parole.significato: To convert into―or make―good; to improve.
parole.testo: From French bonifier.

parole.significato: Good morning; hello.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bonjour (“good afternoon/good day/good morning”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Pierre Bonnard (1867–1947), French painter and artist, known for the stylized decorative qualities of…
parole.testo: From French Bonnard + -ian.

parole.significato: A French nursemaid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bonne.

parole.significato: A gourmet titbit.
parole.testo: Coined in English from French bonne bouche (“agreeable taste”, literally “good mouth(ful)”).

parole.significato: A hosier or maker of garments of similar material.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bonnetier.

parole.significato: Excellent; wonderful.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Gallicism, derived from French bon (“good”) + toujours (“always”); literally, “always good”.

parole.significato: A Buddhist monk or priest in East Asia.

parole.significato: Remarkable; wonderful; excellent; terrific.

parole.significato: A tail feather from an ostrich.

parole.significato: A mistake or error.

parole.significato: A mixture of copper sulfate and lime that is sprayed on plants as a fungicide.
parole.testo: Calque of French bouillie bordelaise, after Bordeaux in France, where it is used on vines.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the city of Bordeaux, Nouvelle-Aquitaine, France.
parole.testo: From French Bordelais/bordelais.

parole.significato: A French sauce made with dry red wine, bone marrow, butter, shallots, and demiglace, and traditionally served with beef.
parole.testo: Partial calque of French sauce bordelaise (literally “sauce of Bordeaux”).

parole.significato: A person from Bordeaux.

parole.significato: A detailed statement, especially one containing a detailed listing of documents or accounts.

parole.significato: A small grove or copse of trees, a thicket.

parole.significato: A black African-born enslaved person in a French (or sometimes other European) colony, especially Haiti (as opposed to…
parole.testo: From French bossale, from Spanish bozal (“wild, untamed, raw; born in Africa and recently enslaved in a colony”). Doublet of bozal and bosal.

parole.significato: Stale brioche, spread with almond cream and sliced almonds and then baked
parole.testo: From French bostock, of uncertain origin; Russian восто́к (vostók, “east”) has been suggested.

parole.significato: The chape, crampet or tag of a scabbard, or a representation thereof in heraldry.
parole.testo: From French bouterolle (or a Middle French predecessor thereof).

parole.significato: A small boot; a lady's boot.

parole.significato: A flowing wide-sleeved robe worn by men in much of West Africa, and to a lesser extent in North Africa.

parole.significato: A bush hammer.

parole.significato: A slit, notch or opening in the edge of a (physical or heraldic) shield, through which the bearer's lance or sword coul…

parole.significato: A social event at which people gather to butcher and make food from an animal, especially a pig.
parole.testo: From French boucherie (“butchershop”), and in American usage (for the event), from Cajun French boucherie.

parole.significato: A piece of tubing forming the pivot holes in watch and clock plates.

parole.significato: A small pastry case filled with a savoury mixture, served as an hors d'oeuvre.

parole.significato: A fabric knitted or woven of uneven yarn with a surface of loops and curls.

parole.significato: A woman's private sitting room, dressing room, or bedroom.

parole.significato: A type of fish soup or stew from Provence, France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bouillabaisse, from Occitan bolhabaissa, bouiabaisso, possibly a compound of bolhir (“to boil”) + abaissar (“to lower (the temperature)”).

parole.significato: Meat stewed with juice.

parole.significato: A mixture; a paste.

parole.significato: A rapidly-played variety of brelan or gleek (a card game resembling poker)

parole.significato: A French or French-style bakery.

parole.significato: A broad, well-paved and landscaped thoroughfare.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French boulevard, from Middle French boulevard, bollevart, boulevars, bolevers, bollewerc (“rampart”), from Middle High German bolewerc, bolwerc (modern German Bollwerk) or Middle Dutch bolwerk (“bulwark, bastion”). Doublet of bulwark; more at bole, work.

parole.significato: A man who frequents the boulevards; thus, a man about town or bon vivant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French boulevardier, from boulevard + -ier.

parole.significato: To change drastically; to overturn or turn upside down.

parole.significato: An arrangement or bunch of cut flowers; a nosegay.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French bouquet, from Old French bochet, from bois, from Early Medieval Latin boscus (“grove”), borrowed from Frankish *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz. Doublet of bosket.

parole.significato: A bundled mixture of herbs or dried herbs used as a flavouring for stews, soups, and sauces.

parole.significato: Alpine ibex (Capra ibex)

parole.significato: A slubby yarn or fabric made of silk waste.

parole.significato: A female member of the bourgeoisie; a wealthy woman

parole.significato: A class of citizens who were wealthier members of the third estate.

parole.significato: Beef bourguignon, or a similar dish replacing beef with some other ingredient.

parole.significato: A mixture of clay and moss or grass, used in construction as a simpler substitute for pierrotage.

parole.significato: A small shop, especially one that sells fashionable clothes, jewelry and the like.

parole.significato: A system of writing using abbreviations or special characters; shorthand.

parole.significato: A litter drawn by a horse, on which a person may be carried.

parole.significato: A sum formerly levied to pay the expense of coinage; seigniorage.

parole.significato: An item of armor (mail or plate) protecting the groin.

parole.significato: An upright standing or hanging metal bowl used for holding burning coal for a source of light or heat.

parole.significato: A biscuit or small cake traditionally eaten in the Christmas period in Alsace and Moselle, France.

parole.significato: A group of people organized for a common purpose.

parole.significato: A hair pomade, making the hair shine brilliantly.

parole.significato: A small brick, typically made of charcoal and used for fuel.

parole.significato: The shattering effect of the energy released in an explosion.

parole.significato: A type of structural sunshade with slats, holes, etc, to keep sunlight from striking fully on a building.

parole.significato: A net curtain (or lace curtain) for the lower half of a window.

parole.significato: The breaking up of anything, such as an ankylosis.

parole.significato: A legal principle usually expressed in Latin, traditionally used to concisely express a wider legal concept or rule.

parole.significato: A heavy brocade fabric with raised designs.

parole.significato: A small skewer or spit on which small pieces of meat, fish or vegetables are roasted or broiled.

parole.significato: A booklet of printed informational matter, like a pamphlet, often for promotional purposes.

parole.significato: Woven with a figure.

parole.significato: to fish for eels by disturbing the waters.

parole.testo: From French bronze (1511); from Italian bronzo (13th c.), of uncertain origin (q.v.). First use appears c. 1721 in the writings of Matthew Prior (for which, see citation below).

parole.significato: Synonym of adelphopoiesis (“a ceremony where males are unionised with one another”).
parole.testo: From brother + -ment; probably a calque of French affrèrement.

parole.significato: A stir; a fuss or uproar.

parole.significato: Also more fully as brubru shrike: a bird in the bushshrike family found in sub-Saharan Africa (Nilaus afer).

parole.significato: An alkaloid related to strychnine, found in several plant species, notably Strychnos nux-vomica (nux vomica).

parole.significato: An abnormal sound in the body heard on auscultation (for example, through using a stethoscope); a murmur.

parole.significato: Consisting of shades of brown, painted or executed with shades of brown, brown monochrome.

parole.significato: Brusqueness; abruptness, bluntness.

parole.significato: Careless introduction of high-rise buildings into traditional residential neighborhoods.

parole.significato: very dry, and not sweet

parole.significato: A form-fitting seat for one passenger in automobiles, aircraft, and other such modes of transport.

parole.significato: A motor car manufactured by this company.

parole.significato: A fruit tree trained on a low stem, the branches closely pruned.

parole.significato: An official who is part of a bureaucracy.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to bureaucracy or the actions of bureaucrats.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bureaucratique, from bureaucrate (“bureaucrat”) or bureaucratie (“bureaucracy”) + -ique (“-ic”), equivalent to bureaucrat + -ic or bureau + -cratic.

parole.significato: To bring under the control of a bureaucracy; to make bureaucratic.
parole.testo: From French bureaucratiser or bureaucrat, bureaucracy + -ize.

parole.significato: office automation
parole.testo: From French bureautique (“office automation”).

parole.significato: A glass tube with fine gradations and a stopcock at the bottom, used in laboratory procedures for accurate fluid dispen…

parole.significato: A chisel with a sharp point, used for engraving; a graver.

parole.significato: A person from Burkina Faso or of Burkinabe descent.
parole.testo: From French burkinabé, from Moore burkĩna (“honest”) + Fula -ɓe (plural ending for a people noun), coined by Burkinabe revolutionary Thomas Sankara.

parole.significato: A cold north wind that blows in the winter in south-central France.

parole.significato: A sauce made of clarified butter emulsified in egg yolks and white wine vinegar and flavored with herbs.

parole.significato: The tripod, pylon, or struts usually at the centre-section of a biplane or high-winged monoplane.

parole.testo: From French classifier. By surface analysis, class + -ify.

parole.significato: A climacteric (period in life, or critical point).
parole.testo: Compare French climactère.

parole.significato: A medical facility, such as a hospital, especially one for the treatment and diagnosis of outpatients.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French clinique, from Late Latin clīnicus (“a bed-ridden person, one baptized on a sick-bed, a physician”), from Ancient Greek κλῑνικός (klīnikós, “pertaining to a bed”), from κλῑ́νη (klī́nē, “bed”), from κλῑ́νω (klī́nō, “to lean, incline”).

parole.significato: Any healthcare practitioner working at the point of care, in clinical practice (e.g., physicians in clinical medicine,…

parole.significato: Glittery; gleaming; sparkling; dressed in, or overlaid with, tinsel finery.

The French term referred to a genre of drama in which the main characters wore cloaks and had swords. parole.significato: A beggar or tramp, especially in France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French clochard.

parole.significato: A glass covering, originally bell-shaped, for garden plants to prevent frost damage and promote early growth.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cloche (“bell”), from Medieval Latin clocca (“bell”). Doublet of cloak and clock.

parole.significato: A partition, dividing fillet or band.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cloison.

parole.significato: A decorative technique for metalwork, especially brass, whereby colored enamel is baked in partitions (cloisons) betwee…

parole.significato: A fabric with an embossed design
parole.testo: From French cloqué (“blistered”).

parole.significato: Having little difference or distance in place, position, or abstractly; see also close to.

parole.testo: Borrowed from French clôture (“closure”). Doublet of closure and clausure.

parole.significato: Something which holds the greatest attention; the chief point of interest.
parole.testo: From French clou. Doublet of clove.

parole.significato: Studded with nails (of a specified tincture).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cloué.

parole.significato: A nonprofit community center in Quebec that offers public health service; a community medical clinic.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French CLSC.

parole.significato: A luxury vacation beach resort.
parole.testo: From the French travel operator Club Med, short for Club Méditerranée, from club+Méditerranée (“Mediterranean”)

parole.significato: A defile or narrow gorge, especially one that cuts transversely through the rock of an otherwise continuous ridge.
parole.testo: In many cases, italicized as a borrowing of French cluse. In Early Modern texts, possibly a continuation of Middle English cluse, Old English clūse (“narrow pass”).

parole.significato: A defensive garment made of metal scales or interlinked metal rings.
parole.testo: Calque of French cotte de mailles.

parole.significato: Synonym of Cochin (“type of domestic hen”).

parole.significato: A rosette or knot of ribbon worn in a hat, especially as an office or party badge.
parole.testo: Partial calque of French cocarde.

parole.significato: A satire or lampoon.

parole.significato: A decal, a design that can be transferred to a surface.

parole.significato: pert; saucy
parole.testo: From French coquet (“coquettish”).

parole.significato: A tall palm tree, Lodoicea maldivica, found in the Seychelles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French coco de mer (“nut of the sea”), because it was originally known only from its nuts found floating in the water.

parole.significato: The silky case spun by the larvae of some insects in which they metamorphose, protecting the pupa within.
parole.testo: From French cocon, a diminutive of coque (“shell”).

parole.significato: small casserole (pot) for individual portions, similar to a Dutch oven
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cocotte.

parole.testo: From French codéine, from Ancient Greek κώδεια (kṓdeia, “capsule of the poppy, poppy head”) + -ine.

parole.significato: The study of codices (early handwritten books).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French codicologie (with ending adapted to -ology), from Latin cōdic- (stem of cōdex) + French -ologie.

parole.significato: The winning of the majority of tricks in the game of ombre.
parole.testo: French

parole.significato: Cooperating.
parole.testo: From French coefficient. Coined by French mathematician François Viète. Or influenced by (New) Latin coefficient-, which is the stem of coefficiens, which is a substantivation of the present active participle of coefficio, which comes from co- and efficio.

parole.significato: A Native American ethnic group of northern Idaho.
parole.testo: From French Cœur d’Alêne, literally “awl heart”. The people were allegedly so called because they had a reputation for shrewdness.

parole.significato: A heart-shaped preparation of cream cheese served with strawberries.
parole.testo: French [Term?]

parole.significato: A small box or chest; casket.
parole.testo: From French coffret.

parole.significato: Reasonable and convincing; based on evidence.
parole.testo: From French cogent, from Latin cōgēns, present active participle of cōgō (“drive together, compel”), from cō + agō (“drive”).

parole.significato: A brandy distilled from white wine in the region around Cognac in France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cognac, from Cognac, a city in France, from Medieval Latin Comniacum, from the name Cominius + Gallo-Roman suffix -acum, from Proto-Celtic *-ākom.

parole.significato: State of cohering, or of working together.
parole.testo: Attested from the late 17th century, borrowed from French cohésion, from Latin cohaesiō, cohaesiōnem.

parole.significato: A male hairdresser.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French coiffeur, from coiffer, from Old French coife, from Late Latin cofia (“cap”).

parole.significato: A female hairdresser
parole.testo: Borrowed from French coiffeuse.

parole.significato: Hairstyle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French coiffure.

parole.significato: To occupy exactly the same space.
parole.testo: From French coïncider, from Medieval Latin coincidere, from con- + incidere, from in- (“into, to”) + cadere (“to fall, fall down, drop”).

parole.significato: Of two or more objects: being in the same location.
parole.testo: The adjective is borrowed from French coïncident, from Medieval Latin coincidentem, an accusative singular form of Latin coincidēns (“coinciding”), the present active participle of coincidō (“to coincide”), from co- (variant of con- (prefix denoting a being or bringing together of several objects))

parole.significato: A dip on a mountain ridge between two peaks.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French col, from Latin collum (“neck”). Doublet of collum.

parole.significato: Having cold hands is an indication of warmheartedness; used as a rejoinder if one finds that another's hands are cold.
parole.testo: A calque translation of French froides mains, chaudes amours.

parole.significato: Severe pains that grip the abdomen or the disease that causes such pains (due to intestinal or bowel-related problems).

parole.significato: A blade, with a hexagonal or diamond-shaped cross section, once used to make small swords.

parole.significato: Any of a class of proteins, secreted by certain strains of bacteria, that kill but do not lyse other strains
parole.testo: From French colicine, from coli- + -cine, with ending formed by analogy from antibiotics like auréomycine, streptomycine, with second element from myc- + -ine.

parole.significato: The American quail or bobwhite, or related species.
parole.testo: From French colin, properly a diminutive of Colas, contracted from Nicolas (“Nicholas”).

parole.significato: The act of collaborating.
parole.testo: Originated 1855–60 from French collaboration, from Late Latin collaboratus + -ion, from Latin con- (“with”) + labōrō (“work”). Morphologically collaborate + -ion.

parole.significato: A person who works with others towards a common goal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French collaborateur.

parole.significato: A picture made by sticking other pictures onto a surface or juxtaposing them digitally in analogous manner.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French collage. Doublet of collagen, colloid, and protocol.

parole.significato: The main structural protein in the extracellular matrix of the connective tissues of many animals.
parole.testo: From French collagène, coined from Ancient Greek κόλλα (kólla, “glue”) and -γενής (-genḗs, “-forming”) (see -gen); it is the main substance that animal glues are derived from.

parole.significato: The transdisciplinary study of the collapse of industrial civilization, and what might succeed it.
parole.testo: From French collapsologie, collapse + -ology.

parole.significato: A small collar, especially as a kind of necklace of lace, fur etc. for women; a ruff

parole.significato: A female college student.

parole.significato: A small hill or mount.

parole.significato: The distribution or selling of publications via carriers, particularly devotional literature.

parole.testo: Borrowed from French colporteur, from comporteur by influence of col (“neck”) (re-analyzed as col + porteur (“porter”)), from verb comporter, from Latin comportō (English comport).

parole.significato: A battle, a fight (often one in which weapons are used).

parole.significato: A band along the top part of the shield, half the height of the chief.

parole.significato: An entertainer who performs in a humorous manner, especially by telling jokes.
parole.testo: From French comédien, from comédie + -ien, from Old French comedie, from Latin cōmoedia, from Ancient Greek κωμῳδία (kōmōidía). By surface analysis, comed(y) + -ian.

parole.significato: A female comedian.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French comédienne, equivalent to comedy + -ienne. Compare doyenne.

parole.significato: A confection, especially of preserved fruit.

parole.significato: A cultivated variety of pear with yellowish-green and reddish skin, and having juicy flesh.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French comice, ellipsis of [Doyenne du] Comice (“[Dean of the] Show”), from comice agricole (“agricultural show”).

parole.significato: A comic actor or singer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French comique.

parole.significato: A commanding officer, usually of a specific force or division.
parole.testo: From French commandant.

parole.significato: A territory under the control of a commander
parole.testo: From French commanderie, from Late Latin commendaria, from Latin commendare. In the Chinese administrative division sense, used as a translation of 府 (fǔ) and 郡 (jùn).

parole.significato: Neither good nor bad; so so; tolerable, passable, indifferent.

parole.significato: Proper; in keeping with etiquette or social standards.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French comme il faut (literally “as is necessary, as must be”).

parole.significato: Like me.

parole.significato: The first existence of anything; act or fact of commencing; the beginning.

parole.significato: The quality of being commensurable or commensurate
parole.testo: From French commensurabilité.

parole.significato: An advertisement in a common media format, usually radio or television.
parole.testo: From French commercial (“of, or pertaining to commerce”), from Late Latin commercialis, from Latin commercium. By surface analysis, commerce + -ial.

parole.significato: An assistant to a chef.

parole.significato: The judge of a bicycle race.

parole.significato: A low chest of drawers on short legs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French commode (literally “convenient”). Doublet of comodo.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a community or a commune.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French communal, from Late Latin commūnālis, from Latin commūnis. Doublet of cominal.

parole.significato: A person who lives in a commune.
parole.testo: From French communard.

parole.significato: An official report or statement, such as a government press release or the report of a conference.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French communiqué (“something communicated”), past participle of communiquer (“to communicate”).

parole.testo: A borrowing from French communisme, which was formed from commun (“common”) (from Latin commūnis) and the suffix -isme (“-ism”). By surface analysis, commune + -ism.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, supporting, or advocating communism.
parole.testo: From French communiste, from commun (“common, communal”) + -iste (“-ist”). By surface analysis, commune + -ist.

parole.significato: Substitution of one thing for another; interchange.
parole.testo: From French commutation, from Latin commūtātiōnem, accusative singular of commūtātiō.

parole.significato: Such that the order in which the operands are taken does not affect their image under the operation.
parole.testo: From French commuter (“to substitute or switch”) + -ative (“tending to”). See commute.

parole.significato: Somebody from one's own country.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French compatriote, itself borrowed from Latin compatriota. By surface analysis, com- + patriot. Displaced native Old English ġelanda.

parole.significato: Able to be compensated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French compensable; by surface analysis, compens(ate) + -able.

parole.significato: Intended to recompense someone who has experienced loss, suffering, or injury.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French compensatoire. By surface analysis, compensate + -ory.

parole.significato: To compensate.
parole.testo: From French compenser. See compensate.

parole.significato: A master of ceremonies, especially for a television, variety, or quiz show.
parole.testo: A borrowing of French compère (“partner, accomplice”), from Old French comper, from Late Latin compater (“godfather”), from Latin com- (“with”) + pater (“father”). Doublet of compeer, compadre, and goombah.

parole.significato: The action of competing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French compétition, from Late Latin competītiō, competītiōnem, from Latin competō, from con- + petō. By surface analysis, compete + -ition.

parole.significato: To piss all over (something); to wet with urine.
parole.testo: From French compisser.

parole.significato: The quality of being complaisant, amiable or agreeable.
parole.testo: From French. See complaisant. By surface analysis, com- + plaisance.

parole.significato: Compliant.
parole.testo: From French complaisant (“willing to please”), from complaire, from Latin complacēre (“please well”), from com- (“with”) + placeō (“please”).

parole.significato: Made up of multiple parts; composite; not simple.
parole.testo: From French complexe, from Latin complexus, past participle of complector (“to entwine, encircle, compass, infold”), from com- (“together”) and plectō (“to weave, braid”). May be analyzed as com- + -plex. See complect. Doublet of complexus.

parole.significato: The state of being complicit; involvement as a partner or accomplice, especially in a crime or other wrongdoing.
parole.testo: From French complicité, from Middle French, from Old French complice (“accomplice”), from Late Latin complic-, stem of complex (“partner, confederate”), from Latin complicō (“fold together”).

parole.significato: Conspiracy theories.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French complotisme.

parole.significato: A conspiracy theorist.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French complotiste.

parole.significato: Divided into a line of squares of alternating tinctures.
parole.testo: From French componé, from Old French compondre, from Latin compōnere (“put together, arrange, compile”). Cognate with English compose, compound.

parole.significato: A person who sets type; a typesetter.
parole.testo: From French compositeur, from Latin compositor.

parole.significato: A dessert made of fruit cooked in sugary syrup.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French compote. Doublet of composite, compost, and kompot.

parole.significato: A dish for holding fruit or compotes.
parole.testo: French

parole.significato: A report by an officer or agent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French compte rendu.

parole.significato: Uncontrolled or reactive and irresistible.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French compulsif, formed from Latin compulsus, past participle of compellere (“to compel”), from com- (“together”) + pellere (“to drive”).

parole.significato: To reckon, calculate.
parole.testo: 17th century. Borrowed from French computer, from Latin computō (“calculate, compute”). Doublet of count.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a count.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French comtal, from oblique stem of Latin comes, comitis (“count, earl, companion, comrade”) + -al. Doublet of comital.

parole.significato: A French count.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French comte. Doublet of comes, conte, and count.

parole.significato: A French countess.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French comtesse.

parole.significato: Roughly chopped or diced; (in particular, of a tomato) diced after the seeds/core and skin have been removed.
parole.testo: From concassé, concasse or its etymon, French concasser (“crush, grind”), + the English past tense -ed.

parole.significato: Food (fish, fruit, vegetables, etc) that has been coarsely chopped or cut into large pieces.
parole.testo: From French concassé (“diced; ground; reduced to small(er) pieces”).

parole.significato: To plan together; to settle or adjust by conference, agreement, or consultation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French concert, from Italian concerto, deverbal from concertare. Doublet of concerto.

parole.significato: One who holds a concession or a right granted (for example, by the government) to conduct a certain business.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French concessionnaire.

parole.significato: Synonym of concher (“machine used to refine the flavour and texture of chocolate”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French conche.

parole.significato: An employee of a hotel who attends to the requirements and wishes of guests.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French concierge (“caretaker; doorkeeper; lodge-keeper of a château”), from Old French conciarge, consierge, consirge, from Medieval Latin consergius; further etymology uncertain, probably from Vulgar Latin *cōnservius, from Latin cōnservus (“fellow servant; fellow slave”), from con- (

parole.significato: Synonym of conciseness (“brevity or terseness”).

parole.significato: An expression of praise.

parole.significato: To bind up; to pack, or bundle up into a pack.

parole.significato: An artwork having a motif of wrapping or concealment.

parole.significato: A pier, a wharf.

parole.significato: Embarrassment; confusion, uncertainty.

parole.significato: An abundance or overabundance of something; too much of a good thing.

parole.significato: An embassy.

parole.significato: To bring (something) into a state of confusion or uproar; to complicate, to confuse, to jumble.

parole.significato: One who has departed their native land, often as a refugee.

parole.significato: a migrant, one who moves from one region to another.

parole.significato: Something which softens or lubricates the skin; moisturizer.

parole.significato: The tail assembly of an aircraft.

parole.significato: An installation that houses a military weapon.

parole.significato: The state of being an employee; employment.

parole.significato: A person who provides labor to a company or another person.

parole.significato: Dated spelling of employee.

parole.significato: A female employee.

parole.significato: Animated cordiality; friendliness, enthusiasm.

parole.significato: To emulate.

parole.significato: A stable suspension of small droplets of one liquid in another with which it is immiscible.

parole.significato: In intaglio; by sinking or hollowing out the design.

parole.significato: A gripping listlessness or melancholia caused by boredom; depression.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French ennui, from Old French enui (“annoyance”), from enuier (modern French ennuyer), from Late Latin inodiō, from Latin in odiō (“hated”). Doublet of annoy.

parole.significato: Affected with ennui; bored.

parole.significato: A woman affected with ennui.

parole.significato: To say or pronounce; to enunciate.

parole.significato: A group of separate things that contribute to a coordinated whole.

parole.significato: The process of producing silage by the fermentation of green fodder.

parole.significato: To preserve (forage) in a silo.

parole.significato: An informal alliance or friendly understanding between two states.

parole.testo: Likely a "relatinized" calque of French éventrer, from Latin ē(x)- (“out”) + Latin venter (“belly”, ventr- in compounds) + -ate (verb-forming suffix); this should have given *eventrate, compare its obsolete doublet eventrate and orienate.

parole.significato: To open the bowels of, disembowel.
parole.testo: Back-formation from eventration on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix) or directly derived from French éventrer. Compare eventerate.

parole.significato: A tumour containing a large portion of the abdominal viscera, caused by relaxation of the walls of the abdomen.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French éventration, from éventrer (“to disembowel”).

parole.significato: A possible event; something that may happen.
parole.testo: Calque of French éventualité, eventual + -ity

parole.significato: To sap the strength of.
parole.testo: From French évertuer.

parole.significato: The scraping-away of diseased tissue.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French évidement, see évider.

parole.significato: To call out; to draw out or bring forth.
parole.testo: From French évoquer, from Latin ēvocō (“to call out, summon”), from ex (“out”) and vocō (“call”). Akin to voice.

parole.significato: Attention to small details; accuracy.
parole.testo: From French exactitude, from exact, from Latin exactus, perfect passive participle of exigō (“demand, claim as due" or "measure by a standard, weigh, test”), from ex (“out”) + agō (“drive”).

parole.significato: To cut out; to remove.
parole.testo: From French exciser, from Latin excisus, past participle of excīdō (“cut out”), from ex (“out of, from”) + caedō (“cut”).

parole.significato: Synonym of excuse me.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French excusez-moi.

parole.significato: A person who executes a dance or piece of music; a performer.
parole.testo: From French exécutant. By surface analysis, execute + -ant.

parole.significato: A space beneath the main design on a coin or medal for the insertion of the date or other minor inscription.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French exergue.

parole.significato: exigent; demanding
parole.testo: From French exigeant. Doublet of exigent.

parole.significato: A demanding woman.
parole.testo: From French exigeante, feminine form.

parole.significato: Exigency.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French exigence.

parole.significato: to be; have existence; have being or reality
parole.testo: From French exister, from Latin existō, exsistō (“I am, I exist, appear, arise”), from ex (“out”) + sistere (“to set, place”) (related to stare (“to stand, to be stood”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *stísteh₂ti, from the root *steh₂- (“stand”); see stand. Compare assist, consist, desist, in

parole.significato: A person who adheres to the philosophy of existentialism.
parole.testo: From French existentialiste, equivalent to existential + -ist.

parole.significato: A French antiship missile.
parole.testo: From French Exocet, from exocet (“flying fish”), from New Latin exocoetus, from Ancient Greek ἐξώκοιτος (exṓkoitos, “a kind of fish resting on shore”), from ἔξω (éxō, “out, outside, without”) + κοῖτος (koîtos, “place of rest, bed”).

parole.significato: An officer of the King's Body Guard of the Yeomen of the Guard.
parole.testo: Apparently an attempt to express the pronunciation of French exempt.

parole.significato: Running or draining to the sea.
parole.testo: From French exorrhéisme (“drainage reaching the sea”). Compare exo- from Ancient Greek ἔξω (éxō, “outer; external”), and -ic (“pertaining to”).

parole.significato: That releases energy in the form of heat.
parole.testo: From French exothermique, from exo- (“outside”) + thermique (“of heat”), both ultimately from Ancient Greek. By surface analysis, exo- + -thermic.

parole.significato: Voluntary migration from one's native land to another.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French expatriation, or from expatriate + -ion.

parole.significato: Great skill or knowledge in a particular field or hobby.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French expertise. Compare gourmandise.

parole.significato: Very specific, clear, or detailed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French explicite, from Latin explicitus (“disentangled, easy”), variant of explicātus.

parole.significato: The act of utilizing something; industry.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French exploitation, from exploiter (“exploit”), from Latin explicō (“unfold, deploy”). By surface analysis, exploit + -ation.

parole.significato: To make use of (something).
parole.testo: Irregular adoption of French exploiter.

parole.significato: A violent release of energy (sometimes mechanical, nuclear, or chemical); an act or instance of exploding.
parole.testo: From French explosion, from Latin explōsiōnis, genitive form of explōsio, from explōdo (“to drive out by clapping”), from ex- and plōdo (“to clap or strike”). For more information see explode.

parole.significato: The act of exposing somebody or something; a shameful showing up.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French exposé.

parole.significato: Moving or operating quickly, as a train not making local stops.
parole.testo: From French exprès, from Latin expressus, past participle of exprimere (see Etymology 2, below).

parole.significato: A movement in the arts in which the artist did not depict objective reality, but rather a subjective expression of thei…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French expressionnisme, equivalent to expression + -ism.

parole.significato: A collective art game in which several collaborating artists assemble a sentence or image, usually by following a promp…
parole.testo: Calque of French cadavre exquis. parole.significato: To exterminate (someone or something); to destroy.
parole.testo: From French exterminer, from Latin extermino.

parole.significato: A day school.
parole.testo: From French externat.

parole.significato: In the works of Jacques Lacan: the quality of being extimate.
parole.testo: Calque of French extimité + English -cy (suffix forming nouns of condition, quality, or state). parole.significato: In the works of Jacques Lacan: simultaneously external and intimate.
parole.testo: From extimacy + -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Extimacy is a calque of French extimité (coined by the French psychiatrist and psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan (1901–1981) in 1959–1960), probably from a blend of French externe (“external”) + intimité (“closeness, intimacy”). The English word can be anal

parole.significato: A small hollow conical instrument for putting out a candle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French extincteur.

parole.significato: To extirpate (something).
parole.testo: From French extirper, from Latin exstirpō (“to uproot”), from ex- (“out of”) + stirps (“the lower part of the trunk of a tree, including the roots; the stem, stalk”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of extirpate.

parole.significato: A formal process by which a criminal suspect held by one government or jurisdiction is handed over to another governmen…
parole.testo: From French extradition, itself from Latin ex- + traditio.

parole.significato: The outer or upper curve of an arch.
parole.testo: From French extradossé (“outer curve”) from Latin extra (“outside”) + dos (“back”) (from Latin dorsum).

parole.significato: Synonym of parfum (“solvent containing around 15% to 40% aromatic compounds”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French extrait.

parole.significato: Extraordinary, remarkable, outstanding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French extraordinaire. Doublet of extraordinary.

parole.significato: Excessive or superfluous expenditure of money.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French extravagance, from Medieval Latin extra + vagor (“to wander”).

parole.significato: External; separable from the thing itself; inessential.
parole.testo: From French extrinsèque, from Latin extrinsecus (“from without, without, on the outside”), from *extrim, an assumed adverbial form of exter (“outer, outward”) + secus (“by, on the side”).

parole.significato: The quality of being exuberant; cheerful or vigorous enthusiasm; liveliness.
parole.testo: From French exubérance, from Latin exuberantia (“superabundance”), from exuberare (“to grow thickly, to abound”); from ex- (“out”) + uber (“udder”), which would have originally referred to a cow or she-goat which was making so much milk that it naturally dripped or sprayed from the udder.

parole.significato: An edifice or building.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fabrique, from Latin fabrica (“a workshop, art, trade, product of art, structure, fabric”), from faber (“artisan, workman”). Doublet of fabrica, borrowed from Latin, and forge, borrowed from Old French.

parole.significato: One who fabricates; a manufacturer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French.

parole.significato: A person who writes, tells, or extensively studies fables.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fabuliste. By surface analysis, fable + -ist, or, by surface analysis, fabula + -ist. Compare fabular.

parole.significato: A kind of counterpoint with a drone bass.
parole.testo: From French faux bourdon. See false, and burden (“a verse”).

parole.significato: The face of a building, especially the front view or elevation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French façade, from Italian facciata, a derivation of faccia (“front”), from Latin faciēs (“face”); compare face.

parole.significato: Any one of the flat surfaces cut into a gem.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French facette.

parole.significato: Treating serious issues with (often deliberately) inappropriate humour; flippant.
parole.testo: From French facétieux, from Latin facētia (“jest, wit, humor”), from facētus (“witty, jocose, facetious”).

parole.significato: To make easy or easier.
parole.testo: Anglicisation of French faciliter (“facilitate”) through -ate (verb-forming suffix), ultimately from Latin facilis.

parole.significato: The act or manner of making or doing anything, especially of a literary, musical, or pictorial production.
parole.testo: From French facture (“a making, invoice”), from Latin factura (“a making”). Doublet of feature. See fact.

parole.significato: Of or relating to faculty, especially to mental faculty.
parole.testo: From French facultatif. By surface analysis, faculty + -ative.

parole.significato: A vapid or meaningless remark; a commonplace; nonsense.
parole.testo: From French fadaise.

parole.significato: A type of tin-glazed earthenware ceramic, used domestically for tableware and in architecture as a decorative material.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French faïence, named after the city of Faenza, Italy, where it was made in the 16th century.

parole.significato: A genre of ballet that developed in the 19th century, featuring fantasy characters and often employing technical effect…
parole.testo: Calque of French ballet-féerie.

parole.significato: A genre of opera, often with magical elements.
parole.testo: Calque of French opéra-féerie.

parole.significato: A folktale or literary story featuring fairies or similar fantasy characters.
parole.testo: Calque of French conte de fées, coined by French writer Madame d'Aulnoy in the late 17th century.

parole.significato: A Cajun dance party.
parole.testo: Originated before World War II, from French [Term?]. Often said to be a mother's command to her infants to go to sleep; but perhaps related to dos a dos.

parole.significato: Something which has already happened, before those affected had the chance to raise objections or queries; especially,…

parole.significato: In roulette, the call made by the croupier when gamblers can place their bets.

parole.significato: A furbelow.

parole.significato: A horse's movement of throwing itself on its haunches two or three times, bending in very quick curvets.
parole.testo: From French falcade, ultimately from Latin falx, falcis (“a sickle or scythe”). By surface analysis, Latin falc- + -ade.

parole.significato: The sport of hunting by using trained birds of prey, especially falcons and hawks.
parole.testo: From French fauconnerie.

parole.significato: A piece of ribbon worn as a streamer.

parole.significato: To alter so as to make false; especially when done with intent to deceive.
parole.testo: From French falsifier, from Late Latin falsificāre (“make false, corrupt, counterfeit, falsify”), from Latin falsificus, from falsus (“false”), corresponding to false + -ify.

parole.significato: A type of beret, decorated with ribbons and badges, traditionally worn by some French students.
parole.testo: From French faluche.

parole.significato: A kind of sweet red apple originating in Canada.
parole.testo: From French fameuse, feminine (after pomme f (“apple”)) of fameux (“famous”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a human family.

parole.significato: A type of Chinese porcelain, primarily from the 18th and 19th centuries, decorated in (chiefly pink) overglaze enamels.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French famille rose. Compare famille verte.

parole.significato: A lighthouse
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fanal, from Ancient Greek φανάριον (phanárion).

parole.significato: A French cake made with puff pastry and a cream filling.

parole.significato: Empty, self-assertive boasting; an instance of such behaviour.
parole.testo: From French fanfaronnade (“bragging, boasting”); other senses influenced by fanfare.

parole.significato: A small flag used for marking positions, especially by soldiers and surveyors.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fanion.

parole.significato: A female science fiction fan.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Gallicism, derived from fan + French -e (feminine suffix).

parole.significato: A genre of literature and film that is characterized by the intrusion of the supernatural into the realistic framework…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French fantastique. Doublet of fantastic.

parole.significato: A traditional cake or dessert from the Brittany region in France, with a base similar in composition to a clafoutis bat…
parole.testo: From French far breton.

parole.significato: The most radical part of the political left wing.

parole.significato: The most right-wing or conservative part of a political faction or grouping.
parole.testo: From far + right, after French extrême droite.

parole.significato: Treatment with faradic electricity; faradization.
parole.testo: From French faradisme, from Farad(ay) + -ism.

parole.significato: A lively chain dance in 6/8 time, of Provençal origin.

parole.significato: A person who writes farces, or who performs in them.

parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French

parole.significato: Scrap material, used to fill space and/or prevent goods from moving about during transport
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fardage. See fardel.

parole.significato: A member of a privileged association in France, before the French Revolution, who collected duties on behalf of the kin…

parole.significato: Sullen or recalcitrant.

parole.significato: The binding up of a limb, etc., with bandages.

parole.significato: To worry; to bother, annoy.
parole.testo: From early modern French fascher (now fâcher), from Latin fastus (“disdain”).

parole.significato: A fop or dandy.

parole.significato: The state proceeding from destiny; invincible necessity, superior to, and independent of, free and rational control.

parole.significato: Susceptible to fatigue; easily able to become physically exhausted.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fatigable, from Latin fatīgābilis, from Latin fatīgō.

parole.significato: To tire or make weary by physical or mental exertion.
parole.testo: From French fatiguer, from Latin fatīgāre (“to weary, tire, vex, harass”).

parole.significato: An outlying part of a city or town, beyond the walls; a suburb, especially of Paris, New Orleans, Montreal, or Quebec C…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French faubourg.

parole.significato: An early European weapon consisting of a curved blade on a long pole.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fauchard. See also -ard.

parole.significato: A zeolite mineral consisting of sodalite cages connected through hexagonal prisms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French faujasite, named after Barthélemy Faujas de Saint-Fond (1741–1819), French geologist, by Alexis Damour, French mineralogist in 1842.

parole.significato: A second rampart, exterior and parallel to the main rampart, and considerably below its level.
parole.testo: From French fausse-braie.

parole.significato: For want of something better; for lack of an alternative; as a makeshift.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French faute de mieux.

parole.significato: An armchair.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French fauteuil, from Germanic. Cognate with Old English fealdestōl (“folding-chair”). Doublet of faldistory, faldstool, and foldstool.

parole.significato: Any of a number of small songbird, such as nightingales or warblers.

parole.significato: An artistic movement of the first decade of the 20th century which emphasized spontaneity and the use of extremely brig…
parole.testo: From French fauvisme, attributed to French art critic Louis Vauxcelles.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to fauvism.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fauviste.

parole.significato: Fake or artificial.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French faux. Doublet of false.

parole.significato: A false friend; one of a pair of words in different languages or dialects that look similar and may be related but that…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French faux-ami, from faux (“false”) + ami (“friend”).

parole.significato: The artistic imitation of wood or wood grains in various media.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French faux bois (“false wood”).

parole.significato: The faux frais of production.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French faux frais.

parole.significato: An embarrassing or tactless blunder.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French faux pas (“faux pas, blunder; misstep, false step”).

parole.significato: A favorite.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French favori. Doublet of favourite.

parole.significato: A fabric having a pattern woven into it, especially one in which the pattern stands out from a sheer background.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French façonné (“fashioned”).

parole.significato: Synonym of antipyretic (“a fever-reducing medication”).
parole.testo: From French fébrifuge, from Latin febrifugus. Doublet of feverfew. Source of -fuge.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being feculent.
parole.testo: From French féculence, from Latin faeculentia. Doublet of feculency.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a league or treaty; derived from an agreement or covenant between parties, especially between nations.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fédéral, from Latin foedus + French -al.

parole.significato: A system of national government in which power is divided between a central authority and a number of regions with deli…
parole.testo: From French fédéralisme. By surface analysis, federal + -ism.

parole.significato: An act of joining together into a single political entity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fédération, from Late Latin foederatio, from Latin foederare; equivalent to federate + -ion.

parole.significato: A movement made to confuse an opponent; a dummy.
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from French feinte (“dummy, feint”), from feindre (“to fake, feign”), from Old French feindre, faindre, from Latin fingere, the present active infinitive of fingō (“to alter the truth to deceive, dissemble, feign, pretend; to fashion, form, shape”). The verb is derived from the

parole.significato: Of an attack or offensive movement: directed toward a different part from the intended strike.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French feint, the past participle of feindre (“to fake, feign”): see etymology 1.

parole.significato: A member of the Front de Libération du Québec, a militant Quebec separatist group founded in the 1960s.
parole.testo: From French felquiste.

parole.significato: A social theory or political movement which argues that legal and social restrictions on women must be removed in order…
parole.testo: From French féminisme circa 1837, ultimately from Latin fēminīnus, from fēmina (“woman”). In the original sense of “women's movement or advocacy”, the French word was probably directly derived from fēmina, as if from Neo-Latin feminismus. parole.significato: An attractive and seductive but ultimately dangerous woman.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French femme fatale (literally “deadly woman”).

parole.significato: A misunderstood or unappreciated woman.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French femme incomprise (literally “misunderstood woman”).

parole.significato: A protected tail rotor of a helicopter, operating like a ducted fan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fenestron (“small window”), ultimately from Latin fenestra (“window”).

parole.significato: A small fox of the species Vulpes zerda, found in the Sahara (excluding the coast) and having distinctive oversized ear…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fennec, from Arabic فَنَك (fanak).

parole.significato: A French variety of apple with a taste like fennel.
parole.testo: From French fenouillet.

parole.significato: Bothrops lanceolatus or other lancehead snakes of genus Bothrops.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fer de lance (“spearhead”).

parole.significato: Synonym of millrind.
parole.testo: French fer-de-moline

parole.significato: The mechanism for closing the breech of a breech-loading firearm, in artillery consisting principally of the breechbloc…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fermeture.

parole.significato: Prepared in a simple rustic style.
parole.testo: From French (à la) fermière, literally, in the manner of a farmer's wife.

parole.significato: A kind of cloth made of silk and wool.
parole.testo: French; compare Old French ferrant (“iron-gray”), from Latin ferrum (“iron”).

parole.significato: Suffering from a deficiency of iron
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ferriprive.

parole.significato: A headband that encircles the wearer's forehead, usually with a small jewel suspended in the centre.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French ferronnière

parole.significato: The act or process of rendering fertile.

parole.significato: To make (the soil) more fertile by adding nutrients to it.
parole.testo: From French fertiliser; equivalent to fertile + -ize.

parole.significato: Having the atmosphere, decoration, or attitude of a festival, holiday, or celebration.
parole.testo: From French festif, from Latin festivus (“pertaining to a feast, gay, lively, joyous”). Equivalent to feast + -ive.

parole.significato: An ornament such as a garland or chain which hangs loosely from two tacked spots.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French feston.

parole.significato: A festival open to the public, the proceeds from which are often given to charity.
parole.testo: * The noun derives from French fête. Doublet of feast, fiesta, and fest. * The verb derives from French fêter.

parole.significato: Something which is believed to possess, contain, or cause spiritual or magical powers; an amulet or a talisman.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fétiche, from Portuguese feitiço, from Latin factīcius (“artificial”). Doublet of factitious.

parole.significato: A bonfire.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being feudal; feudal form or constitution.
parole.testo: Compare French féodalité.

parole.significato: A member of a reformed branch of the Bernardines, founded in 1577 at Feuillans, near Toulouse, in France.

parole.significato: Crispy flakes of crêpe used in desserts.

parole.significato: A section of a European newspaper typically dedicated to arts, culture, criticism, and light literature.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French feuilleton.

parole.significato: A male waiter (especially at a French restaurant).
parole.testo: From French garçon m (1788), from Old French garçon, oblique case of gars (“servant”), from Medieval Latin garciō m, from Frankish *wrakkjō (“servant, boy”), from Proto-Germanic *wrakjô (“exile, driven one”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreg- (“to drive”). parole.significato: A bachelor pad.
parole.testo: From French garçonnière.

parole.significato: Boastful talk.
parole.testo: From French gasconnade, from Gascon (“native of Gascony”) + -ade, equivalent to Gascon (“native of Gascony”) + -ade, literally "to talk like a Gascon". See French gasconnade.

parole.significato: Rubbish, particularly on board a ship or aircraft.
parole.testo: From French gâcher (“to waste, to mess up”) or gâchis (“waste, a mess”), likely borrowed into English by ships' crews in the 19th century. Became increasingly vulgar by association with Etymology 1.

parole.significato: An apparatus used to store or measure gas or the flow of gas, particularly in a laboratory setting.
parole.testo: From French gazomètre, corresponding to gaso- + -meter.

parole.significato: An alewife (type of fish).
parole.testo: From French gaspereau, a variant of gaspareau.

parole.significato: A syrupy reduction of vinegar (or wine) and sugar
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gastrique. Doublet of gastric.

parole.significato: a lover of good food; a connoisseur or gourmet
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gastronome.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to gastronomy.
parole.testo: From French gastronomique.

parole.significato: The art of preparing and eating good food.
parole.testo: From French gastronomie, from Ancient Greek γαστρονομία (gastronomía), from γαστήρ (gastḗr, “stomach”) + νόμος (nómos, “knowledge, law”); by surface analysis, gastro- (“cooking”) + -nomy (“a system of rules or laws about a particular field”).

parole.significato: Any member of a class of molluscs (Gastropoda) that includes snails, slugs, and limpets; univalve mollusc.
parole.testo: From French gastéropode, from gastro- + -poda, New Latin, from Ancient Greek γαστήρ (gastḗr, “stomach”) and πούς (poús, “foot”).

parole.significato: A rich, usually iced, cake.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gâteau. Doublet of wastel.

parole.significato: A disease of silkworms, caused by parasitic fungi.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gattine.

parole.significato: Awkward or lacking in social graces; bumbling; apt to make gaffes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gauche (“left, awkward”), from gauchir (“to veer, turn”), from Old French gaucher (“to trample, walk clumsily”), from Frankish *walkan (“to full, trample”), from Proto-Germanic *walkaną (“to full, roll up”). Akin to Old High German walchan (“to knead”), Old English wealcian (“to

parole.significato: A person or people claiming to be socialist but living a luxurious lifestyle that is inconsistent with such beliefs, im…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gauche caviar.

parole.significato: A socially tactless or awkward act.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gaucherie.

parole.significato: To plait, crimp, or flute
parole.testo: From French gaufrer (“to figure cloth, velvet, and other stuffs”), from gaufre (“honeycomb, waffle”); of Germanic origin. See waffle, wafer, and compare goffer, gopher (“an animal”).

parole.significato: A waffle (flat pastry).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gaufre.

parole.significato: A kind of waffle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gaufrette.

parole.significato: A French political ideology based on Charles de Gaulle's thoughts and actions.
parole.testo: French gaullisme, from Charles de Gaulle.

parole.significato: To apply a dressing of gauze; to cover with gauze.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gaze, from Arabic قَزّ (qazz, “silk”).

parole.significato: A process of force-feeding a goose for foie gras
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gavage, from gaver (“to stuff or cram”).

parole.significato: A French dance, in either 4/4 or 2/2 time.
parole.testo: From French, from Provençal gavoto (“dance of the mountain people”), from Old Occitan Gavot (“Alp native”, literally “glutton, boor”), from gaver (“force feed”), from Old Provençal gava (“crop”); attested since the 1690s.

parole.significato: A lesbian.
parole.testo: From gay + French -elle (“feminine suffix”).

parole.significato: A newspaper; a printed sheet published periodically.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gazette, from Italian gazzetta, from Venetan gazeta, from gazeta dele novità (literally “a gazeta (halfpenny) of news”), named for the cost (one gazeta) of the newspaper. Compare penny dreadful, dime novel. See gazzetta for more.

parole.significato: A person who writes for a gazette or newspaper; a journalist; (specifically) a journalist engaged by a government.
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from French gazettier (archaic), gazetier (“journalist, newspaperman”) + English -eer (suffix forming agent nouns denoting people associated with or engaged in a specified activities). parole.significato: One of the pieces of sod used to line or cover parapets and the faces of earthworks.
parole.testo: Borrowing from French gazon, from Middle French gazon, from Old French gason, wason (“piece of ground covered with grass, turf”), from Old Frankish *wasō (“ground, turf, sod”), from Proto-Germanic *wasô (“moisture; ground”), from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“moist, damp, wet”). Cognate with German Wa

parole.significato: The perineum.
parole.testo: From French guiche.

parole.significato: A semi-solid to almost solid colloid of a solid and a liquid, such as jelly, cheese or opal.
parole.testo: Coined by Thomas Graham in the mid 19th century as a clipping of gelatin, from French gélatine, from Italian gelatina, diminutive form of gelata (“iced”), from Latin gelata, past participle of gelo (“to freeze”), from gelu (“frost”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”). For the meaning developme

parole.significato: A protein derived through partial hydrolysis of the collagen extracted from animal skin, bones, cartilage, ligaments, e…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gélatine (“jelly, gel”), from Italian gelatina (“jelly, gel”), from gelare (“to freeze”), from Latin gelō (“to freeze”).

parole.significato: Jelly-like.
parole.testo: From gelatine + -ous; probably modeled on French gélatineux.

parole.significato: Any gelled suspension made for culinary purposes.
parole.testo: From the French gelée. Doublet of jelly.

parole.significato: The hazel grouse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gélinotte.

parole.significato: Synonym of gemma (“an asexual reproductive structure, as found in animals such as hydra (genus Hydra) and plants such a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gemmule, from Latin gemmula (“small bud; small gem”), from gemma (“bud of a plant; gem, jewel; thing made of precious stones”) (further etymology uncertain; possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to beget, give birth; to produce”), but see further at that entry) + -ula (fem

parole.significato: A member of the gendarmerie, a military body charged with police duties.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gendarme, a back-formation from gendarmes, from gens d'armes (“people of arms, armed people”), from gens + d' + armes.

parole.significato: A military body charged with police duties among the civilian population.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gendarmerie.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the chin.
parole.testo: From French génien, from Latin genianus, from Ancient Greek γένειον (géneion, “chin”) + Latin -ānus (“-an”).

parole.significato: A jinn, a being descended from the jann, normally invisible to the human eye, but who may also appear in animal or huma…
parole.testo: From French génie (“genius, genie”), a phono-semantic matching of Arabic جِنِّيّ (jinniyy).

parole.significato: A variety of apple that ripens very early
parole.testo: Probably from a diminutive of French Jean (“John”), so named as becoming ripe about St. John’s Day, June 24.

parole.significato: One who was involved in committing (perpetrating) the Rwandan Genocide.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French génocidaire. Piecewise doublet of genocider.

parole.significato: A classic European sponge cake.
parole.testo: From French, named after the city of Genoa.

parole.significato: A metal plate used as armour for the knee.
parole.testo: From French genouillère, from Old French genoilliere, which was also borrowed earlier as Middle English genulere.

parole.significato: A kind; a stylistic category or sort, especially of literature or other artworks.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French genre, from Old French gen(d)re, borrowed from Latin genere. Doublet of gender and genus.

parole.significato: Affectedly proper or refined; somewhat prudish refinement; excessively polite.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gentil (“gentile”), from Latin gentīlis (“of or belonging to the same people or nation”), from gēns (“clan; tribe; people, family”) + adjective suffix -īlis (“-ile”). Doublet of gentle, gentile, and jaunty. See also gens, gender, genus, and generation.

parole.significato: Non-Jewish.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gentil (“gentile”), from Latin gentīlis (“of or belonging to the same people or nation”), morphologically from gēns (“clan; tribe; people, family”) + adjective suffix -īlis (“-ile”). parole.significato: A French gentleman.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gentilhomme.

parole.significato: gentianin
parole.testo: From gentian + -in, from French gentianine, from gentiane + -ine.

parole.significato: neat; trim
parole.testo: From French gentil. Compare jaunty.

parole.significato: A nodule of stone having a cavity lined with mineral or crystal matter on the inside wall.

parole.significato: The shortest curve between two points on a specific surface.
parole.testo: From French géodésique. By surface analysis, geodesy + -ic.

parole.significato: The discipline which deals with the measurement and representation of Earth, its gravitational field and geodynamic phe…
parole.testo: From French géodésie, from Medieval Latin geōdaesia, from Ancient Greek γεωδαισία (geōdaisía), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) + δαίω (daíō, “to divide”). By surface analysis, geode + -esy.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to geology or a geologic time scale.
parole.testo: From geology + -ic, perhaps after French géologique.

parole.significato: The discipline of gathering, storing, processing, and delivering geospatial information.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French géomatique, a blend of géodésie (“geodesy”) and geoinformatique (“geoinformatics”); see informatics § Etymology for more.

parole.significato: A thin lightweight silk or cotton fabric with a matte finish.
parole.testo: From French georgette, named after Georgette de la Plante, French dressmaker.

parole.significato: The manager or acting partner of a company, publication etc.
parole.testo: French gérant.

parole.significato: A (wheat) sheaf.
parole.testo: Late 16th century, borrowed from French gerbe (“sheaf”). Doublet of garb.

parole.significato: A member of one of several species of small, jumping, mouselike rodents of the subfamily Gerbillinae, native to Africa,…

parole.significato: Dated spelling of gerbil.
parole.testo: French gerbille. Compare jerboa.

parole.significato: A Mediterranean herb, of species Teucrium chamaedrys, historically grown for medicinal use but now mostly as an ornamen…

parole.significato: A gesture or position serving to interrupt dystonic symptoms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French geste antagoniste (literally “antagonising gesture”).

parole.significato: The act of managing, conducting or administrating something.
parole.testo: Likely from French gestion.

parole.significato: To annoy or infuriate someone.

parole.significato: A kind of saponifying vulcanic clay used for hair and skin care.

parole.significato: A demon said to feed on corpses.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French goule, from Persian غول (ġul) from Arabic غُول (ḡūl).

parole.significato: A non-Muslim, especially a Christian, an infidel; especially as used by Turkish people with particular reference to Chr…

parole.significato: wildfowl; game
parole.testo: From French gibier.

parole.significato: A small, arboreal ape of the family Hylobatidae with long limbs, which they use to travel through tropical rainforests…

parole.significato: A type of stew made from rabbit or fish, in white wine and broth, originating from France.

parole.significato: the use of inkjet printing to manufacture artistic prints

parole.significato: Very large; like a giant; gigantic.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being gigantic; being of abnormally large size.
parole.testo: From French gigantisme, from Latin gigans (“giant”).

parole.significato: An Irish dance, derived from the jig, used in the Partita form (Baroque Period).

parole.significato: A waistcoat worn by a man.

parole.significato: A yellow vest, a member of a French protest movement which started in 2018.

parole.significato: A form of zincography.

parole.significato: Clove pink.
parole.testo: By folk etymology (with influence from flower) from French girofle, gilofre, from Late Latin caryophyllum, from Ancient Greek καρυόφυλλον (karuóphullon, “dried flower buds of the clove tree”).

parole.significato: A kind of pouch worn at the girdle.
parole.testo: French gibecière (“a game pouch or game pocket”). Compare gibbier.

parole.significato: An ornamental branched candle holder, sometimes with a mirror behind.

parole.significato: chanterelle (mushroom)

parole.significato: A member of a moderate political faction in France during the French Revolution.

parole.significato: The practice of frequently altering one's views and opinions to follow current trends.

parole.significato: The process of covering with a glacier, or the state of being glaciated; the production of glacial phenomena; an ice age

parole.significato: A large body of ice which flows under its own mass, usually downhill.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French glacier, from Franco-Provençal gllaciér, from Vulgar Latin *glaciārium, a derivative of Latin glaciēs (“ice”), of uncertain origin. First attested in English in 1744 per the OED.

parole.significato: Characteristic, composed, or of the nature of icy; icy.
parole.testo: From obsolete French glacieux, from Latin glaciēs (“ice”).

parole.significato: A gentle incline.

parole.significato: having a glossy surface
parole.testo: Borrowed from French glacé, past participle of glacer (“to glaze or freeze”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a gland or glands.
parole.testo: Mid 18th century borrowing from French glandulaire, from glandule (“small gland”) + -aire (“-ar, -ary”, adjectival suffix), from Latin glandulae (“glands of the throat”); equivalent to glandule + -ar.

parole.significato: The situation and structure of the secretory vessels in plants.
parole.testo: French

parole.significato: A sliding, as down a snow slope in the Alps.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French glissade.

parole.significato: The locus described by any point attached to a curve that moves continuously along another fixed curve, the movable cur…
parole.testo: From French glissette, from glisser (“to slip”).

parole.significato: Roughly spherical in shape; globe-shaped.
parole.testo: From French globulaire or Medieval Latin globulāris.

parole.significato: A small round particle of substance; a drop.
parole.testo: From French globule, from Latin globulus, from globus (“globe”).

parole.significato: A pavilion or similar structure in an elevated position in parkland.

parole.significato: The absorption or replacement of minor languages or dialects by major ones.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French glottophagie, coined by Louis-Jean Calvet. By surface analysis, glotto- + -phagy.

parole.significato: linguistic xenophobia, linguicism; discrimination against people based on their native language or dialect.
parole.testo: From glotto- + -phobia, derived from the French word French glottophobie, which was defined by Philippe Blanchet in 2008.

parole.significato: A simple monosaccharide (sugar) with a molecular formula of C₆H₁₂O₆; a principle source of energy for cellular metaboli…

parole.significato: lodicule

parole.significato: Synonym of gliadin.

parole.significato: Synonym of glycerol

parole.significato: A polysaccharide that is the main form of carbohydrate storage in animals; converted to glucose as needed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French glycogène. By surface analysis, glyco- + -gen.

parole.significato: A figure carved in relief or incised, especially representing a sound, word, or idea.
parole.testo: First attested in 1727. Borrowed from French glyphe, from Ancient Greek γλυφή (gluphḗ, “carving”), from γλύφω (glúphō, “I carve, engrave”).

parole.significato: Relating to glyptography, the art of engraving on precious stones.
parole.testo: From glyptography + -ic. Compare French glyptographique.

parole.significato: A room or building devoted to displaying works of sculpture.
parole.testo: From French glyptothèque, from Ancient Greek γλυπτός (gluptós, “carved, engraved”) + Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē, “box or chest”).

parole.significato: A museum or similar exhibition of statues and sculptures.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French glyptothèque, from Ancient Greek γλῠπτόν (glŭptón, “statue, sculpture”) + Ancient Greek -θήκη (-thḗkē, “-place, -house”).

parole.significato: Any member of an ethnic group and Sufi religious order in Morocco.
parole.testo: From French Gnaoua, from Moroccan Arabic ڭناوة (gnāwa), from Tashelhit agnaw (“stutterer, a person of sub-Saharan origin”).

parole.significato: An elemental (spirit or corporeal creature associated with a classical element) associated with earth.
parole.testo: From French gnome (“gnome”), from New Latin gnomus, used by Paracelsus as a synonym for pygmaeus (“pygmy”).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to gnomes (sententious sayings).
parole.testo: From French gnomique, ultimately from Ancient Greek γνωμικός (gnōmikós), from γνώμη (gnṓmē, “thought, judgement”), akin to γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “know”). By surface analysis, gnome + -ic.

parole.significato: A female gnome
parole.testo: From French gnomide.

parole.testo: Borrowed from French gnomon, or directly from its etymon Latin gnōmōn, or directly from its etymon Ancient Greek γνώμων (gnṓmōn, “discerner, interpreter; carpenter’s square; gnomon of a sundial; (geometry) gnomon”), from γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to be aware of; to perceive; to know”), ultimately from Pr

parole.significato: To not need to be said or mentioned; to be obvious, apparent, clear, or already established.

parole.significato: An oaf or fool.
parole.testo: * Diarmuid Ó Muirthile says it derives from gobbalew, southwest England dialect for a coastguard exciseman, from French gobe-a-l'eau "one who seizes things on water".

parole.significato: A naive, gullible person.

parole.significato: A naive, gullible person.

parole.significato: An English person, from the perspective of a French person or in the context of French history, originating during the…

parole.significato: A dildo.
parole.testo: From French godemichet.

parole.significato: An ornament produced by notching or carving a rounded moulding.
parole.testo: From French godron (“round plait, godroon”).

parole.significato: A white tern, of species Gygis alba.

parole.significato: A schooner.
parole.testo: From French goélette.

parole.significato: A complex mixture of several substances extracted from the seaweed Irish moss (Chondrus crispus).

parole.significato: To make wavy; to crimp.

parole.significato: A geological concretion, similar in its shape to marleka and imatrankivi.

parole.significato: A member of a habitation colony at Stadacona founded by Samuel de Champlain, where Quebec City now lies.
parole.testo: From French habitant.

parole.significato: One who frequents a place.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French habitué, past participle of habituer (“to frequent”), from Late Latin habituare (“to habituate”), from habitus.

parole.significato: In massage, a hacking or chopping stroke repeated in succession with the edge of the extended fingers or with the whole…

parole.significato: a cleaver, similar to an ax but with a wider cutting edge
parole.testo: From French hacher, from Proto-Germanic *hakkōną (“to chop; hack”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *keg-, *keng- (“to be sharp; peg; hook; handle”).

parole.significato: A line on a map indicating the steepness of a slope.⁷
parole.testo: From French hachure (“crosshatching”), from hacher (“to hatch”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the deepest parts of the ocean.
parole.testo: From French hadal, from Hadès + -al. By surface analysis, had- + -al.

parole.significato: A hemisphere.
parole.testo: From half + world, in later use after French demi-monde.

parole.significato: A small railroad station, usually unstaffed or with very few staff, and with few or no facilities.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French halte. See also Etymology 2.

parole.significato: A rich goblet, especially one used on state occasions.
parole.testo: From French hanap, from Frankish *hnapp, from Proto-Germanic *hnappaz (“cup, bowl”). Doublet of nap.

parole.significato: A large garagelike structure where aircraft are kept.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hangar (“shed, hangar”), from Middle French hanghart (“enclosure near a house”), from Old French hangart, *hamgart, from Old Frankish *haimgard (“fence around a group of houses”), from *haim (“home, village, hamlet”) + *gard (“yard”). parole.significato: An impassioned, disputatious public speech.

parole.significato: snowy owl
parole.testo: Borrowed from French harfang, itself borrowed from Swedish harfång.

parole.significato: Synonym of common bean.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French haricot (“bean”).

parole.significato: A stew of lamb and vegetables.
parole.testo: From French haricot, from Middle French haricot, a deverbal derivation of Old French harigoter (“to tear up, shred, slice up, slice into pieces”), from Frankish *hariōn (“to ruin, lay waste, ravage, plunder, destroy”), from Proto-Germanic *harjōną (“to plunder, lay waste, harry”).
