parole.significato: An Algerian Muslim who fought with the French during Algeria’s war of independence from 1954-1962; loosely, an Algerian…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Harki, from Algerian Arabic حركي (ḥarkī), from حركة (ḥarka, “military operation”) (standard Arabic حركة (ḥaraka, “movement”)).

parole.significato: A pantomime-like comedy featuring the harlequin or clown.
parole.testo: From French arlequinade.

parole.significato: A small keyboard instrument that consists of a series of reed pipes, which sound when one of the keys is pressed to ope…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French harmonium, coined by French harmonium inventor Alexandre Debain in 1840. By surface analysis, harmony + -ium. First attested in 1847.

parole.significato: To be in harmonious agreement.
parole.testo: From French harmoniser. By surface analysis, harmony + -ize.

parole.significato: A harpoon.
parole.testo: From French harper (“to grasp strongly”). See harpoon.

parole.testo: Early 1600s, borrowed from French harpechord (“harp string”), from New Latin harpichordium, from harpa (“harp”) + chorda (“string”). parole.significato: An obsolete matchlock firearm.
parole.testo: From French harquebuse, borrowed from Middle Low German hakebusse or Middle Dutch hakebus, hagebus (modern Dutch haakbus), from hôk (“hook”) + busse (“box; firelock”), from Old Saxon hōk + *buhsa, from Proto-Germanic *hōkaz + *buhsā.

parole.significato: A vicious and scolding woman, especially an older one.
parole.testo: Perhaps a modification of French haridelle (“old horse, nag”).

parole.significato: Food, especially meat and potatoes, chopped and mixed together.
parole.testo: From French hacher (“to chop”), from Middle French hacher, from Old French hacher, from Old French hache (“axe”), from Frankish *happjā (“axe”). Compare also Old English ġehæċċa (“sausage meat”, literally “that which is hacked or chopped up”).

parole.significato: A concept involving the return or persistence of elements from the social or cultural past.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hantologie: equivalent to haunt + -ology, and a near-homophone to ontologie (“ontology”); apparently coined by Jacques Derrida in Spectres of Marx (1993).

parole.significato: A kind of graduated breech sight for a small arm or cannon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hausse.

parole.significato: A gorget (armor for the neck and/or upper chest).
parole.testo: From French hausse-col; see that entry for more.

parole.significato: A slight taint of decay, particularly in wild game meat, that used to be considered desirable; approximately, gaminess.
parole.testo: From French hautgoût, from haut (“high”), goût (“taste”).

parole.significato: High fashion; fashionability.
parole.testo: From French.

parole.significato: A dais.
parole.testo: From French [Term?].

parole.significato: Any of a family of organ stops that contain reeds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hautbois. Doublet of oboe and hautboy.

parole.significato: high (especially in terms of fashion, cookery or anything considered to be typically French)
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French, extracted from terms such as haute cuisine and haute couture.

parole.significato: The upper middle class in France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French haute bourgeoisie.

parole.significato: High fashion as produced in Paris and imitated in other fashion capitals such as New York, London, and Milan.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French haute couture (“haute couture, high fashion”), from haute (“high, elegant”) + couture (“sewing”).

parole.significato: Elaborate or skillfully style or manner of preparing food, especially that of France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French haute (“high”) + cuisine (“cookery”). Literally, “high(-class) cookery”. First attested in 1829. Usually in italics until 1960s.

parole.significato: cultural activities or items that achieve the highest standards.
parole.testo: French

parole.significato: Synonym of passguard, neck guard (plate on shoulder-armor to protect neck)
parole.testo: From French haute pièce.

parole.significato: The highest of the male modal voices (i.e. not a countertenor); it is lower than the female contralto and higher than t…
parole.testo: From French haute-contre.

parole.significato: Higher or better.
parole.testo: French haut + English -er.

parole.significato: Highest or best.
parole.testo: French haut + English -est.

parole.significato: Haughtiness or arrogance; loftiness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hauteur.

parole.significato: A small, strong bag carried on the back or the shoulder, usually with only one strap, and originally made of canvas.
parole.testo: From French havresac, from Low German Haaversack and/or German Habersack, Hafersack (literally “oat-sack”), from Hafer + Sack. Compare also Dutch haverzak.

parole.significato: Synonym of haüynite.
parole.testo: From French haüyne, named for French mineralogist René Just Haüy (1743–1822).

parole.significato: An alleged medical condition, described as an unpleasant sensation of pain and heaviness in the lower limbs.
parole.testo: Calque of French jambes lourdes

parole.significato: A unit of surface area (symbol ㏊) equal to 100 ares (that is, 10,000 square metres, one hundredth of a square kilometre…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hectare, formed from Ancient Greek ἑκατόν (hekatón, “hundred”) + are, equivalent to hect- + are.

parole.significato: The quality of being hectic (very busy with activity and confusion).
parole.testo: From French hecticité or hectic + -ity.

parole.significato: hundred
parole.testo: From French hecto-, from Ancient Greek ἑκατόν (hekatón, “hundred”). Doublet of hecato- and centi-.

parole.significato: An SI unit of mass equal to 10² grams. Symbol: hg
parole.testo: From French hectogramme. By surface analysis, hecto- + gram.

parole.significato: A unit of volume or capacity equivalent to 100 litres. Symbol: hL
parole.testo: From French hectolitre. By surface analysis, hecto- + litre.

parole.significato: An old measure of volume equal to one hundred cubic metres.
parole.testo: French hectostère.

parole.significato: Someone who will become an heir (usually to a monarchy) only if no-one with a higher-ranking claim is born.
parole.testo: A calque of French héritier présomptif, hence the unusual order of adjective following noun.

parole.significato: Any of various papilionid butterflies of the genus Papilio.
parole.testo: From French Hélène, from Latin Helena, from Ancient Greek Ἑλένη (Helénē). Doublet of Elaine.

parole.testo: Borrowed from French hélicoptère, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix, “spiral”) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing”). Doublet of helicopteron. By surface analysis, helico- + -pter. The dragonfly sense is from a dragonfly's ability to hover and fly in any direction, like the flying machine.

parole.significato: rotogravure (process or engraving)

parole.significato: An approximate half-line of verse, separated from another by a caesura, often for dramatic effect.
parole.testo: From French hémistiche, from Latin hēmistichium, from Ancient Greek ἡμιστίχιον (hēmistíkhion), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “half”) + στίχος (stíkhos, “verse”).

parole.significato: A thing having seven parts or divisions.
parole.testo: From French heptaméride, from Ancient Greek ἑπτά (heptá, “seven”) + French méride (compare meridian).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to heraldry or heralds.
parole.testo: From herald + -ic; probably modelled on French héraldique.

parole.significato: An Old World plant (Paris quadrifolia) related to the trillium.
parole.testo: From French herbe paris, from Latin par (“equal”), in reference to the regularity of its leaves, petals, etc. See image.

parole.significato: A mixture of bay leaves, parsley, sage, rosemary and thyme.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French herbes de Provence.

parole.significato: An organism that feeds chiefly on plants; an animal that feeds on herbage or vegetation as the main part of its diet.
parole.testo: From French herbivore, from Latin herbivorus. By surface analysis, herb (“herbage”) + -i- + -vore.

parole.significato: The act of herborizing (collecting and classifying plants during an excursion).

parole.significato: To seek and classify new or previously known plant species.

parole.significato: A beam or bar armed with iron spikes, and turning on a pivot, used to block up a passage.

parole.significato: The branch of biology dealing with reptiles (Reptilia) and amphibians (Amphibia).
parole.testo: Derived from French herpétologie, from Ancient Greek ἑρπετόν (herpetón, “reptile”) + -logie (suffix indicating a field of study or work), equivalent to herpet- + -logy.

parole.significato: The dragging of a harrow over a field.

parole.significato: A herse.

parole.significato: Having six petals.
parole.testo: From hexa- + petalous. Compare French hexapétale.

parole.testo: From French haie (“hedge”), with reference to the weaving patterns used in hedgelaying. Doublet of hedge and quay.

parole.significato: The act or result of hierarchizing; the establishment of a hierarchy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hiérarchisation, equivalent to hierarchize + -ation.

parole.significato: A physical manifestation of the holy or sacred, serving as a spiritual eidolon for emulation or worship.

parole.significato: Finance focused on large-scale operations involving substantial amounts of capital.
parole.testo: Calque of French haute finance.

parole.significato: Hindi-speaking.
parole.testo: From Hindi + -phone or French hindiphone.

parole.significato: Hindu.

parole.significato: A horse racing course.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hippodrome, a learned borrowing from Latin hippodromos, borrowed from Ancient Greek ῐ̔ππόδρομος (hĭppódromos), from ῐ̔́ππος (hĭ́ppos, “horse”) + δρόμος (drómos, “street”). By surface analysis, hippo- + -drome.

parole.significato: a mythical beast, half griffin and half horse, supposedly the offspring of a griffin and a filly.
parole.testo: From French hippogriffe, from Ancient Greek ἵππος (híppos, “horse”, English hippo-) + γρύψ (grúps, “griffin”).

parole.significato: An early automobile invented by Étienne Lenoir in 1863.
parole.testo: From French hippomobile.

parole.significato: Relating to the tissues of the body.
parole.testo: 19th century. From French histique, from Ancient Greek ἱστός (histós, “web”).

parole.significato: Historical quality or authenticity based on fact.
parole.testo: Probably from French historicité, or from Latin historicus + -ity. Equivalent to historic + -ity.

parole.significato: Synonym of storiette /storyette (“short story or tale”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French historiette. By surface analysis, history + -ette.

parole.significato: A voyageur who wintered in First Nations camps.
parole.testo: From French hivernant (“wintering, winterer”).

parole.significato: A hautboy or oboe.

parole.significato: A hockey player.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hockeyeur or Dutch hockeyer.

parole.significato: A strong, unpleasant smell.
parole.testo: From French haut-goût.

parole.significato: An item of armor worn in the 16th century, consisting of overlapping lames to protect the buttocks.

parole.significato: An emulsion of butter and lemon juice using egg yolks as the emulsifying agent, used in French cooking.
parole.testo: From French sauce hollandaise (literally “Dutch sauce”).

parole.significato: Of a geologic epoch within the Quaternary period from about the year 10 000 BC to the present; the age of man.
parole.testo: From French Holocène, based on holo- (“whole”) + Ancient Greek καινός (kainós, “fresh, new”). By surface analysis, holo- + -cene.

parole.significato: A homage, especially something in an artwork which has been done in respectful imitation of another artist.
parole.testo: From French hommage.

parole.significato: man of letters, a literary man
parole.testo: Borrowed from French homme de lettres, from homme (“man”) + de (“of”) + lettres (“humanities, arts”).

parole.significato: An ultimately seductive and dangerous man; a womanizer.
parole.testo: Adapted borrowing from French homme fatal (literally “fatal man”), after femme fatale.

parole.significato: homogeneous
parole.testo: Compare French homogène (“homogeneous”).

parole.significato: Something homologous; a homologous organ or part, chemical compound, chromosome, gene, or cultural element.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French homologue, From Ancient Greek ὁμόλογος (homólogos, “agreeing, of one mind”), equivalent to homo- + -log.

parole.significato: A word which is pronounced the same as another word but differs in spelling or meaning or origin.
parole.testo: From French homophone; equivalent to homo- (“same”) + -phone (“sound”).

parole.testo: Internationalism, from French homophonie, from Ancient Greek ὁμοφωνία (homophōnía, “unison”), from ὁμόφωνος (homóphōnos, “of the same sound or tone”). By surface analysis, homo- + -phony.

parole.significato: To grumble.
parole.testo: French hogner (“to grumble”), which could be a cross of honnir (“to disgrace, shame”) and grogner (“to grunt”).

parole.significato: A bustling to-do, excited speech or noise.
parole.testo: Earlier houp-la, hoop la, first attested in c. 1877, probably from French houp-là, oup-là (“upsadaisy, upsy-daisy”), a cry to various animals close to humans like horses and dogs, of likely onomatopoeic origin (but see là). Compare interjections like whoop, ahoy, hoo.

parole.significato: The toughest category of climbs, tougher than category 1. One of six categories of climbs, HC, 1, 2, 3, 4, and not clas…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hors catégorie (literally “beyond category”).

parole.significato: A small, light, and usually savory first course in a meal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hors-d'œuvre.

parole.significato: Out of action; disabled; no longer able to fight.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hors de combat (literally “out of combat”), which is obsolete in contemporary French.

parole.significato: Occupying a full page by itself, rather than among the prose (such as a full-page image).
parole.testo: From French hors-texte.

parole.significato: A lodging for pilgrims or the destitute, normally provided by a monastic order.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hospice, from Old French hospise, from Latin hospitium (“hospitality, an inn”). Doublet of hospitium.

parole.significato: a children's game in which a blindfolded person had to guess who was hitting them.
parole.testo: From French hautes-coquilles. Compare French main chaude (“hot hand”), referring to the same game. By surface analysis, hot + cockle.

parole.significato: Someone who owns or runs a hotel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hôtelier.

parole.significato: A breed of rabbit, characterized by having short ears and being all white except for black rings around the eyes.
parole.testo: Ellipsis of Blanc de Hotot, from French Blanc de Hotot (“White of Hotot”), after Hotot-en-Auge (a commune in Normandy, France).

parole.significato: Chlamydotis undulata, a bustard, chiefly of North Africa and south-east Asia.
parole.testo: In this spelling, from French houbara, and later also directly from Arabic حُبَارَى (ḥubārā).

parole.significato: A beautiful virgin girl supposed to dwell in Paradise for the enjoyment of the faithful.
parole.testo: From French houri, from Persian حوری (hurî), from Arabic حُورِيّ (ḥūriyy) and Arabic حُورِيَّة (ḥūriyya), adjective and feminine singulative of حُور (ḥūr) from Classical Arabic حُورٌ عِينٌ (ḥūrun ʕīnun, “fair maidens, black-eyed ones”). parole.significato: A licensed brothel.
parole.testo: Calque of French maison de tolérance.

parole.significato: A society where kinship and political relations are organized around membership in corporately-organized dwellings rath…
parole.testo: Calque of French société à maison, coined by Claude Lévi-Strauss.

parole.significato: A covering, usually of textile (or mail) and attached to a saddle; a saddlecloth.
parole.testo: French housse.

parole.significato: The fervent admiration of the works and literary theories of French writer Victor Hugo (1802–1885).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hugolâtrie, equivalent to Hugo + -latry.

parole.significato: An admirer of French writer Victor Hugo (1802–1885).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hugophile, equivalent to Hugo + -phile.

parole.significato: A member of the Protestant Reformed Church of France during the 16th and 17th century.
parole.testo: From French huguenot (“Huguenot”), of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: The religion or doctrine of the Huguenots
parole.testo: From Huguenot + -ism; French huguenotisme.

parole.significato: A doorman; a domestic officer who guarded the doors to chambers in a mansion or similar large establishment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French huissier. Doublet of usher and possibly ostiary.

parole.significato: An officer of the court in several European countries who serves processes and notices, seizes and auctions off propert…
parole.testo: From French huissier de justice (“justice usher, court usher”).

parole.significato: A French poem, a kind of octastich.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French huitain.

parole.significato: A political philosophy that focuses on human rights.
parole.testo: From human rights + -ism, calque of French droits-de-l'hommisme.

parole.significato: One of various early modern perfumes and elixirs made of rosemary, camomile or later lavender infused in various alcoho…
parole.termine_origine: Eau de la Reine de Hongrie

catena.termine: Eau de la Reine de Hongrie

parole.testo: Ellipsis of Queen of Hungary's water, possibly a calque of French Eau de la Reine de Hongrie, after its supposed origin.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the Hyblaean Mountains in southeastern Sicily, Italy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Hybléen, via Latin hyblaeus, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὑβλαῖος (hublaîos, “Hyblaean”).

parole.significato: A solid compound containing or linked to water molecules.
parole.testo: From French hydrate, from Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + -ate.

parole.significato: Pertaining to water.
parole.testo: From French hydraulique, from Latin hydraulicus, from Ancient Greek ὑδραυλικός (hudraulikós, “of a water organ”), from ὕδραυλις (húdraulis, “water organ”), from ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + αὐλός (aulós, “pipe”).

parole.significato: An abnormal build-up of fluids at a site in the body, especially in the membranes around a testicle.
parole.testo: From French hydrocèle or Latin hydrocēlē, from Ancient Greek ὑδροκήλη (hudrokḗlē), from ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + κήλη (kḗlē, “tumour”).

parole.significato: The lightest chemical element (symbol H), with an atomic number of 1 and atomic weight of 1.008.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hydrogène (“hydrogen”), coined by the French chemists Louis-Bernard Guyton de Morveau (1737–1816) and Antoine Lavoisier (1743–1794) from hydro- (prefix meaning ‘water’) + -gène (suffix denoting a producer of something), from the fact that water is produced as a compound when hyd

parole.significato: Divination by water or other liquid.
parole.testo: From French hydromancie or Late Latin hydromantia, from Ancient Greek ὑδρομαντεία (hudromanteía); corresponding to hydro- + -mancy.

parole.significato: A hydrophobic compound or material.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hydrophobe, from Latin hydrophobus, from Ancient Greek ὑδροφόβος (hudrophóbos), from ὑδρο- (hudro-, “water”) + φόβος (phóbos, “fear, dread”).

parole.significato: A hyena.
parole.testo: From French hyène.

parole.significato: The science of health, its promotion and preservation.
parole.testo: From French hygiène, from Ancient Greek ὑγιεινή (τέχνη) (hugieinḗ (tékhnē), literally “art of health”), from ὑγιεινός (hugieinós, “of health, good for the health, wholesome, sound, healthy”), from ὑγιής (hugiḗs, “healthy, sound”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to hygiene; clean, sanitary, free of disease.
parole.testo: From French hygiénique. Displaced earlier hygienal.

parole.significato: An instrument that measures the humidity of the air or other gases, especially the relative humidity.
parole.testo: From French hygromètre, from hygro- + -meter.

parole.significato: Readily taking up and retaining water, especially from the atmosphere.
parole.testo: From French hygroscopique.

parole.significato: The ability of a substance to attract and hold water molecules from the surrounding environment.
parole.testo: From French hygroscopie.

parole.significato: Shaped like a U, or like the letter upsilon (υ).
parole.testo: Borrowing from French hyoïde, from New Latin hȳoīdēs, from Ancient Greek ῡ̔οειδής (hūoeidḗs, “shaped like the letter "υ"”), from ὖ (û, “the Greek letter upsilon”) + -ο- (-o-) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-like, -oid”).

parole.significato: A shop combining elements of a department store and a supermarket.
parole.testo: From hyper- + market, calque of French hypermarché.

parole.significato: An increase in the size of an organ or tissue due to the enlargement of its individual cells.
parole.testo: From French hypertrophie, from Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér, “over, excessive”) + τροφή (trophḗ, “nourishment”), equivalent to hyper- + -trophy.

parole.significato: That induces sleep; soporific, somniferous.
parole.testo: From French hypnagogique, from Ancient Greek ὕπνος (húpnos, “sleep”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “leading”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to hypnosis or hypnotism.
parole.testo: From French hypnotique (“inclined to sleep, soporific”), from Late Latin hypnoticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “inclined to sleep, putting to sleep, sleepy”), from ὑπνοῦν (hupnoûn, “to put to sleep”), from ὕπνος (húpnos, “sleep”).

parole.significato: The hypochondrium.
parole.testo: From French hypocondre (“hypochondrium”).

parole.significato: Related to, or affected by hypochondria.
parole.testo: From French hypocondriaque, from Ancient Greek ὑποχονδριακός (hupokhondriakós, “of the region between the ribs and navel”), from ὑποχόνδριος (hupokhóndrios, “the space between the ribs and the navel”), from ὑπό (hupó, “below”) + χόνδρος (khóndros, “cartilage”). See also hypochondrium, hypochondria,

parole.significato: The beliefs and policies of the Hébertists: advocating the dechristianization of France and extreme Terror.
parole.testo: French hébertisme, named after the populist journalist Jacques Hébert (1757–1794).

parole.significato: A member of a radical revolutionary political group that came to power during the Reign of Terror and played a signific…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hébertiste, named after the populist journalist Jacques Hébert.

parole.significato: The chief hospital in a French city.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hôtel-Dieu.

parole.significato: A woman who owns or runs a hotel.
parole.testo: From French hôtelière.

parole.significato: I am able to think, therefore I exist; a proof of existence based on the fact that someone capable of any form of thoug…
parole.testo: Calque of French je pense, donc je suis or perhaps of Latin cōgitō, ergō sum. First written in French by René Descartes, a 17th century French philosopher, in Discourse on the Method (1637) as je pense donc je suis, which he later expressed in Latin in Principles of Philosophy (1644).

parole.significato: A metrical foot in verse consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable.
parole.testo: From French iambe in the mid-1800s, from Latin ïambus, from Ancient Greek ἴαμβος (íambos). Displaced iambus which shares the same classical origin.

parole.significato: A naturally-occurring psychoactive compound found in a number of plants, principally iboga (Tabernanthe iboga), and use…
parole.testo: From French ibogaïne, from Myene iboga.

parole.significato: One who destroys religious images or icons, especially an opponent of the Orthodox Church in the 8th and 9th centuries,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French iconoclaste and its etymon Medieval Latin īconoclastēs, from Byzantine Greek εἰκονοκλάστης (eikonoklástēs, literally “image breaker”). By surface analysis, icono- + -clast.

parole.significato: A freshwater fish of the family Cyprinidae, found across northern Europe and Asia, especially Leuciscus idus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ide, from Scientific Latin idus (species name), from Swedish id.

parole.significato: Pertaining to ideas, or to a given idea.
parole.testo: From French idéal, from Late Latin ideālis (“existing in idea”), by surface analysis, idea + -al, from Latin idea (“idea”); see idea. In mathematics, the noun ring theory sense was first introduced by German mathematician Richard Dedekind in his 1871 edition of a text on number theory. The concept w

parole.significato: One who adheres to idealism.
parole.testo: From French idéaliste, from Late Latin idealis (“ideal”), from Latin idea (“idea”), equivalent to ideal + -ist.

parole.significato: Identical.
parole.testo: From French identique, from Medieval Latin identicus (“the same”), from Latin identi-, from idem (“the same”).

parole.significato: The act of identifying (i.e., which one, which thing).
parole.testo: From French identification.

parole.significato: To establish the identity of someone or something.
parole.testo: From French identifier, from Medieval Latin identicus + Latin faciō.

parole.significato: One who advocates an ideology, especially as an official or preeminent advocate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French idéologue. By surface analysis, ideo- + -logue. First attested in the 19th century.

parole.significato: Doctrine, philosophy, body of beliefs or principles belonging to an individual or group.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French idéologie, from idéo- + -logie (equivalent to English ideo- + -logy). Cognate with, but not derived from, idea. Coined 1796 by Antoine Destutt de Tracy. Modern sense of “doctrine” attributed to use of related idéologue (“ideologue”) by Napoleon Bonaparte as a term of abuse towar

parole.significato: The state or condition of being an idiot; the quality of having an intelligence level far below average.
parole.testo: From French idiotie, from Old French idiot. Displaced earlier idiotacy, idiotry. Equivalent to idiot + -cy. By surface analysis, idio- + -cy.

parole.significato: A person who exhibits an extraordinary ability in one subject (often mathematics) while being intellectually disabled i…
parole.testo: From French idiot savant, literally ‘wise idiot’.

parole.significato: Idea, occurring only in certain set phrases which are borrowings from French
parole.testo: Borrowed from French idée (“idea”). Doublet of idea.

parole.significato: An idea dominating the mind and maintained despite evidence to the contrary; (loosely), an obsession.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French idée fixe (literally “fixed idea”).

parole.significato: A fundamental idea or guiding principle, seen as giving rise to something.
parole.testo: From French idée mère.

parole.significato: A received, or accepted, idea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French idée reçue.

parole.significato: Please.
parole.testo: The construction is unusual since the infinitive to please originally meant only “to satisfy”, not “to be satisfied”. One solution entails interpreting you as an object pronoun and please as a verb in the third-person singular subjunctive, such that if you please actually meant if it may please you.

parole.significato: Great dishonor, shame, or humiliation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ignominie, from Latin ignōminia, from ig- (“not”) + nomen (“name”) (prefix assimilated form of in-).

parole.significato: Designating an order of friars founded in 1495 who ministered to the poor, especially in France.
parole.testo: From French ignorantin.

parole.significato: To deliberately not listen or pay attention to.
parole.testo: From French ignorer, from Latin ignōrō (“to have no knowledge of, mistake, take no notice of, ignore”), from ignārus (“not knowing”), from in- (“not”) + gnārus (“knowing”), from gnōscō, nōscō; see know.

parole.significato: Relating to the ilium.
parole.testo: From French iliaque, from Late Latin īliacus, Latin īlium.

parole.significato: Contrary to, forbidden, or not authorized by law, especially criminal law.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French illégal, from Medieval Latin illegalis, from Latin legalis, by surface analysis, il- + legal. In senses relating to immigration, via clipping of illegal alien or illegal immigrant.

parole.significato: the state of being illegal
parole.testo: From French illégalité, equivalent to il- + legality or illegal + -ity.

parole.significato: Not approved by law, but not invalid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French illicite, from Latin illicitus, from in- (“not”) + licitus (“allowed, permitted”), from licet (“it is allowed”). By surface analysis, il- + licit.

parole.significato: Synonym of Illinois (“member of the Illinois (Algonquian people)”)
parole.testo: From French Illinois.

parole.significato: A member of the above-mentioned tribe.
parole.testo: From French Illinois, an adaptation of an Algonquian (perhaps Ojibwe) name derived from Miami ilenweewa (“he speaks the regular way”).

parole.significato: Something that illuminates.
parole.testo: From French.

parole.significato: One of the Illuminati (various groups).
parole.testo: French

parole.significato: A person's essential or favorite works of art, regarded as a collection that could be brought together as a single idea…
parole.testo: Calque of French musée imaginaire.

parole.significato: Beardless.
parole.testo: From French imberbe, from Latin imberbis.

parole.significato: A set of tiles or shingles that overlap like the scales of a fish.
parole.testo: From French imbrication, from Latin imbricātus, from imbricō, from imbrex. By surface analysis, imbricate + -ion.

parole.significato: Capable of being imitated or copied.
parole.testo: From French imitable, from Latin imitābilis. See imitate.

parole.significato: A person who imitates or apes another.
parole.testo: From French imitateur, derived from Latin imitātor, equivalent to imitate + -or.

parole.significato: The state of being immanent; inherency.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French immanence.

parole.significato: Naturally part of something; existing throughout and within something; intrinsic.
parole.testo: Entered English around 1530, via French, from Late Latin immanēns, present participle of Latin immanēre, from im- (“in”) + manēre (“to dwell, remain, stay”). Cognate with remain and manor.

parole.significato: That is beyond memory; ancient.
parole.testo: From French immémorial. By surface analysis, im- + memorial.

parole.significato: The act or process of preventing a thing from moving.
parole.testo: From French immobilisation or im- + mobilization or immobilize + -ation.

parole.significato: To render motionless; to stop moving or stop from moving.
parole.testo: From French immobiliser, equivalent to immobile + -ize.

parole.significato: Any of various papery flowers, often dried and used as decoration.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French immortelle.

parole.significato: The process by which a person is safely exposed in a controlled manner to a material that is designed to prime their im…
parole.testo: From French immunisation. Coined by Albert Calmette. Equivalent to immunize + -ation or immune + -ization.

parole.significato: To make someone or something immune to something.
parole.testo: From French immuniser, equivalent to immune + -ize.

parole.significato: Printed.
parole.testo: Abbreviation of French imprimé (“printed”) and imprimeur (“printer”).

parole.significato: A road with no exit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French impasse.

parole.significato: The act of making into paste.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French impastation. See impaste and impasto.

parole.significato: the quality of being impermeable
parole.testo: Borrowed from French imperméabilité.

parole.significato: Not personal; not representing a person; not having personality.
parole.testo: From French impersonnel, from Latin impersōnālis, from im- (“not”) + persōnālis (“personal”), equivalent to im- + personal.

parole.significato: The action of imploring; begging, beseeching.
parole.testo: From French imploration, from Latin implorationem.

parole.significato: Being easily influenced (especially of young people).
parole.testo: From French impressionnable, equivalent to impression + -able. See also impressible.

parole.significato: An art movement characterized by visible brushstrokes, ordinary subject matter, and an emphasis on light and its changi…
parole.testo: From French impressionnisme.

parole.significato: One who adheres to the theory or method of impressionism.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French impressionniste.

parole.significato: Synonym of printer, printing house, &c., a self-employed printer or printing establishment.
parole.testo: From French imprimerie, from imprimer (“to print, to imprint”) + -erie (“-ery”), from im- (“in-”) + primer (“to print”). Equivalent to imprint + -ery.

parole.significato: Improvised; without prior preparation, planning, or rehearsal.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French impromptu.

parole.significato: The condition of being improper.
parole.testo: From French impropriété, from Latin improprietās. By surface analysis, improper + -iety or im- + propriety.

parole.significato: The act or art of composing and making music, poetry, and the like, extemporaneously
parole.testo: From French improvisation. Morphologically improvise + -ation.

parole.significato: Someone who improvises; improviser.
parole.testo: From improvise + -ator, after French improvisateur and Italian improvvisatore.

parole.significato: To make something up or invent it as one goes on; to proceed guided only by imagination, intuition, and guesswork rathe…
parole.testo: From French improviser; ultimately from Latin improvisus.

parole.significato: Immodest.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French impudique. Equivalent to im- + pudic.

parole.significato: weak; feeble; lacking power
parole.testo: French, from prefix im- (“not”) + puissant. See puissant.

parole.significato: Shared with one or more others.
parole.testo: Possibly a calque of French en commun. Compare Italian in comune, Spanish en común and Portuguese em comum.

parole.significato: Resulting from the actions of parties.
parole.testo: From fact (“deed, action”) (now obsolete, except in law). Perhaps ultimately a calque of French en fait.

parole.significato: With someone's favour or blessing.
parole.testo: Possibly a calque of French en paix. Compare Spanish en paz and Italian in pace.

parole.significato: Appropriate, relevant, pertinent.
parole.testo: Calque of French à propos, c. 1658.

parole.significato: All things considered; when all is said and done; in conclusion, basically and fundamentally.
parole.testo: Calque of French en dernière analyse.

parole.significato: Fashionable.
parole.testo: Partial calque of French en vogue.

parole.significato: Unable to be hung (or sold), especially because of sexual content.
parole.testo: Literally "unhangable", from French accrocher (“to hang”).

parole.significato: Lack of action or activity or labor
parole.testo: From French inaction. Morphologically in- + action.

parole.significato: Not active, temporarily or permanently.
parole.testo: From French inactif. Piecewise doublet of unactive.

parole.significato: Not admissible.
parole.testo: From French inadmissible, from Middle French inadmissible. Morphologically in- + admissible.

parole.significato: Lack of affability or sociability; unfriendliness.
parole.testo: Compare French inaffabilité.

parole.significato: Not subject to being alienated, that is, surrendered, taken away, or transferred to another.
parole.testo: Borrowed around 1645 from French inaliénable, from in- + aliénable (“alienable”), equivalent to in- + alienable.

parole.significato: The property of being inane, of lacking material of interest or satisfaction, emptiness.
parole.testo: From French inanité, from Latin inānitās (“emptiness”), equivalent to inane + -ity.

parole.significato: The state of being inapplicable.
parole.testo: From French inapplicabilité.

parole.significato: Not apt.
parole.testo: From French inapte, from Middle French, equivalent to in- + apt.

parole.significato: The quality of being inapt.
parole.testo: From French inaptitude, probably from Renaissance Latin inaptitūdō.

parole.significato: Lack of attention, or failure to pay attention
parole.testo: From French inattention.

parole.significato: Of inauguration; as in a speech or lecture by the person being inaugurated.
parole.testo: From French inaugural, from inaugurer, from Latin augurare (“to take omens”).

parole.significato: the emission of visible light by a hot body
parole.testo: Borrowed from French incandescence. Morphologically incandesce + -ence.

parole.significato: Emitting light as a result of being heated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French incandescent, from Latin incandescens, from incandesco (“be heated, glow”), from in- (intensifying prefix) + candesco (“become white”), from candidus (“white”).

parole.significato: Of the pale pink or pale red colour of flesh; carnation.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from French incarnadin, incarnadine, from Italian incarnadino, a variant of incarnatino (“carnation; flesh colour”), from incarnato (“embodied, incarnate”) + -ino (suffix forming adjectives denoting composition, colour, or other qualities). Incarnato is derived from Ecclesia

parole.significato: Beginning; of or relating to inception.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French inceptif, from the Latin inceptīvus, from incipiō (“to begin”).

parole.significato: A call to act; encouragement to act, often in an illegal way.
parole.testo: From French incitement, from Latin incitāmentum (“incentive; incitement”), from incitō (“urge; quicken; incite”, verb). Equivalent to incite + -ment.

parole.significato: To make (someone) uncomfortable; to discomfort, to disturb, to trouble.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French incommoder (“to bother, disconcert, incommode”), from Latin incommodāre, the present active infinitive of incommodō (“to inconvenience”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + commodō (“to accommodate, adapt; to bestow, provide; to hire, lend”) (from com- (a variant of con-

parole.significato: Synonym of incommodious.
parole.testo: The adjective is a learned borrowing from French incommode (“causing discomfort; inconvenient; troublesome; undesirable, unwanted, unwelcome”), from Latin incommodus (“inconvenient; disagreeable, troublesome; unfit, unsuitable, unseasonable”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + commodus (“becoming, s

parole.significato: Of two or more things: that cannot coexist; not congruous because of differences; unable to function together due to di…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French incompatible.

parole.significato: An inability to perform; a lack of competence; ineptitude.
parole.testo: From French incompétence, equivalent to in- + competence.

parole.significato: Lacking the degree of ability and responsibility necessary to do a task successfully.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French incompétent, from Late Latin incompetentem, from Latin incompetēns, equivalent to in- + competent.

parole.significato: The time elapsed between an exposure to a pathogenic organism, a chemical or radiation, and the appearance of signs and…
parole.testo: Since 1850s, from earlier period of incubation, attested in that now obsolete sense since late 1820s, which is a calque of French période d'incubation (attested since mid-1810s), itself a calque from Latin periodus incubationis (attested since 1770s).

parole.significato: The inability to decide on a course of action, especially if two or more possibilities exist.
parole.testo: From French indécision.

parole.significato: That one cannot decline; unavoidable.
parole.testo: From French indéclinable, from Middle French, from Latin indeclinabilis. Equivalent to in- + declinable.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being independent; lack of dependence; the state of not being reliant on, or controlled by, oth…
parole.testo: From French indépendance. Analyzable as in- + de- + pend + -ence or in- + dependence.

parole.significato: The doctrine that all human actions are not so much determined by the preceding events, conditions, causes or karma as…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French indéterminisme, equivalent to in- + determinism.

parole.significato: One who believes the doctrine of indeterminism.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French indéterministe, equivalent to in- + determinist.

parole.significato: The adjustment of an economic variable (such as a salary) according to an index (such as that of inflation).
parole.testo: From French indexation.

parole.significato: A type of elaborately patterned textile produced in Europe between the 17th and 19th centuries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French indienne

parole.significato: Lack of discipline.
parole.testo: From French indiscipline, from Middle French [Term?], from Late Latin indisciplina.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being indissoluble.
parole.testo: Compare French indissolubilité.

parole.significato: The tendency for a person to act without reference to others, particularly in matters of style, fashion or mode of thou…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French individualisme, equivalent to individual + -ism.

parole.significato: Habitually lazy, procrastinating, or resistant to physical labor.
parole.testo: From French indolent or directly from Late Latin indolēns, from in- (“not”) + dolēns (“hurting”), from doleo (“to hurt”). The later sense of “living easily, slothful” perhaps developed in French.

parole.significato: Of or relating to industry, notably manufacturing.
parole.testo: From French industriel. By surface analysis, industry + -al.

parole.significato: A process of social and economic change whereby a human society is transformed from a preindustrial to an industrial st…
parole.testo: From French industrialisation. Analyzable as industrial + -ization or industrialize + -ation.

parole.significato: To develop industry; to become industrial.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French industrialiser.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being ineligible.
parole.testo: From French inéligibilité, from Middle French.

parole.significato: Not eligible; forbidden to do something.
parole.testo: From French inéligible.

parole.significato: That cannot be told; indescribable, inexpressible, unspeakable.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French inénarrable, from Latin inēnārrābilis (“indescribable”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + ēnārrābilis (“describable, explainable”). Ēnārrābilis is derived from ēnārrāre + -bilis (suffix forming adjectives indicating a capacity or worth of being acted upon); ēnārrāre is

parole.significato: A government characterized by incompetent leaders.
parole.testo: From inept, from French inepte (“feckless”) + -o- + -cracy, from Ancient Greek κράτος (krátos, “strength, power”).

parole.significato: unfair, unequal or unjust.
parole.testo: From French inéquitable. Morphologically in- + equitable.

parole.significato: Unable to move or act; inanimate.
parole.testo: From French inerte, from Latin iners (“inactive, inert”).

parole.significato: Imperfectly conforming; exceeding or falling short in some respect.
parole.testo: From French inexact.

parole.significato: A lack of exactness; something inexact or imprecise
parole.testo: From French inexactitude, equivalent to in- + exactitude.

parole.significato: A lack of experience.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French inexpérience, from Late Latin inexperientia.

parole.significato: The murder of an infant.
parole.testo: From French infanticide, from Latin īnfanticīdium. By surface analysis, infant + -i- + -cide.

parole.significato: The murderer of a child: a person who has committed infanticide.
parole.testo: From French infanticide, from Latin īnfanticīda. By surface analysis, infant + -i- + -cide.

parole.significato: Infantile; childish.
parole.testo: From French infantin, variant of enfantin.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being inflexible, or not capable of being bent or changed; unyielding stiffness
parole.testo: From French inflexibilité, from Old French inflectibilité. Equivalent to in- + flexibility or inflexible + -ity.

parole.significato: The process of becoming based on information and information technology.
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from French informatisation. By surface analysis, information + -isation or informatise + -ation.

parole.significato: An underlying base or foundation for a building, organization, or system.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French infrastructure, equivalent to infra- + structure.

parole.significato: An innocent, unsophisticated, naive, wholesome boy or young man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ingénu (“guileless”), especially as used by Voltaire in L'Ingénu, from Latin ingenuus (“ingenuous”). Doublet of ingenuous.

parole.significato: To dye with a fast or lasting colour.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English engreynen, from the French phrase en grain; reinforced by the phrase (dyed) in grain. See grain.

parole.significato: Serving to initiate.
parole.testo: From French initiative, from Medieval Latin *initiativus (“serving to initiate”), from Late Latin initiare (“to begin, to initiate”), from Latin initium (“beginning”), from ineo (“enter, begin”). By surface analysis, initiate + -ive.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or being an injection: such that each element of the image (or range) is associated with at most one e…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French injectif.

parole.significato: Lack of observation.
parole.testo: Compare French inobservation.

parole.significato: Stainless steel.
parole.testo: From French inox. By surface analysis, a clipping of inoxidable or of inoxidizable.

parole.significato: Any of various substances used to kill insects.
parole.testo: From French insecticide, as insect + -icide.

parole.significato: Insect-eating animal or plant.
parole.testo: From French insectivore. In the zoological sense, coined by English philosopher and historian of science William Whewell in 1840 as an adaptation of Cuvier's coinage, French insectivore. The French terms reflect scientific New Latin origins. By surface analysis, insect + -i- + -vore.

parole.significato: The scientific study of insects.
parole.testo: From French insectologie; equivalent to insect + -ology. Compare Latin īnsectum and īnsecta.

parole.significato: Unappetizingly flavorless.
parole.testo: From French insipide, from Latin īnsipidus (“tasteless”), from in- (“not”) + sapidus (“savory”). In some senses, perhaps influenced by insipient (“unwise, foolish, stupid”).

parole.significato: The incident radiant energy emitted by the sun which reaches a unit area over a period of time, typically measured over…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French insolation, from Latin insolatio (“a setting or placing in the sun”).

parole.significato: Carelessness, heedlessness, indifference, or casual unconcern.
parole.testo: From French insouciance, from in- (“not”) + souciant (“worrying”).

parole.significato: Casually unconcerned; carefree, indifferent, nonchalant.
parole.testo: From French insouciant, from in- (“not”, prefix) + souciant (“worrying”), 1828.

parole.significato: An organization founded to promote a cause
parole.testo: From French institut, from Middle French, from Latin īnstitūtum.

parole.significato: Rebellious or defiant to authority; contumacious.
parole.testo: From in- + subordinate, on model of French insubordonné.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being insubordinate; disobedience to lawful authority; specifically, an employee's failure or r…
parole.testo: From in- + subordination, on the model of French insubordination.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being intangible; intangibleness.
parole.testo: Compare French intangibilité.

parole.significato: Able to be integrated.
parole.testo: From French intégrable, equivalent to integr(ate) + -able.

parole.significato: The office or employment of an intendant.
parole.testo: From intendant + -cy. Compare French intendance.

parole.significato: The administrator of an opera house or theater.
parole.testo: Originally and usually from French intendant, but translating Spanish or Chinese equivalents in some contexts.

parole.significato: Any molecule that intercalates, or is inserted, between two others
parole.testo: Borrowed from French intercalant, from Latin intercalantem, accusative of intercalans.

parole.significato: Interceding: Passing between; mediating
parole.testo: Probably by way of French intercedent (adjective), which seems to be more commonly attested than this English adjective. Ultimately from Latin intercedens, present participle of intercedere, and possibly borrowed twice by English, with the later borrowing being a learned borrowing.

parole.significato: A grouping of communes or municipalities that share some services.
parole.testo: Calque of French intercommunalité; intercommunal + -ity

parole.significato: The act of interdicting or something interdicted.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from French interdiction, itself a borrowing from Latin interdictiō.

parole.significato: An intertie.
parole.testo: Compare French entre-deux, literally "between two".

parole.significato: Mutual liaison between multiple entities.
parole.testo: Possibly borrowed from French interliaison, equivalent to inter- + liaison.

parole.significato: A decree of a court.
parole.testo: From French interlocutoire, from Latin interlocūtōrium.

parole.significato: A female interlocutor
parole.testo: Borrowed from French interlocutrice.

parole.significato: A short musical dramatic piece, of a light, pleasing, and sometimes burlesque character.
parole.testo: From French intermède, from Latin inter (“between”) + medius (“middle”). Compare Italian intermedio. Doublet of intermezzo.

parole.significato: That intermediates.
parole.testo: From French intermédiaire, adjusted to simulate a borrowing from Medieval Latin *intermediārius.

parole.significato: A person who is interned, forcibly or voluntarily.
parole.testo: From French interner, from interne (“inner, internal”), from Latin internus (“within, internal”), compare Etymology 2.

parole.significato: A student or recent graduate who works in order to gain experience in their chosen field.
parole.testo: From French interne (“inner, internal”), from Latin internus (“within, internal”), from inter (“between”); compare Etymology 1.

parole.significato: An abrupt change in elements, with continuation of the first idea.
parole.testo: From French interpolation, from Latin interpolatio. Morphologically interpolate + -ion.

parole.significato: An interregnum.
parole.testo: Compare French interrègne.

parole.significato: The nonstandard punctuation mark ⟨‽⟩ (a combination of ⟨?⟩ and ⟨!⟩), which may be used at the end of a sentence to expr…
parole.testo: A blend of French (point d')interrogation (“question mark”) or the equivalent term in another Romance language + bang (“exclamation mark, exclamation point”), coined in a 1962 article in the journal TYPEtalks by American advertising executive Martin Kiehra Speckter (1915–1988), who invented the symb

parole.significato: The idea that a given text is a response to what has already been written, be it explicit or implicit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French intertextualité.

parole.significato: The political practice of intervening in a sovereign state's affairs.
parole.testo: From French interventionnisme. By surface analysis, intervention + -ism.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to interventionism, or an advocate thereof.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French interventionniste, equivalent to intervention + -ist.

parole.significato: Serving to intervene or interpose; intervening.
parole.testo: From intervene + -ive cognate with French interventive.

parole.significato: The swapping of positions within a sequence; transposition or permutation.
parole.testo: From French interversion.

parole.significato: The act of making timid or fearful or of deterring by threats; the state of being intimidated.
parole.testo: From intimidate + -ion. Compare French intimidation; perhaps modeled on it.

parole.significato: To entitle; to give a title to.
parole.testo: Compare French intituler. See entitle.

parole.significato: The state of being intolerant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French intolérance, itself from in- (“not”) + tolérance or borrowed from Latin intolerantia (“insolence, insufferableness; (very rare) intolerance”). By surface analysis, in- + tolerance.

parole.significato: The rise and fall of the voice in speaking.
parole.testo: From French intonation, from Medieval Latin intonatio, from intonō + -tiō.

parole.significato: The inner curve of an arch or vault.
parole.testo: From French, from Latin intra (“within”) + French dos (“back”) (from Latin dostrum).

parole.significato: Unwillingness to change one's views or to agree.
parole.testo: From French intransigeance, noun form of intransigeant, borrowed from Spanish intransigente at the end of the nineteenth century. Morphologically, from in- + transiger + -ant, literally "uncompromising".

parole.significato: Unwilling to compromise or moderate a position; unreasonable; stubborn.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French intransigeant, from Spanish intransigente, from Latin in- (“un-, not”) + trānsigēns, present participle of trānsigō (“to come to an understanding”), from trāns (“across”) + agō (“to do”).

parole.significato: Fearless; bold; brave.
parole.testo: From French intrépide, from Latin intrepidus, from in- (“not”) + trepidus (“anxious, nervous”).

parole.significato: Entanglement or intricacy
parole.testo: Borrowed from French intrication.

parole.significato: A female intriguer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French intrigante.

parole.significato: A complicated or clandestine plot or scheme intended to affect some purpose by secret artifice; conspiracy; stratagem;…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French intrigue, from Italian intricare, from Latin intrīcō (“to entangle, perplex, embarrass”). Doublet of intricate.

parole.significato: The invagination of one portion of a tubular anatomical structure (especially intestines or blood vessels) within the n…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French intussusception, or directly from Latin intussusceptiō, from intus (“within”) + susceptiō (“susception”).

parole.significato: Conspicuous bract, bract pair or ring of bracts at the base of an inflorescence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French involucre, from Latin involūcrum (“wrapper”). Doublet of involucrum.

parole.significato: The state of being invulnerable.
parole.testo: From French invulnérabilité.

parole.significato: Synonym of iodine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French iode.

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol: I) with an atomic number of 53; one of the halogens.
parole.testo: From French iode + -ine, from Ancient Greek ἰοειδής (ioeidḗs, “violet”). Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1814.

parole.significato: One of the Native Americans formerly occupying the region now included in the state of Iowa.
parole.testo: From French Aiouez/Ayoés, an early transliteration of the name for the Iowa tribe, from Dakota ayúxba (“the sleepy ones”).

parole.significato: Having irises of a specified colour or kind.
parole.testo: From iris + -ed; as a synonym of iridescent and irisated, perhaps a calque of French irisé.

parole.significato: Synonym of Iroquois
parole.testo: From French Iroquois.

parole.significato: Lack of reflection or consideration.
parole.testo: From French irréflexion.

parole.significato: The state of being irreligious; irreligious sentiment or thought.
parole.testo: From French irréligion, from Latin irreligiō. By surface analysis, ir- + religion.

parole.significato: Free from blame, not open to reproach or criticism; blameless.
parole.testo: First attested in 1630. Borrowed from French irréprochable, from Middle French inreprochable. See also ir- + reproachable.

parole.significato: Undecided or unsure how to act.
parole.testo: First attested in 1580. Borrowed from French irrésolu or composed from ir- + resolute.

parole.significato: Capable of being irritated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French irritable, from Latin irritabilis.

parole.significato: Causing irritation or inflammation.
parole.testo: From French irritant, equivalent to irritate + -ant.

parole.significato: The religion of Muslims; Islam.
parole.testo: Appearing in English in the 1740s, from French islamisme (1720s), paralleling the French christianisme and judaïsme. By surface analysis, Islam + -ism.

parole.significato: Distinctive regions of tissue in the pancreas, which contain its endocrine cells.
parole.testo: Translating French îlots de Langerhans; named after Paul Langerhans, the German anatomist who discovered these regions in the pancreas.

parole.significato: isocheimal
parole.testo: From French isochimène, from iso- + Ancient Greek χειμαίνω (kheimaínō, “to be wintry”), from χεῖμα (kheîma, “winter”).

parole.significato: To set apart or cut off from others.
parole.testo: Back-formation from isolated, from French isolé, from Italian isolato, from Latin īnsulātus (whence also insulate), see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3).

parole.significato: Placed or standing apart or alone; in isolation.
parole.testo: A rendering into English of French isolé.

parole.significato: The state of being isolated, detached, or separated; the state of being away from other people.
parole.testo: First attested in 1800. From French isolation, from isolé, placed on an island (thus away from other people). Equivalent to isolate + -ion.

parole.significato: An isotherm connecting points on a map with equal mean summer temperature.
parole.testo: From French isothère, from iso- + Ancient Greek θέρος (théros, “summer”).

parole.significato: A line on a graph or chart, such as a weather map, along which all the points have the same temperature.
parole.testo: From the French isotherme (“of equal temperature”, adjective), itself from Ancient Greek ἴσος (ísos, “equal”) + θέρμη (thérmē, “warmth”). By surface analysis, iso- + -therm.

parole.significato: an extinct lynx, of species †Lynx issiodorensis, that inhabited Europe during the Pleistocene epoch.
parole.testo: From French lynx d'Issoire, named after the town of Issoire.

parole.significato: It is understood without being said (but will be or was said anyway).
parole.testo: Calque of French ça va sans dire.

parole.significato: It is absurd or laughable.
parole.testo: Calque of French c'est à rire

parole.significato: Of a procedure that involves repetition of steps (iteration) to achieve the desired outcome; in computing this may invo…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French itératif.

parole.significato: The (often chaotic) movement of electrons through a material
parole.testo: From French itinérance. By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ance.

parole.significato: An inducted abortion (in the context of a country like France).
parole.testo: From languages in which "voluntary interruption of pregnancy" has the initials IVG, like French interruption volontaire de grossesse, Italian interruzione volontaria di gravidanza, Portuguese interrupção voluntária da gravidez, etc.

parole.significato: Ivorian
parole.testo: From French Ivoirien, ivoirien.

parole.significato: A sheltered, overly-academic existence or perspective, implying a disconnection or lack of awareness of reality or prac…
parole.testo: Calque of French tour d'ivoire, based on a biblical phrase, coined by Charles Augustin Sainte-Beuve to compare the poet Alfred de Vigny (more isolated) with Victor Hugo (more socially engaged). First attested in English in a translation of Laughter by French philosopher Henri Bergson (1911). The ter

parole.significato: A Pyrenean chamois (Rupicapra pyrenaica).
parole.testo: From French isard; further derivation uncertain.

parole.significato: An accusation, especially one made publicly.
parole.testo: Borrowing from French J'Accuse ("I accuse"), the title of an 1898 open letter from writer Emile Zola to the president of France during the Dreyfus Affair.

parole.significato: Spoken by a player before adjusting a piece on the chessboard, to indicate that one is not making a move in the game.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French j'adoube (“I adjust”), from je (“I”) + adouber (“to adjust”).

parole.significato: A person dressed up as a devil-like character, in Caribbean carnivals, who carries a whip used for hitting other devils.
parole.testo: From a patois variety, originally from French diable (“devil”).

parole.significato: A cascading or ornamental frill down the front of a blouse, shirt, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jabot.

parole.significato: Any of certain wild canids of the genera Lupulella and Canis, native to the tropical Old World and smaller than a wolf.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chacal, chacale, checale, schakal, ciacale, from Turkish çakal, from Ottoman Turkish چقال (çakâl), from Classical Persian شغال (šaġāl), borrowed from Sanskrit शृगाल (śṛgāla, “jackal”), the alternative form of सृगाल (sṛgāla).

parole.significato: Synonym of Jacobin, especially as a feminine form.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Jacobine.

parole.significato: The principles of the Jacobins; especially the violent opposition to legitimate government.
parole.testo: From Jacobin + -ism, compare French jacobinisme.

parole.significato: A revolt organized by peasants, typically violent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jacquerie, from Jacquerie (derogatory nickname for peasants, literally “James”) + -erie. First attested in the early 1500s. In reference to the Jacquerie uprising of 1358 during the Hundred Years' War.

parole.significato: A game resembling backgammon.
parole.testo: French jacquet

parole.significato: Boasting; bragging; showing off.
parole.testo: From French jactance.

parole.significato: A semiprecious stone, either nephrite or jadeite, generally green or white in color, often used for carving figurines.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French le jade, rebracketing of earlier l'éjade (“jade”), from Spanish piedra de ijada (“flank stone”), via Vulgar Latin *iliata from Latin ilia (“flank”). (Jade was thought to cure pains in the side.)

parole.significato: A component in a ventilation system.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jalousie. Doublet of jealousy.

parole.significato: A sense of unfamiliarity with, or of never having experienced or seen before, something that should be familiar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jamais (“never”) + vu (“seen”).

parole.significato: A leg, of an animal or person.
parole.testo: From Middle English jambe, jaumbe, French jambe. Doublet of gam, gamb, gamba, and jamb.

parole.significato: A foot rest.
parole.testo: French?

parole.significato: A square puff pastry containing ham and cheese.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jambon (“ham”). Doublet of gammon and jamon.

parole.significato: A kind of almond meringue dessert.
parole.testo: From French japonaise (literally “Japanese”).

parole.significato: Art objects made in the Japanese style.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French japonaiserie.

parole.significato: An influence of Japanese art and culture on European art and design.
parole.testo: From French japonisme.

parole.significato: An influence of Japanese art and culture on European art and design.
parole.testo: From French japonisme.

parole.significato: An influence of Japanese art and culture on European art and design.
parole.testo: From French japonisme.

parole.significato: The inclusions and fissures within an emerald.
parole.testo: From French jardin (“garden”), from the mossy appearance. Doublet of garden.

parole.significato: An ornamental pot for the display of live or cut flowers; a planter; a plantstand or flowerpot, especially one made of…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jardinière. Doublet of giardiniera.

parole.significato: A variety of pear.
parole.testo: From French jargonelle, diminutive of jargon.

parole.significato: A variety of zircon.
parole.testo: From French jargon, from Italian giargone, from Arabic زَرْقُون (zarqūn). Doublet of zircon.

parole.significato: Any of several plants, of the genus Jasminum, mostly native to Asia, having fragrant white or yellow flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jasmin, from Arabic يَاسَمِين (yāsamīn).

parole.significato: Veined or clouded like imitation jasper.
parole.testo: From French jaspé, past participle of jasper (“to colour motley, so as to imitate jasper”), from jaspe (“jasper”), from Latin iaspis, from Ancient Greek ἴασπις (íaspis).

parole.significato: Airy; showy; finical.
parole.testo: Formerly spelt janty, from French gentil. See gentle, and compare genty. Doublet of genteel, gentile, and gentle.

parole.significato: A dance popular in France in the early 20th century.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French java.

parole.significato: A type of slang used in the French language, where an extra syllable -av- or -va is placed inside a word as an infix.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French javanais.

parole.significato: sodium hypochlorite, the earliest chemical bleach.
parole.testo: Calque of French eau de Javel, after the village (now Parisian neighbourhood) where it was produced.

parole.significato: An indefinable quality that makes something distinctive or attractive.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French je ne sais quoi (literally “I don't know what”).

parole.significato: A hill, a mountain (especially in the Middle East or North Africa).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French djebel, from Arabic جَبَل (jabal, “mountain”).

parole.significato: A long speech or prose work that bitterly laments the state of society and its morals, and often contains a prophecy of…
parole.testo: From French jérémiade, from Jérémie, from Latin Ieremias, from Hebrew ירמיה (yirm'yá, “Jeremiah”). Named after biblical prophet Jeremiah, who lamented the moral state of Judah and predicted her downfall.

parole.significato: A collimated stream, spurt or flow of liquid or gas from a pressurized container, an engine, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jet (“spurt”, literally “a throw”), from Old French get, giet, from Vulgar Latin *iectus, *jectus, from Latin iactus (“a throwing, a throw”), from iacere (“to throw”). See abject, ejaculate, gist, jess, jut. Cognate with Spanish echar.

parole.significato: an operation that takes a differentiable function f and produces a polynomial, the Taylor polynomial (truncated Taylor…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jet.

parole.significato: A stream of water spouting from a fountain or pipe (especially from one arranged to throw water upward), used as an orn…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French jet d'eau (literally “jet of water”).

parole.significato: A leap from one foot to the other in which one leg appears to be "thrown" in the direction of the movement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jeté.

parole.significato: A counter or token.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jeton.

parole.significato: A witticism; a witty comment or composition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jeu d'esprit (“game of the spirit”).

parole.significato: A precursor of lawn tennis, originally played by hitting the ball with the palm of the hand instead of with a racquet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jeu de paume (“game of the palm”).

parole.significato: A construction that defines an equivalence relation on the set of skew standard Young tableaux.
parole.testo: From French jeu de taquin (“15 puzzle”, literally “teasing game”).

parole.significato: actor who plays young hero/lover roles
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French jeune premier; first used in the early 1800s.

parole.significato: Young people who are dazzlingly rich, elegant, etc.; the youthful part of fashionable society.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jeunesse dorée (“gilded youth”).

parole.significato: A brave, visionary, or martial woman.
parole.testo: Appellativisation of Joan of Arc (Jeanne d'Arc), the name of a 15th century French folk heroine revered as a martyr. parole.significato: A Mona Lisa.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French La/la Joconde, itself a calque of Italian la Gioconda using Middle French joconde, feminine of jocond, from Latin iūcundus. Doublet of Gioconda.

parole.significato: A light almond sponge cake.
parole.testo: Thought to be named after the Mona Lisa (French La Joconde).

parole.significato: Enjoyment of living; happiness, ebullience, zest for life.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French joie de vivre (literally “joy of living”).

parole.significato: An itinerant entertainer in medieval England and France; roles included song, music, acrobatics etc.; a troubadour.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jongleur. Doublet of juggler.

parole.significato: A fragrant bulb flower (Narcissus jonquilla), a species of daffodil.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jonquille, itself a borrowing from Spanish junquillo. Possible doublet of junket.

parole.significato: A series of presentations and/or performances, discussions or similar events that happen on a fixed day every month (or…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jour fixe (literally “fixed day”).

parole.significato: The amount of land that can be worked in a day.
parole.testo: From French journal. Doublet of diurnal and the journal from Middle English.

parole.significato: The aggregating, writing, editing, and presenting of news or news articles for widespread distribution, typically in el…
parole.testo: From French journalisme (beginning of 19th century). By surface analysis, journal + -ism.

parole.significato: The total time spent melting and working one piece.
parole.testo: Reborrowing from French journée (day's activities), originally an unadapted borrowing from French journée, from Old French jornee, from Vulgar Latin *diurnāta.

parole.significato: The state of being jovial; jollity or conviviality.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jovialité.

parole.significato: Under the astrological influence of the planet Jupiter.
parole.testo: From jovial + -ly (suffix forming adverbs from adjectives). Jovial is borrowed from French jovial (“jolly, jovial”), from Italian gioviale (“jolly, jovial; (obsolete) born under the influence of the planet Jupiter”), from Latin ioviālis (“relating to the Roman god Jupiter”), from Iuppiter, Iovis (“t

parole.significato: A female prostitute.
parole.testo: Calque of French fille de joie.

parole.significato: The houseleek.
parole.testo: From the French joubarbe, jousbarbe, from the Latin Iovis barba (“Jove's beard”).

parole.significato: Synonym of rood screen.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jubé.

parole.significato: A public officer authorized to hear and decide cases in a court of law.
parole.testo: As a European official, a calque of French huissier de justice (“court usher”) employing officer because of usher's lack of legal associations in English.

parole.significato: Having, characterized by, or done with good judgment or sound thinking.
parole.testo: From French judicieux, ultimately derived from Latin iudico. Related to judge, judicial.

parole.significato: A fetish or charm believed by West Africans to have magical or supernatural powers.
parole.testo: From a West African language, probably originally from French joujou.

parole.significato: A garnish of vegetables cut into long, thin strips.
parole.testo: From French julienne (1722), from given name Jules or Julien, presumably from an otherwise unknown chef of that name. Originally used in potage julienne (“Julienne potage, soup in the manner of Jules/Julien”), meaning “soup made from thin slices”; this sense is now known as chiffonade.

parole.significato: The fabled offspring of a bull and a mare.
parole.testo: Derived from French jument (“mare”).

parole.significato: Twin; paired; said of various objects made or formed in pairs, such as a binocular opera glass, a pair of gimmal rings,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jumelle.

parole.significato: A jupon with a very short skirt.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jupette.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the second period of the Mesozoic era, a time still dominated by dinosaurs.

parole.significato: The juices given off as meat is cooked.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French jus (“juice”). Doublet of juice and ukha.

parole.significato: One who believes in following something through to the very end.

parole.significato: An extremist; a hardliner.

parole.significato: A knee-length coat worn by men in the 17th and 18th centuries.

parole.significato: To place side by side, especially for contrast or comparison.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French juxtaposer, corresponding to juxta- + pose, derived from Latin iuxtā (“near, next to”) + pōnō (“place”).

parole.significato: The nearness of objects with little or no delimiter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French juxtaposition, from Latin iuxtā (“near”) (from Latin iungō (“to join”)) + French position (“position”) (from Latin pōnō (“to place”)).

parole.significato: A type of thin buckwheat pancake in Breton cuisine.

parole.significato: An indigenous Melanesian inhabitant of New Caledonia.

parole.significato: A hard raised growth of scar tissue at the site of an injury.

parole.significato: A gambling game, a variety of lotto, played with balls or knobs, numbered, and cards also numbered.

parole.significato: A cap with a flat circular top and a visor, particularly associated with French uniforms.
parole.testo: From French képi, from Switzerland German Käppi, diminutive of Kappe, from Middle High German kappe, from Old High German kappa, from Latin cappa. Akin to English cap.

parole.significato: Inflammation of the cornea.

parole.significato: Any part of a letter which extends into the space used by another letter.

parole.significato: The adjustment of the horizontal space between selected pairs of glyphs in a typeface.
parole.testo: From kern (“part of a letter which extends into the space used by another letter”) + -ing, from French carne (“corner”).

parole.testo: Calque of French logique du chaudron. parole.significato: The title of the hereditary monarch of Egypt from 1805–1914, nominally ruling as a viceroy of the Sultan of Turkey.
parole.testo: From French khédive, from Ottoman Turkish خدیو (ḫediv, ḫıdiv), from Persian خدیو (xadêw, xedêw, “lord, master, king”), from Bactrian χοαδηο (khoadēo, “lord”).

parole.significato: The total distance travelled, in kilometres.
parole.testo: From French kilométrage. By surface analysis, kilometre + -age.

parole.significato: An SI unit of length equal to 10³ metres. Symbol: km
parole.testo: From French kilomètre, from Ancient Greek χίλιοι (khílioi, “thousand”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”); equivalent to kilo- + metre.

parole.significato: The branch of mechanics concerned with objects in motion, but not with the forces involved.
parole.testo: French cinématique, from Ancient Greek κίνημα (kínēma, “motion”) + -ics.

parole.significato: A decorative cake distributed among friends or visitors on Epiphany. In many traditions it contains a pea, a trinket or…
parole.testo: Probably a calque of French galette des rois (literally “galette of the kings”), meaning the three Magi who visited the baby Jesus at Epiphany.

parole.testo: From French quincajou, from an Algonquian word, probably originally meaning ‘wolverine’ (compare Algonquin Kwingwaage, Ojibwe gwiingwa'aage (“wolverine”)), which was later transferred to the South American animal. Related to carcajou.

parole.significato: Kinshasan

parole.significato: A small enclosed structure, often freestanding, open on one side or with a window, used as a booth to sell newspapers,…

parole.significato: Those sailing together on a ship, both crew and passengers.
parole.testo: An aphetic form of French équipage.

parole.significato: A cocktail made with a measure of crème de cassis topped up with white wine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French kir, named after Félix Kir, mayor of Dijon.

parole.significato: A clear brandy made from black cherries: kirschwasser.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French kirsch, from German Kirschwasser (“cherry water”). Doublet of cerise and cherry.

parole.significato: A kitchen staff that operates under the brigade system.

parole.significato: A footpad, thief, or sharper.

parole.testo: From French Akoroa (also Courouais), most likely from a Native American word.

parole.significato: A fermented drink made from mare's milk, common among peoples of the Central Asian steppes.
parole.testo: Via French koumis, German Kumiss, from Russian кумы́с (kumýs), borrowed from a Turkic source. Compare Tatar кымыз (qımız), Kazakh қымыз (qımız), Kyrgyz кымыз (kımız), Southern Altai кымыс (kïmïs), Turkish kımız, Azerbaijani qımız, Northern Altai кымыс (kïmïs), etc.

parole.significato: a fortified traditional village in North Africa.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ksar, from a Maghrebi form of Arabic قَصْر (qaṣr). Doublet of qasr and castrum

parole.significato: A dance rhythm from the Congo (DRC), where the hips move back and forth while the hands move to follow the hips.
parole.testo: Perhaps from the French quoi ça? (“what is it?”).

parole.significato: A long rigmarole.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French kyrielle.

parole.testo: Borrowed from French esprit de l’escalier (literally “mind of the staircase”), with the definite article le (“the”) at the beginning of the term. parole.significato: Used to signify one's exercise of power in a dictatiorial, repressive and/or charismatic manner.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French l'état, c'est moi (“I am the state”), which apocryphally attributed to Louis XIV per an anecdote representing the tyranny of France before the French Revolution.

parole.significato: Prefixed to the name of a woman, with ironic effect (as though an opera prima donna).
parole.testo: From French la, Italian la.

parole.significato: Characteristic of lac, such as in laccic acid.

parole.significato: A type of lace consisting of patterns darned on to net.

parole.significato: The disaccharide sugar of milk and dairy products, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, a product of glucose and galactose used as a food and in…

parole.significato: A lacunar stroke or infarct.

parole.significato: Dated spelling of lagoon.

parole.significato: A section of verse concerning a single theme; tirade.

parole.significato: A monastery for lamas.

parole.testo: Borrowed from French lambdoïde, from the New Latin lambdoīdēs, from the Ancient Greek λαβδοειδής (labdoeidḗs).

parole.significato: A scarf or other piece of material used as a covering for a helmet.

parole.significato: A small oil lamp.

parole.significato: A fabric made from gold or silver threads and silk, wool or cotton.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French lamé.

parole.significato: A cavalry soldier armed with a lance weapon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French lancier (“lancer”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Languedoc, an area and historical region of France.

parole.significato: Any of a class of German mercenaries of the 15th and 16th centuries, most of whom were pikemen and foot soldiers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French lansquenet, from German Landsknecht, from Lands (“of the land”) + Knecht (“servant”). Doublet of Landsknecht.

parole.significato: A meaningless chant or refrain.

parole.significato: An artistic movement associated with the slogan "art for art's sake".

parole.testo: Borrowed from French lassitude, from Latin lassitūdō (“faintness, weariness”), from lassus (“faint, weary”), perhaps for *ladtus, and thus akin to English late.
