parole.significato: A member of the Congregation of the Priests of the Mission founded by St Vincent de Paul.

parole.significato: the
parole.testo: Borrowed from French le (“the”). Popularized especially by the expression le sigh.

parole.significato: A sigh of longing or disappointment.
parole.testo: Used by Pepé Le Pew, stereotypically French skunk character in Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies cartoons; combination of French le (“the”) and English sigh.

parole.significato: To raise; to levy.

parole.significato: The principal phospholipid in animals; it is particularly abundant in egg yolks, and is extracted commercially from soy…

parole.significato: legendary in act or function.

parole.significato: A person who is neither a citizen nor colonial/imperial subject of the state whose military they join.

parole.significato: An iguana.

parole.significato: The fruit or seed of leguminous plants (as peas or beans) used for food.

parole.significato: Any of a group of globulins, resembling casein, found mostly in legumes and grains.

parole.significato: the state of being luminous, or a luminous object; brilliance or radiance
parole.testo: Borrowed from French luminosité or else a native formation from luminous + -ity.

parole.significato: A concave figure formed by the intersection of the arcs of two circles on a plane, or on a sphere the intersection betw…
parole.testo: From French lune, from Latin luna.

parole.significato: A charge formed by four crescents in cross with their horns pointing inwards.
parole.testo: From French lunel, a heraldic term based on lune (“moon”). Compare Spanish lunel, Italian lunello.

parole.significato: A small opening in a vaulted roof of a circular or crescent shape.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French lunette, diminutive of lune (“moon”).

parole.significato: A sudden forward movement, especially with a sword.
parole.testo: From French allonge, from Old French alonge, from alongier, from Vulgar Latin *allongare, from ad + Late Latin longare, from Latin longus. Doublet of allonge.

parole.significato: Anything crescent-shaped; a crescent-shaped part or mark; a lunula or lune.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French lunule, from Latin lūnula, diminutive of lūna (“moon”). By surface analysis, luna + -ule.

parole.significato: A sudden or unsteady movement.
parole.testo: Originally a nautical term, found in lee-larches (“the sudden and violent rolls of a ship to the leeward in high seas”), of unknown origin. Possibly the same as lurch (“to move stealthily, evade by stooping”) (see below), or from French lâcher (“to let go”).

parole.significato: A glossy silk fabric; lutestring.
parole.testo: From French lustrine, Italian lustrino, from lustrare (“to polish”), Latin lustrare. See luster and compare lutestring.

parole.significato: A plain, stout, lustrous silk, used for ladies' dresses and for ribbon.
parole.testo: Corrupted form of French lustring, probably influenced by lute.

parole.significato: The leatherback (turtle).
parole.testo: French

parole.significato: The craft of making stringed musical instruments.
parole.testo: From French lutherie (“manufacture of stringed instruments”). Doublet of luthiery.

parole.significato: A dormer-window.
parole.testo: From French lucarne (“a dormer, dormer window, garret window”), Latin lucerna (“lamp”), from lucere (“to be light or clear”), from lux (“light”).

parole.significato: A person who, or a business which, makes or repairs stringed wooden musical instruments, such as lutes, violins, and gu…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French luthier, from luth (“lute”).

parole.significato: Luxury.
parole.testo: From French luxe, from Latin luxus. Cognate with English lock.

parole.significato: Synonym of Luxembourgish.
parole.testo: From French luxembourgeois and Luxembourgeois.

parole.significato: lycopodium powder (an inflammable yellow powder found in species of lycopodium, or club moss).
parole.testo: From French lycopode.

parole.significato: A public secondary school in France.
parole.testo: From French lycée. Doublet of lyceum.

parole.significato: Pure water.
parole.testo: Borrowing from French lymphe and/or Latin lympha (“clear water”), from Ancient Greek νῠ́μφη (nŭ́mphē, “bride; spring water”). Doublet of nymph.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Lyon.
parole.testo: From French lyonnais. By surface analysis, Lyon + -ese.

parole.significato: Cooked with onions, especially caramelized onions.
parole.testo: From French lyonnaise (“in the manner of Lyon”).

parole.significato: a lyophilic substance
parole.testo: From lyo- + -phile, c. 1900, US, perhaps from French lyophile (“lyophilic”).

parole.significato: A lyophobic substance.
parole.testo: From lyo- + -phobe, first use appears c. 1900 in the US, perhaps from French lyophobe (“lyophobic”).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to a type of poetry (such as a sonnet or ode) that expresses subjective thoughts and feelings, often in…
parole.testo: From French lyrique, or its source, Latin lyricus, from Ancient Greek λυρικός (lurikós), from λύρα (lúra, “lyre”). Its English equivalent would be lyre + -ic. parole.significato: The crime of violating majesty, an offense against the dignity of a reigning sovereign or against a state.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French lèse-majesté, from Latin laesa maiestās (“injured majesty”).

parole.significato: Syncopic form of monsieur.
parole.testo: From French m'sieur.

parole.significato: Representing or personifying death.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French macabre, whose etymology is uncertain. Possibly from the term danse macabre, most commonly believed to be from corruption of the biblical name Maccabees; compare Latin Chorea Machabaeorum. parole.significato: Any of several species of lemur, including the white-headed lemur, ruffed lemur, and ring-tailed lemur.
parole.testo: From French mococo, probably ultimately from Malagasy maka, maki (“lemur”).

parole.significato: Any of a group of Old World monkeys of the genus Macaca.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French macaque, from Portuguese macaco, of uncertain origin (see macaco for more). Doublet of macaco.

parole.significato: Any of various confections made with almond and egg white, traditionally made in France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French macaron. Doublet of macaroon.

parole.significato: The step in making macarons where the wet and dry ingredients are carefully folded together.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French macaronage.

parole.significato: A macaroon.
parole.testo: From French macaron. Doublet of macaron.

parole.significato: A mixture of diced vegetables or fruit served as a salad.
parole.testo: From French Macédoine (“Macedonia”). Doublet of Macedonia.

parole.significato: A machicolation.
parole.testo: French mâchicoulis.

parole.significato: A constructor of machines and engines; someone knowledgeable about machines.
parole.testo: From French machiniste, from machine (“machine, mechanical device”), from Latin māchina, from Ancient Greek μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “machine”).

parole.significato: A dry red or white burgundy wine produced around Mâcon or extremely similar to such wines.
parole.testo: An anglicized form of French Mâcon, from earlier Mascon and Medieval Latin Masconis, a syncopated form of Madasconis and Matisco, probably from Gaulish matus (“bear”) and a suffix equivalent to -iscus (“-ish: forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: A type of oar blade with an elliptical shape which is squared off at the end, with a ridgeline running down the centre…

parole.significato: A form of decorative textile made by knotting and weaving.
parole.testo: 1865, borrowed from French macramé, from Italian macramè, from Ottoman Turkish مقرمه (makrame), from Arabic مِقْرَمَة (miqrama, “ornamental fringe, embroidered veil”), from مِقْرَم (miqram, “bedspread”), from قَرَمَ (qarama, “to gnaw”), from Proto-Semitic *q-r-m.

parole.significato: large
parole.testo: From French, from Latin, from Ancient Greek μακρο- (makro-), combinging form of μακρός (makrós, “long”). By surface analysis, macr- + -o-.

parole.significato: A type of dish containing a mixture of many types of fruits, or many types of vegetables.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French macédoine.

parole.significato: A French type of small gateau or sponge cake, often shaped like an elongated scallop shell.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French madeleine, from earlier gâteau à la Madeleine, after the given name Madeleine (“Magdalene”), of uncertain reference: attributed in some sources to a 19th-century pastry cook Madeleine Paulmier, whose existence is now considered dubious. In sense 2, used with reference

parole.significato: A courtesy title for an unmarried woman in France or a French-speaking country.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French mademoiselle.

parole.significato: To oxidize.
parole.testo: From French madériser, from Madeira, as the wines are oxidized.

parole.significato: A large fish pound used for the capture of tuna in the Mediterranean, now a forbidden practice in places.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French madrague.

parole.significato: A coral of the genus Madrepora or of the order Madreporaria.
parole.testo: From French madrépore, from Italian madrepora (from madre (“mother”)), from Latin mater + poro (“pore”), from Latin porus.

parole.significato: A thick plank, used for several mechanical purposes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French madrier (“thick plank”).

parole.significato: Reminiscent of a madrigal.
parole.testo: From French madrigalesque.

parole.significato: A type of consommé flavored with tomatoes and served either as a warm broth or chilled and jellied.
parole.testo: From French (consommé) madrilène (literally “consommé in the style of Madrid”).

parole.significato: Relating to the late Paleolithic culture typical of La Madeleine, c. 17000 to 12000 BCE.
parole.testo: From French Magdalénien, Magdalene + -ian, after the Magdalene Shelter, an archaeological site in the Dordogne département of South-Western France.

parole.significato: A color which is close to the equal mixture of red and blue which is an additive secondary color but a subtractive prim…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French magenta, from Italian Magenta, in commemoration of the Franco-Italian victory at the Battle of Magenta in 1859. parole.significato: A palindromic square word arrangement, usually in the form of a magic amulet.
parole.testo: As magical square by 1670 and magic square by 1701 (see Citations). Calque of French quarré magique or Latin quadratum magicum. Magic refers to its original function as a talisman.

parole.significato: A silkworm farm.
parole.testo: From French magnanerie, from magnan (“silkworm”).

parole.significato: Any of several units of magnetic moment of an atom, molecule or subatomic particle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French magnéton, from magnétique + -on, equivalent to magnet + -on.

parole.significato: The Barbary macaque (Macaca sylvanus) native to the Atlas Mountains of Algeria and Morocco along with a small populatio…
parole.testo: From French magot.

parole.significato: The breast meat of the mulard duck, known for its superior quality.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French magret.

parole.significato: A person from Mayotte or of Mahoran descent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Mahorais.

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to Mayotte or its people or language.
parole.testo: From French mahorais / Mahorais (with the ending replaced with -an).

parole.significato: Made without meat (and thus permitted to be eaten on a fast day).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French maigre. Doublet of meager.

parole.significato: Nickel silver.
parole.testo: From French maillechort.

parole.significato: A one-piece swimsuit (for women).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French maillot (“shirt, leotard”).

parole.significato: A basket for gathering grapes.
parole.testo: Uncertain, possibly from French main (“hand”).

parole.significato: In musical notation, an instruction for the pianist to use the right hand.
parole.testo: From the French main (“hand”) + droit (“right”).

parole.significato: In musical notation, an instruction for the pianist to use the left hand.
parole.testo: French, meaning "left hand".

parole.significato: A relatively large dagger, especially popular in the 17th century. It was held in the left hand (the non-dominant hand)…
parole.testo: French, left hand.

parole.significato: A low-class hotel where rooms are rented out by the hour, especially to prostitutes and their clients.
parole.testo: From French maison de passe.

parole.significato: A licensed brothel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French maison de tolérance.

parole.significato: A small house.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French maisonnette. Doublet of mansionette.

parole.significato: A function, or an element of a set, that dominates others or is greater than all others.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French majorant, present participle of majorer (“to majorate, to dominate”), from Latin maior. By surface analysis, major + -ant.

parole.significato: primogeniture
parole.testo: Borrowed from French majorat.

parole.significato: mostly; predominantly.
parole.testo: From majority + -ary + -ly. Perhaps a calque of French majoritairement or equivalents in other Romance languages.

parole.significato: A capital letter, especially one used in ancient manuscripts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French majuscule, from Latin majuscula (littera).

parole.significato: To cooperate, to enter into an alliance for a shared goal.
parole.testo: Possibly a calque of French faire cause commune, first attested in the same period (1787).

parole.significato: An item's composition.
parole.testo: Deverbal from make up. Noun sense 2 is a semantic loan from French maquillage, from maquiller (“to make up, fabricate”).

parole.significato: A ring-tailed lemur (Lemur catta).
parole.testo: From French maki, from Malagasy maky.

parole.significato: seasickness
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mal de mer (literally “sickness of sea”).

parole.significato: homesickness
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mal du pays.

parole.significato: Apathy and world-weariness, involving pessimism towards the current state of the world, often along with nostalgia for…

parole.testo: From French mal du Suisse (literally “Swiss disease”); coined in 1688 by Johannes Hofer (1669–1752), based on its frequent occurrence in Swiss mercenaries who in the plains of Switzerland were pining for their landscapes. At the time it was thought to be accompanied by serious symptoms such as faint

parole.significato: The study of molluscs.
parole.testo: From French malacologie, contraction of malacozoologie, from the (obsolete) taxonomic name Malacozoa + French -ologie (“-ology”), Malacozoa being in turn from Ancient Greek μαλακός (malakós, “soft”) + ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”). Equivalent to malaco- + -logy.

parole.significato: Homesickness.
parole.testo: From French maladie du pays (“homesickness”).

parole.significato: Sickly.
parole.testo: From French maladif.

parole.significato: sickly
parole.testo: From French maladieux. Equivalent to malady + -ous.

parole.significato: sick; ill
parole.testo: From French.

parole.significato: Not adroit; awkward, clumsy, inept.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French maladroit, from mal- (“bad, badly”) + adroit (“skilful”), equivalent to mal- + adroit.

parole.significato: A feeling of general bodily discomfort, fatigue or unpleasantness, often at the onset of illness.
parole.testo: From French malaise (“ill ease”), from mal- (“bad, badly”) + aise (“ease”). Compare ill at ease.

parole.significato: A crusty rash in the bend of the knee of the foreleg of a horse.
parole.testo: French malandres, from Latin malandria (“blisters or pustules on the neck, especially in horses”).

parole.significato: The blundering use of an absurdly inappropriate word or expression in place of a similar-sounding one.
parole.testo: From the name of Mrs. Malaprop, a character in the play The Rivals (1775) by Richard Brinsley Sheridan + -ism. parole.significato: out of place; inappropriate
parole.testo: From French mal à propos, from mal (“bad, badly”) and à propos (“appropriate, relevant”).

parole.significato: A variety of grape used in making red wine, originally from France, but now predominantly grown in Argentina.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French malbec, said to be named after a Hungarian winemaker who brought it to France.

parole.significato: The state of an organism or an organisation that did not develop in the "normal" way (used in medicine, e.g. "brain mal…
parole.testo: From French maldéveloppement, introduced as a human and social development term in France in the 1990s, to replace the words malformation or développement anormal. The word can be broken down as mal- (“ill”) + development.

parole.significato: Of or relating to malfeasance or misconduct.
parole.testo: From malfeasance, after such pairs as assistance, assistant, or adapted from French malfaisant.

parole.significato: Contrary to their desires or ambitions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French malgré (“against”) and French lui (“him”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to apples.
parole.testo: From French malique, from Latin mālum.

parole.significato: Mechelen (kind of lace)
parole.testo: Via French from Dutch/West Flemish Mechelen.

parole.significato: To feign illness, injury, or incapacitation in order to avoid work, obligation, or perilous risk.
parole.testo: From French malingrer, from adjective malingre (“delicate, fragile”).

parole.significato: A manufacturer of trunks (containers).
parole.testo: From French malletier.

parole.significato: Hollandaise sauce with blanched orange zest and the juice of blood orange.
parole.testo: From French sauce maltaise.

parole.significato: To treat badly, to abuse.
parole.testo: From mal- + treat, after French maltraiter.

parole.significato: Corrupt behaviour, illegitimate activity, especially by someone in authority.
parole.testo: From French malversation, from malverser, from Latin male versari (“behave badly”). Compare Spanish malversación (“embezzlement”).

parole.significato: To disrespect. To wish ill on someone.
parole.testo: French mal "bad", "badly" + veuille, the second-person singular subjunctive form vouloir, "to want".

parole.significato: A circular armor plate (of metal, leather, etc) worn over the breast of a fighter to hold chains to which the sword, da…
parole.testo: From French mamelière, from mamelle + -ière.

parole.significato: A hillock; a rounded elevation or protuberance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mamelon.

parole.significato: a subsidiary chapel in Ancient Egypt attached to a larger temple and associated with the nativity of a god
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mammisi, a neologism coined by Jean-François Champollion as if from Bohairic Coptic *ⲙⲁⲙ̀ⲙⲓⲥⲓ (*mam̀misi) (a term otherwise unattested), from ⲙⲁ (ma, “place”) + ⲛ̀- (ǹ-, “of”) + ⲙⲓⲥⲓ (misi, “birth”) as a calque of earlier Egyptian pr-ms (“mammisi”, literally “house of birth”).

parole.significato: bird of paradise
parole.testo: Borrowed from French.

parole.significato: A lawyer, a lawman.
parole.testo: Calque of French homme de loi.

parole.significato: A literary man; a scholar or author.
parole.testo: Calque of French homme de lettres.

parole.significato: A sleeve used as a charge in French heraldry

parole.significato: Ellipsis of mandarin orange:
parole.testo: From French mandarine, feminine of mandarin, probably formed as Etymology 1, above, from the yellow colour of the mandarins' costume.

parole.significato: The status of holding a position as a mandarin.
parole.testo: From French mandarinat, corresponding to mandarin + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, a body of people performing it, the concrete charge of it).

parole.significato: A stringed instrument of the lute family, having eight strings in four courses, frequently tuned as a violin, and with…
parole.testo: From French mandoline, from Italian mandolino, diminutive of mandola, a large stringed instrument.

parole.significato: An early form of lute that gave rise to the mandolin.
parole.testo: from French mandore

parole.testo: From French mandrin, probably from Vulgar Latin *mamphurinum, from Latin mamphur (“a bow drill”), ultimately from Oscan or Ancient Greek μαννοφόρον (mannophóron, “wearing a collar”), from μανά (maná, “collar”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear”); first element cognate with Latin monile (“collar”).

parole.significato: A metal wire or stylet inserted into a flexible catheter to give it shape and firmness while passing through a hollow t…

parole.significato: A French comic (bande dessinée) inspired by Japanese manga.

parole.significato: A vegetable pea (Pisum sativum) eaten when immature.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mangetout, from mange (“eat”) + tout (“all”), since even the pod is edible.

parole.significato: A mongoose.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mangouste.

parole.significato: The cusimanse, a genus of mongoose, Crossarchus.
parole.testo: From French manger.

parole.significato: A cosmetic treatment for the fingernails.

parole.significato: A protester; someone participating in a protest.

parole.significato: The practice of manipulating or the state of being manipulated.

parole.significato: A type of manor or country house.

parole.testo: From French manqué.

parole.significato: Unfulfilled due to the vagary of circumstance, some inherent flaw or a constitutional lack.

parole.significato: having two slopes on each side, the lower being steeper than the upper

parole.significato: A cloak or gown, especially of a kind popular with women in the 17th and 18th centuries.

parole.significato: An article of loose clothing popular in 17th- and 18th century France.

parole.significato: Maintenance, upkeep of a person, place or thing.

parole.significato: A towel used by a priest during liturgy.

parole.significato: A preliminary model or sketch used in preparation for making a sculpture.

parole.significato: A member of a resistance or guerrilla movement, originally and chiefly that of the French during the German occupation…

parole.significato: Margin; edge; brink or verge.

parole.significato: An oxeye daisy (Leucanthemum vulgare).
parole.testo: From French marguerite. Doublet of Margaret (and various forms, q.v.), margarita, margarite, and Margherita, and related to margarine.

parole.significato: A kind of bellflower, Campanula trachelium.

parole.significato: A puppet, usually made of wood, which is animated by the pulling of strings.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Mari.

parole.significato: A member of any of several Roman Catholic organizations named after the Virgin Mary

parole.significato: Something which people either love or hate.

parole.significato: A chef's assistant; kitchen boy.
parole.testo: From French marmiton.

parole.significato: A heavy crepe fabric of silk, wool, or both, having a cross-ribbed texture, used for apparel.

parole.significato: An escaped black slave of the Caribbean and the Americas or a descendant of such a person.

parole.significato: A rich dark red, somewhat brownish, color.

parole.significato: The fact or state of being a maroon.

parole.significato: Leather made from goatskin.

parole.significato: Pertaining to French poet Clément Marot, or characteristic of his light, graceful style.
parole.testo: From French marotique, from Marot, the name of French poet Clément Marot (1496-1544).

parole.significato: A jester's dummy, bauble, or sceptre.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French marotte.

parole.significato: A brand of a manufactured product, especially of a motor car.

parole.significato: A large tent with open sides, used for outdoors entertainment.
parole.testo: From marquise, from French marquise. Ultimately from same root as march (“border country”), margin (“edge”). Ultimately cognate with marque.

parole.significato: A marchioness, especially one who is French.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French marquise.

parole.significato: A sheer cotton fabric used for mosquito nets and curtains
parole.testo: Diminutive of French marquise

parole.significato: A sweet chestnut.

parole.significato: A chestnut preserved in sugar or syrup and flavoured with vanilla.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French marron glacé (literally “iced chestnut”).

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the city of Marseille, Bouches-du-Rhône department, Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French marseillais, from Marseille + -ais. Doublet of Marseillese.

parole.significato: A small kind of hammer, once used by marble workers and sculptors.
parole.testo: French

parole.significato: A country cottage or farmstead in Occitan-speaking territories.

parole.significato: A carved, ornamental face, either human-like or grotesque, whose alleged function was originally to frighten away evil…

parole.significato: Something thought to bring good luck.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mascotte, from Occitan mascòta (“sortilege”), feminine diminutive of masca (“witch”), from Old Occitan masca, from Medieval Latin masca (“specter, nightmare”). More at mask.

parole.significato: The degree or property of being masculine or manly; manliness.
parole.testo: From French masculinité, from Old French, equivalent to masculine + -ity. Earlier in same sense was masculineness.

parole.significato: A metal-headed golf club with a moderate loft, the equivalent of a five iron in a modern set of clubs.

parole.significato: A balcony in North Africa enclosed with carved wooden latticework.

parole.significato: A suspension of sugar crystals in a mother liquor, after boiling of syrup; produced in a sugar factory.

parole.significato: A stroke made with the cue held vertically that causes a billiard ball to move in an arc.

parole.significato: Inflammation of a breast.

parole.significato: Sexual stimulation of one's genitalia or other erotic regions, often to the point of orgasm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French masturbation, New Latin masturbātiō, masturbātiōnem. By surface analysis, masturbat(e) + -ion.

parole.significato: A heavy fabric, composed of two layers of cloth, used to form a quilted surface.

parole.significato: A social practice of same-sex civil union among seafarers in the 17th and 18th centuries.

parole.significato: The state of being a mother; motherhood.

parole.significato: A showing of a movie, sporting event, or theatrical performance in the morning or afternoon.

parole.testo: From French matricide, from Latin mātricīda (“person who kills his own mother”) and mātricīdium (“the murder of one's mother”). By surface analysis, matri- + -cide.

parole.significato: An underground storage place for grain.

parole.significato: A brief unpleasant period; a bad yet quick experience.

parole.significato: A rich purple synthetic dye, which faded easily, briefly popular c. 1859‒1873 and now called mauveine.

parole.significato: a purple color similar to mauve

parole.significato: The hawthorn bush or its blossoms.

parole.significato: An interdisciplinary approach to the study of culture, created by Régis Debray in 1979, that pays specific attention to…

parole.significato: A psychopathological condition characterized by delusional fantasies of wealth, power, or omnipotence.

parole.significato: An instrument for determining longitude by observation of the stars.

parole.significato: To make melancholy.

parole.significato: A type of reed organ, similar to a harmonium.

parole.significato: A kind of drama having a musical accompaniment to intensify the effect of certain scenes.
parole.testo: From French mélodrame, the second element refashioned by analogy with drama; ultimately from Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “limb”, “member”, “song”, “tune”, “melody”) + δρᾶμα (drâma, “deed”, “theatrical act”). Compare melodrame. Cognate to German Melodram and Spanish melodrama.

parole.significato: Synonym of melomaniac.

parole.significato: An abnormal love of music.
parole.testo: From melo- + -mania, after French mélomanie.

parole.significato: An aubergine; an eggplant.

parole.significato: Any of various kinds of accordion, especially a handheld free reed instrument of 19th-century France.

parole.significato: Granny; nana.

parole.significato: A firearm, similar to a musket but with a shorter barrel and a large bore.
parole.testo: From musket + -oon, after French mousqueton. Compare Italian moschettone.

parole.significato: Any of several varieties of thin cotton cloth.
parole.testo: From French mousseline, from Italian mussolina, from Mussolo (“Mosul”), that is Mosul in northern Iraq (compare 1875 Knight, Edward H., Knight's American Mechanical Dictionary, V2 p1502: "Muslins are so called from Moussol in India."). Doublet of mousseline.

parole.significato: A sort of coarse or light cotton muslin.
parole.testo: French mousselinette.

parole.significato: The noseband of a horse's bridle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French muserolle.

parole.significato: A process for prematurely stopping the fermentation of the must of grapes, used in winemaking to make sweet wine.
parole.testo: French

parole.significato: In the French language usage of the letter h at the start of a word which allows liaison with a preceding consonant.
parole.testo: Calque of French h muet.

parole.significato: Someone who participates in mutiny.
parole.testo: From French mutinier.

parole.significato: Mutiny.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mutinerie.

parole.significato: The inability to speak, be it from psychological or physical cause.
parole.testo: From French mutisme, from Latin mutus (“mute”), equivalent to mute + -ism.

parole.significato: Forming muscle fibres; pertaining to myogenesis.
parole.testo: From myo- + -genic, after French myogénique.

parole.significato: innumerable: myriad, myriapod
parole.testo: From French myria-, ultimately from Ancient Greek μυρίος (muríos, “ten thousand”).

parole.significato: Ten thousand; 10,000
parole.testo: From French myriade, from Late Latin mȳriadem (accusative of mȳrias), from Ancient Greek μυριάς (muriás, “number of 10,000”), from μυρίος (muríos, “numberless, countless, infinite”). By surface analysis, myria- + -ad.

parole.significato: 10,000 ares, or one square kilometre.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French myriare. See myria- and are (as in hectare).

parole.significato: In Greece, a funeral song composed and sung by a woman on the death of a friend.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French myriologue, from Greek μοιρολόγι (moirológi), from μοίρα (moíra, “fate”) + λόγος (lógos, “word”).

parole.significato: A myriologue.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French myriologue + -y, from Greek μοιρολόγι (moirológi), from μοίρα (moíra, “fate”) + λόγος (lógos, “word”).

parole.significato: The quality of being mystic or mystical.
parole.testo: From mystic + -ity, after French mysticité.

parole.significato: The act of mystifying or the condition of being mystified.
parole.testo: From French mystification.

parole.significato: To thoroughly confuse, befuddle, or bewilder.
parole.testo: From French mystifier, from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós, “secret, mystic”) + Latin -ficare.

parole.significato: An aura of heightened interest, meaning or mystery surrounding a person or thing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mystique (“a mystic”), from Latin mysticus. See also the doublet mystic.

parole.significato: Someone who suffers from mythomania.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mythomane. By surface analysis, mytho- + -mane.

parole.significato: Someone who suffers from mythomania.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mythomane. By surface analysis, mytho- + -maniac. Attested in English since 1950s.

parole.significato: The constitutive myth that gives an ethnic group its sense of purpose.
parole.testo: French; first used in this context by Ramon d'Abadal i de Vinyals, and later taken up by John Armstrong in his book Nations before Nationalism.

parole.significato: Valerianella locusta, a small dicot annual plant of the family Caprifoliaceae often cultivated as a salad green or herb.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mâche.

parole.significato: A household; a domestic situation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ménage; compare Middle English menage, a parallel borrowing from an earlier form of the French word.

parole.significato: Masturbation or an act of masturbation, especially by a woman.
parole.testo: Blend of ménage à trois + French moi (“me”).

parole.significato: A household or relationship whereby four people live together as lovers.
parole.testo: From ménage à trois (“household whereby three people live as lovers; sexual act involving three people”), from French ménage à trois. The number trois (“three”) is replaced by quatre (“four”).

parole.significato: A household or relationship whereby three people live together as lovers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ménage à trois (literally “household of three”).

parole.significato: An asymmetrical daybed with a high head-rest, and a lower foot-rest, joined by a sloping piece.
parole.testo: From French méridienne, feminine of méridien (“meridian; noon (attributive)”), from its typical use: rest in the middle of the day, when the sun is near the meridian.

parole.significato: Marriage with a person of inferior social position.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mésalliance, from mésallier (“to misally”).

parole.significato: Any activity that is pursued as a trade or profession; a calling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French métier. Doublet of mister (“employment, trade”).

parole.significato: In manège, a movement comprising a series of levades with small steps between.
parole.testo: From French mezzair, later mézair, from Italian mezz'aria, from mezzo (“middle”) + aria (“air”) (because it was originally a movement at height halfway between terre-à-terre and curvet).

parole.significato: Used to form tag questions.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French n'est-ce pas (“isn't it?”).

parole.significato: A shade of bright red-orange.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nacarat, from Spanish or Portuguese nacarado, ultimately derived from Arabic نَقَّارَة (naqqāra, “small drum”), from نَقَرَ (naqara, “to hollow out”). Related to English nacre, English naqareh and nagada.

parole.significato: The compartment that holds passengers on a dirigible, hot-air balloon, or other aerostat; a gondola.
parole.testo: PIE word  *néh₂us Borrowed from French nacelle (“rowing boat, skiff; gondola (of a hot-air balloon, etc.); structure on an aircraft to house an engine”), Middle French nacelle (“rowing boat, skiff”), from Old French nacele, from Late Latin naucella, nāvicella (“small boat or ship”), from Latin nāvis

parole.significato: A basic aluminium silicate clay that is a polymorph of kaolinite
parole.testo: From French nacre (“mother-of-pearl”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Having an iridescence like that of nacre, or mother-of-pearl.
parole.testo: French

parole.significato: The bohor reedbuck, Redunca redunca.
parole.testo: From French [Term?], said to have been named by Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon, from earlier nanguer; compare Nanger.

parole.significato: Lacking worldly experience, wisdom, or judgement; unsophisticated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French naïve, feminine form of naïf, from Latin nātīvus (“native, natural”). Doublet of native.

parole.significato: rhea (large, flightless birds)
parole.testo: From French nandou from Spanish ñandú from Paraguayan Guarani ñandu guasu.

parole.significato: To cover (something) with a sauce. (usually in the passive)
parole.testo: From French napper, from nappe (“nape”).

parole.significato: A product formed by the oxidation of naphthalamine (also called naphthylamine), which was observed to produce blue prec…
parole.testo: From French naphtaméine. By surface analysis, naphth(a) + -am + -ein.

parole.significato: Either of two isomeric phenols derived from naphthalene; they are used in the preparation of dyes and many other compou…
parole.testo: From naphtha + -ol, after French naphtole.

parole.significato: Finished, dead, no more, gone; non-existent.
parole.testo: World War I British and ANZAC army slang, probably a corruption of French “il n′y a plus” (“there is no more”).

parole.significato: The profile of a body of water flowing over an obstruction in a vertical drop.
parole.testo: From French nappe. Doublet of map, mop, and nape.

parole.significato: A disorder characterized by sudden and uncontrollable attacks of deep sleep, often brief, sometimes accompanied by para…
parole.testo: From French narcolepsie. By surface analysis, narco- + -lepsy, from Ancient Greek ναρκόω (narkóō, “put to sleep”) + λῆψις (lêpsis, “seizure”).

parole.significato: A large Oriental tobacco pipe wherein the smoke is drawn through water to filter and cool it.
parole.testo: From French narghilé, from Turkish nargile, from Persian نارگیله (nârgile) from نارگیل (nârgil, “a coconut”), which was formerly used to construct the bowl, likely ultimately from Sanskrit नारिकेल (nārikela, “a coconut”), from a Dravidian language.

parole.significato: The study of narrative structure.
parole.testo: From narrate + -ology, after French narratologie.

parole.significato: A kind of pessary of medicated wool or cotton.
parole.testo: French nascale.

parole.significato: The act or process of nationalising:
parole.testo: From French nationalisation. By surface analysis, nationalise + -ation.

parole.significato: A more extreme form of patriotism; the idea of a more extreme support for one's country, people or culture.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nationalisme, equivalent to national + -ism.

parole.significato: Legal membership of a particular nation or state, by origin, birth, naturalization, ownership, allegiance or otherwise.
parole.testo: From national + -ity, perhaps after French nationalité; ultimately from Latin nātio (“nation, people”).

parole.significato: To make into, or to become, a nation.
parole.testo: From French nationaliser. By surface analysis, national + -ize.

parole.significato: A crystalline mixture of hydrous sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate, with the chemical formula Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.
parole.testo: From French natron, from Spanish natrón, from Arabic نَطْرُون (naṭrūn), from Ancient Greek νίτρον (nítron, “nitre”), ultimately from Egyptian nṯrj (“natron”): R9 Doublet of niter and trona.

parole.significato: Surface decoration or diaper resembling plaited or interlaced work.
parole.testo: From French nattes.

parole.significato: An image depicting inanimate objects; a still life.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nature morte (literally “dead nature”).

parole.significato: The belief in or practice of going nude in social settings, often in mixed-gender groups, specifically either in cultur…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French naturisme. By surface analysis, natur(e) + -ism.

parole.significato: shipwreck
parole.testo: From French naufrage (“shipwreck”), from Latin naufragium (“shipwreck”), from nāvis (“ship”) + frangere (“to break”).

parole.significato: A stew of mutton and vegetables.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French navarin, probably from navet (“turnip”), a traditional ingredient. However, a connection with the 1827 Battle of Navarino has been suggested. (See Wikipedia.)

parole.significato: A shuttle bus in France.
parole.testo: From French navette. By surface analysis, Latin nav- + -ette.

parole.significato: Naive.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French naïf. Doublet of native and neif.

parole.significato: Lack of sophistication, experience, judgement or worldliness; artlessness; gullibility; credulity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French naïveté. See also nativity.

parole.significato: Edged in a deeply wavy line, intended to represent clouds.
parole.testo: French nébulé.

parole.significato: A small case for holding personal items, especially toiletries.
parole.testo: From French nécessaire. Doublet of necessary.

parole.significato: Used when giving a former name. Originally known as.
parole.testo: From French née (“(f)”) and né (“(m)”), past participle of naître, to be born. Mix of both gendered terms due to their homophony, resulting in a unisex term in English.

parole.significato: An extravagant table ornament and container used in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, made in the shape of a ship.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nef. Doublet of nave and nau.

parole.significato: business; occupation or enterprise
parole.testo: From French négoce. See negotiate.

parole.significato: A wine merchant who purchases grapes, grape juice, or wine in bulk from vineyards, and bottles the wine for sale.
parole.testo: Borrowing from French négociant.

parole.significato: Someone who conducts negotiations; a negotiator, an agent.
parole.testo: From French négociant, or its source, Latin negōtiant-, probably via Italian negoziante (“merchant”).

parole.significato: A black female.
parole.testo: From French négresse, from nègre. Equivalent to Negro + -ess.

parole.significato: The fact of being of black African descent, especially a conscious pride in the values, cultural identity etc. of Afric…
parole.testo: From French négritude (coined by Aimé Césaire), from nègre (“Negro”) + -itude.

parole.significato: A capsule, in certain cnidarians, containing a barbed, threadlike tube that delivers a paralyzing sting
parole.testo: Formed as nemato- + cyst after the French nématocyste.

parole.significato: One of the dimorphic forms of the species of Dicyema, which produce vermiform embryos
parole.testo: Formed as nemat- + -o- + -gen, in zoölogical use after the French nématogène. Compare nematogenous and nematogenic, as well as the scientific Latin Nēmatogena.

parole.significato: Describing a style of French painters and architects of the mid-19th century.
parole.testo: * From French néo-grec * neo- + Greek

parole.significato: An adherent of neo-Nazism, any of various (far right, authoritarian, or bigoted) post-World War II Nazi ideologies.
parole.testo: Originally from postwar French néonazi which first appears in 1952, equivalent to neo- + Nazi, and used to describe any number of movements, which saw themselves as believers of Nazi ideology or whose ideology had similar attributes. The term spread throughout the Western world acquiring a broader u

parole.significato: A word or phrase which has recently been coined; a new word or phrase.
parole.testo: From French néologisme, from Ancient Greek νέος (néos, “new”) + λόγος (lógos, “word”) + -ism.

parole.significato: The favoring of relatives (most strictly) or also personal friends (more broadly) because of their relationship rather…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French népotisme, from Italian nepotismo, from Latin nepōs (“nephew”), a reference to the practice of popes appointing relatives (most often nephews) as cardinals (cardinal-nephew) during the Middle Ages and Renaissance.

parole.significato: A rare apple-green nickel silicate mineral.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French népouite, after Népoui in New Caledonia, where it was first discovered.

parole.significato: More fully neroli oil or oil of neroli: an essential oil distilled from the blossoms of the bitter orange or Seville or…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French néroli (“neroli”), from Nerola, a town and comune in the Metropolitan City of Rome, Lazio, Italy. Marie Anne de La Trémoille, princesse des Ursins (1642–1722), Princess of Nerola but originally from France, is thought to have made neroli popular as a fragrance in her country of

parole.significato: A nervous disorder, especially neurasthenia.
parole.testo: From French nervosisme.

parole.significato: A vein in the wing of an insect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nervure.

parole.significato: An antipsychotic drug.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French neuroleptique, coined by Jean Delay and Pierre Deniker in 1955. Constructed from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “neuron”) and λῆψις (lêpsis), noun form of λαμβάνω (lambánō, “take hold of”).

parole.significato: The act of neutralising.
parole.testo: From French neutralisation. By surface analysis, neutralise + -ation.

parole.significato: The act of neutralizing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French neutralisation. By surface analysis, neutral + -ization or neutralize + -ation.

parole.significato: To make (something) even, inactive or ineffective.
parole.testo: From French neutraliser (first attested in 1642). By surface analysis, neutral + -ize.

parole.significato: Chiefly of a person: having a neutral gender (being neither male nor female), and having or seeking to have no or reduc…
parole.testo: Apparently a blend of French neu(tre) (“neuter”, adjective) or its etymon Latin neu(ter) (“neuter”, adjective) + French trois (“three”) (referring to the third gender), coined by Holly A. Burnham in 1995 as a self-description.

parole.significato: Synonym of nouveau réalisme
parole.testo: In modern art, a calque of French nouveau réalisme.

parole.significato: Any of several movements in music and film which are or were considered cutting edge.
parole.testo: Calque of French Nouvelle Vague.

parole.significato: A Native American people who live in the Pacific Northwest region (Columbia River Plateau) of the United States.
parole.testo: From French nez percé (“pierced nose”).

parole.significato: A young hawk; an eyas.
parole.testo: French niais. See eyas and nyas.

parole.significato: A cavity, hollow, or recess, generally within the thickness of a wall, for a statue, bust, or other erect ornament.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French niche, from Middle French niche, from Old French niche, from nicher (“to make a nest”) (modern French nicher), from Vulgar Latin *nīdicāre, from Latin nīdus (“nest”). Doublet of nidus and nide via Latin and nest via Proto-Indo-European; also related to nyas.

parole.significato: A white waxy amino acid with a hot, bitter taste, extracted from tobacco leaves.
parole.testo: From French nicotianine.

parole.significato: An alkaloid (C₁₀H₁₄N₂), commonly occurring in the tobacco plant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nicotine, equivalent to Nicot + -ine, named after Jean Nicot (1530–1604), the French ambassador to Portugal, who sent tobacco seeds back to France in 1561. The etymology of the surname itself is unclear.

parole.significato: rotenone
parole.testo: From French, from the former taxonomic name Robinia nicou.

parole.significato: Extremely dark black.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nielle. Doublet of nigella.

parole.significato: The niello process.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French niellure?

parole.significato: A person from Niger or of Nigerien descent.
parole.testo: From French Nigérien, from Niger + -ien.

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to Niger or the Nigerien people.
parole.testo: From French nigérien, from Niger + -ien.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Nice.
parole.testo: From French nissard, from Occitan niçard. Compare Italian nizzardo.

parole.significato: A nightclub or nightspot.
parole.testo: From nite and French + -erie, as in eaterie.

parole.significato: Any salt or ester of nitric acid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nitrate.

parole.significato: The chemical element (symbol N) with an atomic number of 7 and atomic weight of 14.0067. It is a colorless and odorless…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nitrogène (coined by French chemist and physician Jean-Antoine Chaptal in 1790). By surface analysis, nitro- + -gen. See also niter.

parole.significato: level, grade, standard
parole.testo: From French niveau; see there for more. Doublet of level and libella.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the city of Nice, the prefecture of the Alpes-Maritimes department, Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur,…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French Niçois.

parole.significato: A dark olive of a cultivar grown primarily in the Alpes-Maritimes region near Nice and the Riviera di Ponente, Italy.
parole.testo: From French niçoise, feminine of niçois (“of Nice (town in France)”), and olive.

parole.significato: The honourable obligation that is the responsibility of those of high rank; in American English this often includes the…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French noblesse oblige (literally “nobility obliges”), primarily used as a phrase. See noblesse and obliger.

parole.significato: A bat, of the genus Nyctalus, that lives in tree hollows.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French noctule, a latinised scientific borrowing of the Italian nottola (refers to various birds or bats), inherited from Late Latin noctula, diminutive of Classical Latin noctua (“night-owl”), ultimately from Latin nox (“night”), from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts. Per the OED, first at

parole.significato: A work in a genre of piano music of moderate tempo with a highly-decorated, improvisatory melody.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nocturne (literally “nocturnal”), from Latin nocturnus. Doublet of notturno.

parole.significato: The junction between root and stem of a plant.
parole.testo: From French nœud vital.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to film noir, or the atmosphere associated with that genre
parole.testo: Shortened from film noir, and from French noir. Doublet of negro.

parole.significato: A small round thick slice of meat (in particular, lamb or veal) that has been deboned.
parole.testo: From French, diminutive of noix (“nut”). The rose takes its name from the French gardener of Charleston, South Carolina, who produced it in 1817.

parole.significato: A pseudonym used by an artist.
parole.testo: From French nom d'artiste (literally “artist's name”).

parole.significato: A pseudonym, particularly one adopted by soldiers, revolutionaries, or resistance fighter.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French nom de guerre (literally “war name”), referring to the pseudonyms used during wars.

parole.significato: A pen name or pseudonym.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Gallicism, derived from nom (“name”) + de (“of”) + plume (“feather”), by analogy with the borrowed nom de guerre.

parole.significato: A pseudonym used while travelling.
parole.testo: French

parole.significato: Navel-gazing.
parole.testo: From French nombrilisme.

parole.significato: A prefecture or unit of regional government in Greece.
parole.testo: From French nome, from Ancient Greek νομός (nomós, “district”), from νέμω (némō, “to divide”). Doublet of nomos.

parole.significato: A term in an algebraic expression.
parole.testo: The sense "term" is from French -nôme, second element of binôme etc., again from Ancient Greek νομός (nomós) here in its sense "division". The name of the special function may be identical or may be an independent borrowing from the Greek.

parole.significato: Capable of being identified using a name.
parole.testo: From French nominable or its etymon Latin nōminābilis, from nōminō (“to name”) + -ābilis (“-able”).

parole.significato: A doctrine that universals do not have an existence except as names for classes of concrete objects.
parole.testo: From French nominalisme. By surface analysis, nominal + -ism.

parole.significato: Not starting; not participating.
parole.testo: From French non partant (“not leaving, not departing”).

parole.significato: An independent politician.
parole.testo: From French non (“not”) inscrit (“registered”).

parole.significato: The principle that a person (particularly a refugee) should not be returned to an area (chiefly their country of origin…
parole.testo: From non- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + refoulement. Refoulement is borrowed from French refoulement (“act of pushing something back (as gunpowder into a gun barrel, or water by a dam); act of water overflowing; forced relocation of a group of people; forced repatriation of asylum-seekers or refugees”),

parole.significato: Indifference, unconcern; carelessness; coolness; disregard, detachment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nonchalance.

parole.significato: Casually calm and relaxed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nonchalant, from Old French nonchaloir (“to be unconcerned”), from non- (“not”) + chaloir (“to have concern for”), from Latin non (“not”) + calēre (“to be warm”).

parole.significato: 10³⁰.
parole.testo: From French nonillion. By surface analysis, non- (“nine”) + -illion.

parole.significato: The whitebait of certain Mediterranean fish.
parole.testo: French nonnat

parole.significato: Synonym of nonpareil.
parole.testo: (printing): From French nonpareille and German Nonpareille (“6-point type”).

parole.significato: An anthropological space of transience where human beings remain anonymous, such as an airport or shopping mall.
parole.testo: Calque of French non-lieu, non- + place.

parole.significato: The sphere of human reason, thought, and consciousness, seen as a theoretical evolutionary stage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French noosphère, from Ancient Greek νόος (nóos, “mind, spirit”) + Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, globe”), developed and perhaps coined by Pierre Teilhard de Chardin and Vladimir Vernadsky, in analogy to atmosphere, biosphere etc. By surface analysis, nous (“mind”) + -sphere.

parole.significato: A plantation of nopal (a prickly pear cactus of the genus Opuntia, especially Opuntia cochinellifera) used as food for…
parole.testo: From nopal + -ery (suffix forming nouns indicating places of arts, crafts, or practices), modelled after French nopalerie. Nopal is borrowed from Spanish nopal, from Classical Nahuatl nohpalli (“cactus of the genus Opuntia”), from Proto-Uto-Aztecan [Term?].

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Nordic countries.
parole.testo: From French nordique, from nord (“north”).

parole.significato: A granular crystalline rock consisting essentially of a triclinic feldspar (such as labradorite) and hypersthene.
parole.testo: From French Norvège (“Norway”) + -ite.

parole.significato: A school for training teachers, especially in mainland Europe and North America.
parole.testo: Calque of French école normale, so called because the norms of pedagogy are taught there.

parole.significato: The state of being normal or usual; normalcy.
parole.testo: From normal + -ity, perhaps modelled on French normalité.

parole.significato: A wooden bar, or iron pin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French normand.

parole.significato: A dairy cow of a particular breed originating from Normandy, France.
parole.testo: From French Normande.

parole.significato: A yearning for something base or vile.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nostalgie de la boue (literally “nostalgia for mud”).

parole.significato: Not worth the cost or trouble.

parole.significato: A cloth made of worsted and cotton, used for making clothes.
parole.testo: From French Orléans, ultimately from Latin Aurelianum, from the name of the Roman emperor Aurelian, who rebuilt the city. More at Aurelius.

parole.significato: Golden or gilded brass or bronze used for decorative purposes.
parole.testo: From French or moulu (literally “ground gold”).

parole.significato: An aircraft that generates lift through the flapping of its wings.
parole.testo: From French ornithoptère, from Ancient Greek ὄρνιθ- (órnith-) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing”), equivalent to ornitho- + -pter.

parole.significato: ornamental
parole.testo: French past participle of orner. Doublet of ornate.

parole.significato: The process of mountain building by the upward folding of the Earth's crust.
parole.testo: From French orogénie, from Ancient Greek ὄρος (óros, “mountain, high ground”) + γενεια (geneia, “creation, birth, making”). By surface analysis, oro- + -geny.

parole.significato: An alloy of copper and zinc or tin that has a gold color, used in making inexpensive jewelry.
parole.testo: From French, from or (“gold”) + Ancient Greek εἶδος (eîdos, “appearance”, “shape”, “form”).

parole.significato: gold prospector, gold panner
parole.testo: Borrowed from French orpailleur.

parole.significato: An orphan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French orphelin. See orphan.

parole.significato: A member of an orphéon.
parole.testo: From French orphéoniste.

parole.significato: A French male choral society.
parole.testo: From French orphéon.

parole.significato: An acid found in certain lichens, such as orchil.
parole.testo: From French orseille (“archil”). See archil.

parole.significato: Of or relating to orthopedics.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French orthopédique.

parole.significato: The study of straight lines, especially in regards to the flight paths that UFOs tend to follow.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French orthoténie.

parole.significato: A sage, of species Salvia viridis.

parole.significato: The slowworm.
parole.testo: From French orvet.

parole.significato: A medicinal preparation made from herbs, wine and honey, thought to be an antidote for any poison.
parole.testo: 17th century: from French orviétan, from Italian orvietano (“of Orvieto”), after the place of origin of its creator.

parole.significato: the act of oscillating or the state of being oscillated
parole.testo: From French oscillation, from Latin oscillatio, from Latin oscillo. By surface analysis, oscillate + -ion.

parole.significato: A skeletal framework; an underlying structure.

parole.significato: A little bone.

parole.significato: Apparent, evident; meant for open display.

parole.significato: Synonym of monstrance.

parole.significato: monstrance
parole.testo: Derived from French ostensoir.

parole.significato: a tumor composed of bone and cartilage
parole.testo: French ostéo-chondrophyte. Surface reading of osteo- (“bone”) + chondro- (“cartilage”) + -phyte (“growth”).

parole.significato: A small, abnormal growth of bone (exostosis, bone spur) that forms along joint margins.
parole.testo: From French ostéophyte. Surface reading of osteo- (“bone”) + -phyte (“growth”).

parole.significato: Synonym of otolith.
parole.testo: A Latinised adaptation (taking the form of a Latin second-declension neuter noun in the nominative case, as if from a Latin *ōtoconium) of the French otoconie (whence otocony, otokony), itself formed from the Ancient Greek οὖς, ὠτ- (oûs, ōt-, “ot-; ear”) + κονία (konía, “dust”).

parole.significato: A poisonous cardiac glycoside, g-strophanthin, found in the seeds of certain lianas.
parole.testo: From ouaba(io) + -in, after French ouabain, ultimately from Somali waabaayo, meaning "arrow poison".

parole.significato: A member of a Native American tribe who lived along the Ouachita River in Louisiana, affiliated with and now subsumed i…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Ouachita.

parole.significato: A howler monkey (Alouatta spp.).
parole.testo: From French ouarine (which see for more), from the same source as English guariba.

parole.significato: A dungeon only accessible by a trapdoor at the top.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French oubliette, from oublier (“to forget”).

parole.significato: A sheep of a certain hardy breed raised for wool.
parole.testo: From French Ouessant (“Ushant island”).

parole.significato: The currency of Mauritania, divided into five khoums.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ouguiya, from Arabic أُوقِيَّة (ʔūqiyya), via Classical Syriac and Ancient Greek from Latin ū̆ncia (“ounce”). Doublet of ounce, inch, uncia, oka, and awqiyyah.

parole.significato: Synonym of yes.

parole.significato: A non-French person who is obsessed with France and French culture, a Francophile.

parole.significato: A marmoset.

parole.significato: The Canada goose.
parole.testo: From French outarde. Doublet of bustard.

parole.significato: An area beyond the sea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French outremer.

parole.significato: Beyond what is customary or proper; extravagant.
parole.testo: French outré, form of outrer (“to go to excess”); see also outre (“beyond”).

parole.significato: Used when referring to a woman: feminine of outré.
parole.testo: From French outrée.

parole.significato: A position in which the feet are apart, or a movement which brings them apart.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ouvert. Doublet of apert and overt.

parole.significato: An usher

parole.significato: An usherette.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ouvreuse.

parole.significato: A French labourer or manual worker.

parole.significato: The glorification of manual laborers, often in opposition to the leadership of labor or socialist movements.
parole.testo: From French ouvrierisme.

parole.significato: A female ouvrier.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ouvrière.

parole.significato: The structure in a plant that develops into a seed after fertilization; the megasporangium of a seed plant with its enc…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ovule (“ovum”), from Latin ōvum (“egg”). Doublet of ovolo.

parole.significato: Any salt or ester of oxalic acid.
parole.testo: From French oxalate, equivalent to oxalic acid + -ate (“salt or ester”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to oxalic acid or its derivatives.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French oxalique, from Oxalis (“the sorrel plant”).

parole.significato: an oxidizing agent
parole.testo: Borrowed from French oxydant.

parole.significato: The combination of a substance with oxygen.
parole.testo: From French oxydation, equivalent to oxide + -ation. See oxidate.

parole.significato: A binary chemical compound of oxygen with another chemical element.
parole.testo: Archaic French oxide (now oxyde), from a blend of ox(ygene) and (ac)ide, coined by G. de Morveau and A. Lavoisier. By surface analysis, ox- + -ide.

parole.significato: Concerning oxygen
parole.testo: Reduced from oxygen which in turn is from French oxygène, from Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús).

parole.significato: The chemical element (symbol O) with an atomic number of 8 and relative atomic mass of 15.9994. It is a colorless and o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French oxygène (originally in the form principe oxygène, a variant of principe oxigine ‘acidifying principle’, suggested by Lavoisier), from Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús, “sharp”) + γένος (génos, “birth”), referring to oxygen's supposed role in the formation of acids. parole.significato: A member of a people of Ozark with a distinct culture, architecture, and dialect.
parole.testo: From French aux arcs (literally “at the arches”), in reference to natural bridge formations in the area, or aux Arcs, a clipping of aux Arcansas (“among the Arkansas”), i.e. the Quapaw people.

parole.significato: A member of the obsolete taxonomic order Pachydermata, grouping of thick-skinned, hoofed animals such as the rhinoceros…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pachyderme, equivalent to pachy- (“thick”) + -derm (“skin”).

parole.significato: The third stage of prophase 1 of meiosis, during which the chromosomes shorten and divide into four chromatids.
parole.testo: From French pachytène, equivalent to pachy- (“thick”) + -tene (“ribbon”). Coined by Hans von De Winiwarter in 1900 and in English by Edmund B. Wilson in 1912.

parole.significato: The support of peace, specifically:
parole.testo: From French pacifisme, from pacifique; pacific + -ism.

parole.significato: One who loves, supports, or favours peace.

parole.significato: Something of little or no value exchanged for something valuable, originally goods exchanged for slaves.

parole.significato: A rich and heavy silk material.
parole.testo: From Padua (“a place name in Italy”) + French soie (“silk”). Compare French pou-de-soie, peau de soie.

parole.significato: The act of creating pages for a document, book, etc., or determining when to truncate text on the pages.

parole.significato: A slice of meat pounded thin and grilled.

parole.significato: An under bed or mattress of straw.

parole.significato: A kind of straw bonnet.

parole.significato: A sequin or spangle.

parole.significato: A thin leaf of metal, for use in gilding or enamelling, or to show through a translucent medium.

parole.significato: A French snack consisting of a pastry, normally similar to a croissant, with chocolate inside.

parole.significato: A spiral pastry containing raisins, originating in France and often eaten for breakfast.
parole.testo: From French pain aux raisins (literally “raisin bread”).

parole.significato: A form of French gingerbread.

parole.significato: A type of bread from France formed in large round loaves.

parole.significato: A type of soft bread made with sugar, with a soft crust and interior.

parole.significato: A case or situation that is different from another.

parole.significato: A heroic champion, especially a knight.

parole.significato: Synonym of pile (“wooden structure used to support prehistoric dwellings”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a palace.

parole.significato: A fur cape or stole worn by women, which covers the neck and shoulders.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the palate or to a palatine bone.

parole.significato: a local creole language, such as Antillean Creole or Jamaican Creole
parole.testo: Probably at least partly from French parler, with repetition to make it sound like babbling.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Paleocene epoch.

parole.significato: The study of the forms of life existing in prehistoric or geologic times, especially as represented by fossils.
parole.testo: Attested since 1836 (as palæontology). From French paléontologie (attested since 1822). By surface analysis, paleo- (“ancient”) + onto- (“being”) + -logy (“study”).

parole.significato: Synonym of vetero-testamentary.

parole.significato: Any extinct mammal of the genus Palaeotherium.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Palaeotherium.

parole.significato: A loose outer jacket, cloak, coat, overcoat, greatcoat, three-quarter coat.

parole.significato: A thin board on which a painter lays and mixes colours.

parole.significato: A Parisian measure of blood let; a cup containing three ounces, formerly used by surgeons.

parole.significato: A thin mattress or under bed stuffed with straw.
parole.testo: French French paillasse, from Old French paille (“straw, chaff”), from Latin palea (“chaff”).

parole.significato: a dense, heavy wood, similar to teak or mahogany, mostly from species of Dalbergia and Pterocarpus, as well as Machaeri…

parole.significato: A motif in decorative art resembling the fan-shaped leaves of a palm tree.
parole.testo: From French palmette. By surface analysis, palm + -ette.

parole.significato: A type of puff pastry biscuit made in the shape of a palm leaf and rolled in sugar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French palmier, ellipsis of feuille de palmier (“palm tree leaf”), the original name of this pastry.

parole.significato: Synonym of pedipalp.

parole.significato: Panache; flamboyant style.

parole.significato: A royal charter confirming to a subject all his possessions.

parole.significato: A formal speech publicly praising someone or something.

parole.significato: A lustrous finish applied to velvet and satin.

parole.significato: A mechanical linkage based on parallelograms causing two objects to move in parallel; notably as a drawing aid.
parole.testo: From French pantographe, from panto- (from Ancient Greek παντός (pantós), genitive singular of πᾶν (pân, “all”)), and -graphe (from γράφειν (gráphein, “to write”)).

parole.significato: A horseshoe to correct a narrow, hoofbound heel.
parole.testo: From French patin. See patten.

parole.significato: To bread; to coat in breadcrumbs or breading.

parole.significato: Breaded; coated in breadcrumbs or breading.

parole.significato: A small piece of aluminum foil or parchment paper, wrapped around food during cooking.

parole.significato: a mailboat

parole.significato: By; with.

parole.significato: By air mail.

parole.significato: Because or on account of one's excellence.

parole.significato: to guard against, to avert, to shield from; to provide protection against, defence from

parole.significato: Synonym of parry in both its literal and figurative senses.
parole.testo: From French parade (“a parry”), from parer (“to parry, to defend oneself”) + -ade, from Italian parata. Doublet of parry.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a paradigm.
parole.testo: From French paradigmatique, from Ancient Greek πᾰρᾰδειγμᾰτῐκός (părădeigmătĭkós).

parole.significato: Someone suffering from paralysis.

parole.significato: A small light umbrella used as protection from the sun.

parole.significato: A windscreen.

parole.significato: A purple liqueur, generally based on curaçao.

parole.significato: Fragrance; perfume.
