parole.testo: From French plage, from Late Latin plagia, from Latin plaga (“region”) (cognate with English flake). Doublet of playa.

parole.significato: An act of pleading; a plea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French plaidoyer.

parole.significato: Synonym of plainsong.
parole.testo: From French plain-chant, from plain + chant, calque of Latin cantus planus.

parole.significato: A jokester.
parole.testo: From French plaisanteur.

parole.significato: A drawing showing technical details of a building, machine, etc., with unwanted details omitted, and often using symbol…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French plan (“flat surface, ground plot, map”), from Latin plānus. Some sources also argue for influence or alteration of French plant, from plantar, from Latin plantāre (“set, fix in place”). Doublet of llano, piano, plane, and plain.

parole.significato: A position where the gymnast is horizontal and face-down, using only the hands as support.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French planche (“board”). Doublet of phalange, phalanx, planch, plancha, and plank.

parole.significato: A floor made of wood.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French plancher.

parole.significato: A flat disk of metal used as a blank for stamping a coin.
parole.testo: From French planchette. By surface analysis, French planche + -et.

parole.significato: A small plank.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French planchette. By surface analysis, French planche + -ette.

parole.significato: An organism having characteristics of both plants and animals; a zoophyte, later chiefly an animal with structural rese…
parole.testo: From plant + animal, after French plant-animal (obsolete), from New Latin plantanimal (16th c.), after Hellenistic Ancient Greek ζωόφυτον (zōóphuton, “zoophyte”).

parole.significato: Plants, vegetation; specifically, the planting or cultivation of plants.
parole.testo: From plant + -age. In later use influenced by French plantage and Dutch plantage.

parole.significato: Of an animal: walking with the entire sole of the foot on the ground.
parole.testo: From French plantigrade, from Latin planta (“sole of the foot”) (from Proto-Indo-European *pléh₂-n̥t-eh₂, from *pleh₂- (“flat”)) + -grade, from Latin gradus (“pace, step”).

parole.significato: The embryo which has begun its development in the act of germination; a seedling.
parole.testo: From French plantule, diminutive of plante (“a plant”), Latin planta.

parole.significato: Any flat, thin piece of clay, ivory, metal, etc., used for ornament, or for painting pictures upon, as a dish, plate, s…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French plaque (“plate, sheet (of metal); slab (of marble); bacteria on teeth”), from French plaquer, Middle French plaquer (“to plate”), from Middle Dutch placken (“to patch, beat metal into a thin plate”), from placke (“disk, patch, stain”), from Old Dutch *plagga (“patch”)

parole.significato: A small metal tablet decorated in bas-relief, usually with a design including figures.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French plaquette (“small plaque”), allegedly coined in the 1860s.

parole.significato: A form of physical exercise that involves rotation of the joints.
parole.testo: From French plastique. Doublet of plastic.

parole.significato: The nearly flat part of the shell structure of a tortoise or other animal, similar in composition to the carapace.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French plastron, from Italian piastrone, augmentive of piastra (“breastplate”), from Latin emplastrum (“plaster”), from Ancient Greek ἔμπλαστρον (émplastron), from ἔμπλαστος (émplastos, “daubed, plastered”), from ἔμπλασσειν (émplassein, “to mould, form”).

parole.significato: The special dish for the day in a restaurant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French plat du jour (literally “dish of the day”). See du jour.

parole.significato: A largely level expanse of land at a high elevation; tableland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French plateau, diminutive of plat (“a plate”); see plate. Doublet of platter.

parole.significato: The part of a printing press which presses the paper against the type and by which the impression is made.
parole.testo: From French platine, from plat (“flat”). See plate, and compare platin.

parole.significato: The removal or excision of the footplate of the stapes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French platinectomie.

parole.significato: An often-quoted saying that is supposed to be meaningful but has become unoriginal or hackneyed through overuse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French platitude, from plat (“flat”).

parole.significato: A unit of thirty to forty soldiers typically commanded by a lieutenant and forming part of a company.
parole.testo: From obsolete French plauton, variant of peloton, from Middle French pelote + -on. Doublet of peloton. Compare pellet.

parole.significato: The replaying of something previously recorded, especially sound or moving images.
parole.testo: From play + back. Sense 2 is from French playback, a pseudo-anglicism of this term.

parole.significato: a form of marital union, often illegal in nature, found in the Caribbean during the colonial period between a Caucasian…
parole.testo: From French.

parole.significato: Used to make a polite request.
parole.testo: Short for if you please, an intransitive, ergative form taken from if it please you which is a calque of French s'il vous plaît, which replaced pray. If it please you is a present subjunctive form, but most current uses of please are not parsed that way.

parole.significato: A direct popular vote on an issue of public importance, such as an amendment to the constitution, a change in the sover…
parole.testo: Sense 1 (“referendum”) is borrowed from French plébiscite, from Latin plēbiscītum, plēbis scītum, plēbī scītum (“law of the common people or plebs”), from plēbis (the genitive singular of plēbs (“common people, plebeians”)) + scītum (“decree, ordinance, statute”). Sense 3 (“law enacted by the common

parole.significato: Synonym of plectrum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French plectre.

parole.significato: Done outdoors.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French plein air.

parole.significato: A weeping figure used as an ornament on a tomb.
parole.testo: French, pleurant (“weeping”).

parole.significato: A certain fold in the crown of the (upper) molars of some horse species.
parole.testo: French pli caballin (“caballine fold”).

parole.significato: A block or slab upon which a column, pedestal, statue or other structure is based.
parole.testo: From French plinthe, from Latin plinthus, from Ancient Greek πλίνθος (plínthos, “brick”).

parole.significato: A vitreous enamelling technique where the enamel is applied in cells, similar to cloisonné, but with no backing in the…
parole.testo: From French plique-à-jour, literally "letting in daylight".

parole.significato: A fabric treated so as to be permanently puckered or crinkled.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French plissé.

parole.significato: A narrow pleat made by gathering fabric with stitches, wetting the fabric, and setting by allowing it to dry under weig…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French plissé.

parole.significato: A smooth and continuous bending of the knees
parole.testo: Borrowed from French plié. Doublet of plicate.

parole.significato: A mixture of hair and tar for covering the bottom of a ship.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ploc.

parole.significato: A slope or sloping down toward the front.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French plongée. See plunge.

parole.significato: Cheap or inferior everyday wine.
parole.testo: From WWI military slang, derived by alteration of French vin blanc (“white wine”) by the law of Hobson-Jobson. Recorded earliest in the playful rhyming slang form plinketty-plonk. Possibly influenced by the sound of wine being poured into a glass.

parole.significato: A kind of Brayon flatbread made with buckwheat flour.
parole.testo: From French.

parole.significato: Bowed, curved.
parole.testo: French. Doublet of plicate.

parole.significato: The business of a plumber; plumbing
parole.testo: French plomberie.

parole.significato: Of or related to a span of several centuries, centuries-old.
parole.testo: From pluri- (“multi-, many”) + secular (“of or related to centuries”), chiefly after French pluriséculaire.

parole.significato: The more it changes, the more it's the same thing (sometimes loosely translated as the more things change, the more the…
parole.termine_origine: plus ça change, plus c'est la même chose

catena.termine: plus ça change, plus c'est la même chose

parole.testo: A short form (specifically, an anapodoton) of French plus ça change, plus c'est la même chose (“the more it changes, the more it's the same thing”).

parole.significato: Very extravagant.
parole.testo: From French peluche (“fluff, plush”). The fact that historically (in past centuries) plush upholstery was so expensive as to be socially exclusive undoubtedly connects the senses of "luxurious" and "soft".

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or produced by rain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pluvial, from Middle French pluvial, borrowed from Latin pluviālis (“pertaining to rain”).

parole.significato: The pneumatic postal system in Paris (abolished 1984), or a letter sent by this system.
parole.testo: From French pneumatique.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to pneumatology.
parole.testo: From pneumatology + -ical. Compare French pneumatologique.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; Probably; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: Wearing a particularly stern and disapproving expression; humourless; priggish.
parole.testo: Uncertain, probably from po, abbreviated slang based on French pot de chambre (“chamber pot”), after the distasteful expression anyone would adopt upon being presented with a full one. Perhaps similarly from pooh; perhaps influenced by poker-faced. Also possibly “poor-faced”.

parole.significato: A rough sketch.
parole.testo: From French pochade.

parole.significato: A small handbag shaped like an envelope.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pochette (“pocket”). Doublet of pocket.

parole.significato: A technique in visual art consisting of applying various stencils (perforated templates).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pochoir.

parole.significato: Areas of an architectural plan or section that are filled in, often by cross-hatching or solid black, to show wall thic…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French poché.

parole.significato: Apathetic, indifferent or nonchalant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pococurante, itself - from Pococurante, a nonchalant Venetian senator in Candide, coined by Voltaire based on Italian poco (“little”) + curante (“caring”).

parole.significato: A French infantryman during the First World War
parole.testo: Borrowed from French poilu (“brave”). Doublet of plew.

parole.significato: A given point or body upon which troops are formed, or by which they are marched in line or column.
parole.testo: From French point d'appui (“point of support”).

parole.significato: A position from which something is seen.
parole.testo: Calque of French point de vue.

parole.significato: Very close; not touching but not more than a few metres (yards).
parole.testo: From French point blanc (“white point”), originally referring to the white spot to be aimed at on a target (see blank's "bull's eye") or alternatively into empty space being fired horizontally.

parole.significato: The tip of the toe; a ballet position executed with the tip of the toe.
parole.testo: From French pointe (“point, tip”). Doublet of point, ponto, puncto, punctum, punt, and punto.

parole.significato: The use of many small areas of color to construct an image.
parole.testo: From French pointillisme, from pointiller (“to dot, to mark with points”), from point (“dot, point”).

parole.significato: of, pertaining to, or in the style of pointillism
parole.testo: From French pointilliste.

parole.significato: Synonym of pointillist.
parole.testo: French

parole.significato: A style of finishing consisting of dotted lines and curves on the covers of a book.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pointillé.

parole.significato: A fishwife, especially in France; specifically, any of the Parisian fishwives or market-women who led riots during the…
parole.testo: From French poissarde.

parole.significato: The Poisson distribution.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French Poisson. The noun sense is named after French mathematician Siméon Denis Poisson (1781–1840).

parole.significato: In a large commercial kitchen, a cook tasked with preparing and cooking (and possibly selecting) fish and fish dishes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French poissonnier, from poisson (“fish”).

parole.significato: A triclinic-pinacoidal mineral containing copper, hydrogen, iron, oxygen, sulfur, and zinc.
parole.testo: Named after Canadian mineralogist Théophile Eugène Poitevin (1888–1978) + -ite. The surname is of French origin, see Poitevin.

parole.significato: A piece of armor for a horse's chest; the breastplate of a horse's armour or harness.
parole.testo: From Middle English: the form poitral is from central/Parisian French poitrel, "introduced into English apparently by Caxton"; the older form peitral (Middle English peitrel, paytrel, etc) was borrowed from Anglo-Norman peitral; both are from Old French poitral (modern French poitrail).

parole.significato: Someone suffering from tuberculosis, or a similar lung disease.
parole.testo: From French poitrinaire, from poitrine (“chest”).

parole.significato: The breastplate of a knight's armour.
parole.testo: From French poitrine or a Middle or Old French predecessor.

parole.significato: A type of sauce (generally a vinaigrette) with pepper as a main ingredient.
parole.testo: From French poivrade.

parole.significato: The production or the condition of polarity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French polarisation. By surface analysis, polarize + -ation or polar + -ization.

parole.significato: To cause to have a polarization.
parole.testo: From French polariser, equivalent to polar + -ize.

parole.significato: A Siberian flying squirrel (Pteromys volans, syn. Sciuropterus volans), native to much of boreal Eurasia, from Finland…
parole.testo: From French polatouche.

parole.significato: A person who writes in support of one opinion, doctrine, or system, in opposition to another; one skilled in polemics;…
parole.testo: From French polémique, from Ancient Greek πολεμικός (polemikós, “of war”), from πόλεμος (pólemos, “war”). By surface analysis, polem- + -ic.

parole.significato: A film telling the fictional story of a police investigation, particularly such a film based on a novel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French policier.

parole.significato: A groove found carved into rock, once used to polish stone axes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French polissoir.

parole.significato: A dishonest or mischievous person; a scamp.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French polisson.

parole.significato: Civility, politeness, courtesy or gallantry; genteel politeness or an instance of this.
parole.testo: From French politesse, from Italian politezza, from polito, past participle of pulire (“to clean”), from Latin polire, present active infinite form of poliō (“to polish”).

parole.significato: A politician, especially one seen as being unprincipled.
parole.testo: From French politique, from Latin politicus. Doublet of politic.

parole.significato: A lively dance originating in Bohemia.
parole.testo: Via French and German from Czech polka, variant of půlka (“half”) as in "half-step"; see půl (“half”).

parole.significato: A stately Polish dance in triple time and moderate tempo.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French polonaise (“Polish”).

parole.significato: Polish.
parole.testo: From French polonais. By surface analysis, Polono- + -ese.

parole.significato: A Pole.
parole.testo: From French Polonais. By surface analysis, Polono- + -ese.

parole.significato: To make Polish as to custom, culture, language, or style; to adapt to the norms of the Republic of Poland.
parole.testo: From Polonia + -ize, perhaps after French poloniser.

parole.significato: Polish-speaking.
parole.testo: From French polonophone; equivalent to Polono- + -phone.

parole.significato: Having multiple dials
parole.testo: From French polycamératique.

parole.significato: A person who can multitask
parole.testo: From French.

parole.significato: A form of government administered by several councils rather than individual ministers; specifically that of Regency Fr…
parole.testo: From French polysynodie.

parole.significato: That teaches applied arts, sciences, technology, engineering and other academic subjects.
parole.testo: First attested in 1805. From French polytechnique, from the École polytechnique, engineering school founded 1794 in Paris; from Greek πολύτεχνος "skilled in many arts," from πολύς "many" (see poly-) + τέχνη "art" (see technic).

parole.significato: The belief in the existence of multiple gods.
parole.testo: From French polythéisme, from Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “many”) and θεός (theós, “god”), corresponding to poly- + theism.

parole.significato: A greasy or waxy substance that is used to style hair, making it look slick and shiny.
parole.testo: From French pommade, from Italian pomata (“ointment, pomade”), from pomo (“apple”) + -ata (“-ade, -ate: forming nouns”), from Latin pōmum (“fruit, apple”). Doublet of pomatum, pomate, and pomace. Early pomades tended to be various kinds of fat mixed with apples for a more pleasing scent.

parole.significato: An ornamental knob.
parole.testo: From French.

parole.significato: A roundel vert (green circular spot), resembling or representing an apple.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pomme (“apple”), ultimately from Latin poma. Doublet of pome.

parole.significato: Psoralea esculenta, the prairie turnip.
parole.testo: French, literally "white apple".

parole.significato: A traditional Belgian-style skin-on shoestring-cut piece of deep-fried potato; French fry, chip.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pomme frite.

parole.significato: A very smooth and creamy mashed potatoes dish/sidedish, usually requiring ricers/foodmills and chinois/strainers to mak…
parole.testo: From French pomme purée.

parole.significato: Synonym of ambarella (fruit (Spondias dulcis))
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pomme cythère, from pomme (“apple”) and Cythère (“Kythira”).

parole.significato: Having the ends terminating in rounded protuberances or single balls; having round shapes on the extremities.
parole.testo: From French pommé (“grown round, or like an apple”), past participle of pommer (“to pome”).

parole.significato: A French dish of sliced layered potatoes cooked in melted butter.
parole.testo: French; perhaps named after the actress Dame Judic (Anna Damiens), or after Anna Deslions.

parole.significato: French fries; plural of pomme frite
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pommes frites.

parole.significato: A women's hairstyle in which the hair is swept upwards from the face and worn high over the forehead.
parole.testo: From French Pompadour, after Madame de Pompadour (1721–1764), mistress of Louis XV.

parole.significato: A pompier hook
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pompier.

parole.significato: A sexual technique the woman uses her pubococcygeus (vagina) muscles to stimulate the man's penis while both partners r…
parole.testo: From French pomper, to pump. Borrowed from Tamil பூம்புகார் (pūmpukār, “Poompuhar”).

parole.significato: A ball made of pieces of soft fabric, tinsel, plastic, or paper streamers, tied together in the middle and left loose a…
parole.testo: Alteration of pompon, from French pompon (“ornamental tuft”); of unknown origin, perhaps related to Old French pomp.

parole.significato: A man living off another's earnings, especially a woman's.
parole.testo: Uncertain, but probably an aphetic form of French alphonse (“kept man”), from the male given name Alphonse. Also sometimes connected to pounce or French pensionnaire (“pensioner, person living without working”).

parole.significato: The stomach of a pig, especially when stuffed as chaudin (a Louisianan food).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French panse (“belly”).

parole.significato: Any of a number of red pigments, some of which are used as indicators.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ponceau.

parole.significato: An unoriginal or uninspired idea; a cliché.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French poncif (“cliché, stereotype”), from French poncif (“stencil”), from poncer (“to copy with pouncing paper”) + -if, from ponce (“pumice”) + -er, from Late Latin pōmex (“pumice”), from Latin pūmex (“pumice”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)poH(y)- (“foam”).

parole.significato: A drawbridge.
parole.testo: From French pont-levis.

parole.significato: A card game in which the object is to obtain cards whose value adds up to, or nearly to, 21 but not exceed it.
parole.testo: Probably from vingt-un, an obsolete variant of vingt-et-un (“twenty-one”), from French.

parole.significato: A supply of resources.
parole.testo: 1. From French poule (“collective stakes in a game”). The French word "poule" in this context is an abbreviation of "poulain, pouliche" (foal, filly), and referred to races with female horses under 3 years old. It then became used by punters to designate bets on that race, and started to be used fro

parole.significato: Female genitalia; the vulva or vagina.
parole.testo: Origin uncertain. Likely from French putain (“prostitute”). Compare Jamaican Creole punani (“female genitalia”); also Tagalog putang ina (“contemptible person”, literally “prostitute-mother”) from Spanish puta (“prostitute”).

parole.significato: A poppyhead finial seen on church pews and occasionally on other types of seating benches.
parole.testo: Likely from French poupe; see poppyhead.

parole.significato: A fabric of many varieties, usually made of silk and worsted; used especially for women's dresses.
parole.testo: An alteration (taken as related to Pope) of French papeline, a distortion of Poperinge, a town in Flanders which was a centre for textile production.

parole.significato: A man's mistress, or a single woman of loose morals; a sweetheart.
parole.testo: Likely a fanciful variant of poplet, ultimately from French poupe (“doll”).

parole.significato: The deliberate slaughter of a people or a nation.
parole.testo: Probably an unadapted borrowing from French populicide (“(noun) slaughter of a people; (adjective) harmful to the people”) (obsolete, rare), from Latin populus (“community; people; nation”) + French -cide (suffix meaning ‘killing’). The French word populicides was coined by the French journalist and

parole.significato: 1838, William Howitt, The Rural Life of England
parole.testo: Diminutive of French porc. See pork.

parole.significato: A pornographer.
parole.testo: From the French pornographe.

parole.significato: The explicit literary or visual depiction of sexual subject matter; any display of material of an erotic nature.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pornographie. By surface analysis, porno- + -graphy.

parole.significato: An exercise in which the arms are moved to different positions, sometimes also incorporating upper-body movements.
parole.testo: From French port de bras (literally “carriage of the arms”).

parole.significato: A portative organ.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French portatif.

parole.significato: A gateway through which horse carriages pass, often into a courtyard.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French porte cochère (literally “coach gateway or coachman's gateway”): porte (“door; gateway”) (ultimately from Latin porta (“door; entrance; gate; passage”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to go through; to carry forth, fare”)) + cochère (from coche (“stagecoach”) + -ièr

parole.significato: An instrument (typically a metallic tube with a clasp) used to hold a pencil, lead etc. for drawing.
parole.testo: From French porte-crayon, from porter (“to carry”) + crayon (“a crayon”).

parole.significato: A wallet.
parole.testo: From French porte-monnaie.

parole.significato: A spokesperson, one who speaks on another's behalf.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French porte-parole.

parole.significato: A strap, buckle or other fastening by which a sword or scabbard is held attached to a person's belt, clothing etc.
parole.testo: From French porte-épée.

parole.significato: An artist's portfolio.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French portefeuille.

parole.significato: A car door.
parole.testo: From French portière, derived from porte (“door”) + -ière.

parole.significato: A chart of European navigable waters based on descriptions of coasts.
parole.testo: From French portulan, from Italian portolano.

parole.significato: A form of tableau vivant consisting of nearly nude women posing, once a form of salacious entertainment.
parole.testo: French poses plastiques

parole.significato: One who affects some behaviour, style, attitude or other condition, often to impress or influence others.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French poseur.

parole.significato: A female poseur.
parole.testo: French

parole.significato: A doctrine that states that the only authentic knowledge is scientific knowledge, and that such knowledge can only come…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French positivisme, from positif (“positive”). By surface analysis, positiv(e) + -ism.

parole.significato: A believer in positivism.
parole.testo: Perhaps borrowed from French positiviste. Equivalent to positive + -ist, after positivism.

parole.significato: The belief that possible things exist, as well as actual things.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French possibilisme. By surface analysis, Latin possibil|is, ~e (“that can be done”) + -ism, from Latin po|ssum, ~(te)sse, ~tuī (“be able”) + -ibil|is, ~e (“-able”). First attested in 1883.

parole.significato: An assigned station; a guard post.
parole.testo: Probably from French poste.

parole.significato: Relating to the collection, sorting and delivery of mail.
parole.testo: From post + -al, modelled on French postal.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a political movement that criticises neoclassical economics and advocates a pluralistic approach.
parole.testo: From post- + autistic, derived from the French autisme-économie (“autism economics”), itself from an older sense of French autisme to mean "abnormal subjectivity" or "acceptance of fantasy rather than reality."

parole.significato: A postal service in which a mail is held at a post office to be collected by the recipient
parole.testo: Borrowed from French poste restante.

parole.significato: Any item of false hair worn on the head or face, such as a false beard or wig.
parole.testo: From French postiche.

parole.significato: A Bible commentary written in its margins.
parole.testo: From French postille (“marginal note”), from Late Latin postilla, probably from post illa (verba) (“after those (words)”).

parole.significato: To place (a word or phrase) after another in a sentence, especially in order to modify it
parole.testo: From French postposer. See post- and pose.

parole.significato: A person seeking admission to a religious order.
parole.testo: From French postulant, present participle of postuler.

parole.significato: Held in position for a prolonged period.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French posé (“placed, posed”).

parole.significato: A thick soup of meat and vegetables cooked together in a large pot.

parole.significato: An octopus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French poulpe. Doublet of polyp.

parole.significato: A puppet.

parole.significato: A tip (extra money given to e.g. a waiter in appreciation of service), especially in French contexts.

parole.significato: A digestif consumed after the coffee course.

parole.significato: A movement, or part of a figure, in the contradance.

parole.significato: A chicken reared to be eaten at a few weeks of age.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French poussin.

parole.significato: A restaurant that specializes in making poutine.

parole.significato: A sweet spice mixture used in medieval cookery.

parole.significato: An extensive area of relatively flat grassland with few, if any, trees, especially in North America.

parole.significato: A little prairie.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French prairillon, from prairie + -illon.

parole.significato: A confection made from almonds and other nuts, caramelized sugar, and sometimes milk or cream.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French praline.

parole.significato: Previous caution or care; caution previously employed to prevent misfortune or to secure good.
parole.testo: From French précaution, Latin praecautio, from praecavere, praecautum (“to guard against beforehand”); prae (“before”) + cavere (“be on one's guard”). See pre-, and caution.

parole.significato: The person who leads songs or prayers in a cathedral, church, monastery, or synagogue and generally facilitates worship.
parole.testo: From French précenteur, from Latin praecentor, from praecentus (“sung before”), from praecinō (“to sing before”) + -or (“agent suffix”), from prae- + canĕre (“to sing”).

parole.significato: Steep, like a precipice
parole.testo: From obsolete French précipiteux, from Vulgar Latin *praecipitōsus, from praeceps, praecipit- (“ precipice”) + -ōsus (“-ful, -ous”), from prae- (“before”) + caput (“head”). Equivalent to precipice (“steep cliff, brink”) + -ous.

parole.significato: precocious
parole.testo: Borrowing from French précoce.

parole.significato: The state of being precocious.
parole.testo: From French précocité.

parole.significato: The belief that all events that occur have already been determined.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French prédéterminisme, equivalent to pre- + determinism or predetermine + -ism.

parole.significato: Capable of being seized.
parole.testo: Compare French préhensible.

parole.significato: Able to take hold of and clasp objects; adapted for grasping especially by wrapping around an object.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French préhensile, from Latin perfect passive participle prehēnsus, from prehendō (“grasp, seize”) + adjective suffix -ile, from Latin -ilis.

parole.significato: prelates in general
parole.testo: From both French prélature and post-Classical Latin praelātūra.

parole.significato: The lead male dancer in a ballet; compare première danseuse.
parole.testo: From French premier danseur (“first dancer”) (unlisted in dictionaries of French); from premier (“first”) + danseur (“dancer”); compare première danseuse.

parole.significato: High-quality dripping, the first fraction to melt from the solid fat.
parole.testo: French premier jus

parole.significato: The first showing of a film, play or other form of entertainment, often held as a special event with celebrity guests.
parole.testo: From French première (“first”).

parole.significato: The lead female dancer in a ballet.
parole.testo: From French première danseuse (unlisted in dictionaries of French); from première, feminine form of premier (“first”) + danseuse, feminine form of danseur (“dancer”); feminine form of premier danseur (“first dancer”).

parole.significato: The power or right of taking a thing before it is offered
parole.testo: Borrowed from French prendre (“to take”), from Latin prehendere (“to take”).

parole.significato: To place or set (something) before; to prefix.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French préposer; prefix pré- (Latin prae before) with poser. See pose.

parole.significato: A premonition; a feeling that something, often of undesirable nature, is going to happen.
parole.testo: From French pressentiment, from Middle French, equivalent to pre- + sentiment.

parole.significato: An ornamental tray, dish, etc. used as a salver.
parole.testo: Compare French présentoir, from present + French -oir.

parole.significato: A presidential candidate considered to have a good chance of winning an election.
parole.testo: From French présidentiable.

parole.significato: A failure to remember something, with the sense that recall is imminent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French presque (“almost”) + vu (“seen”).

parole.significato: A device used to measure the stress in soil under pressure
parole.testo: From French pressiomètre.

parole.significato: pressure

parole.significato: payable
parole.testo: From Middle or early Modern French prestable, compare Modern French prêtable. By surface analysis, prest + -able.

parole.significato: A performance of or skill in performing magic or conjuring tricks with the hands.

parole.significato: One who performs feats of prestidigitation; a sleight-of-hand artist.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French prestidigitateur.

parole.significato: The quality of how good the reputation of something or someone is, how favourably something or someone is regarded.
parole.testo: From French prestige (“illusion, fascination, enchantment, prestige”), from Latin praestīgium (“a delusion, an illusion”). Despite the phonetic similarities and the old meaning of “delusion, illusion, trick”, the word has a different root than prestidigitator (“conjurer”) and prestidigitation.

parole.significato: Motivated by an inappropriate, excessive, or unjustified desire to impress others.
parole.testo: From French prétentieux, from prétention, from Latin praetēnsus (“false or hypocritical profession”), past participle of praetendō. parole.significato: A valiant knight; any gallant gentleman.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French preux chevalier.

parole.significato: A going before; anticipation in sequence or order.
parole.testo: French prévenance.

parole.significato: To precede (come before) or anticipate.
parole.testo: From French prévenir, Latin praevenire. See prevent.

parole.significato: foreseeing; prescient
parole.testo: Borrowed from French prévoyant.

parole.significato: A kneeling figure, in French sepulchral art.
parole.testo: From French priant (“praying”).

parole.significato: Any of several species of stonecrop, such as Petrosedum rupestre, formerly used as ingredients of vermifuge medicines.
parole.testo: From French trique-madame. Compare Dutch tripmadam.

parole.testo: From French prie-Dieu, from prie (“pray”) + Dieu (“God”).

parole.significato: A mammal of the order Primates, comprising of apes (including humans), monkeys, lemurs, tarsiers, lorisids, and galagos.
parole.testo: First attested in 1876. From French primate, from the substantivization of Latin prīmās, prīmātis (“one of the first, chief, excellent, noble”), same as Etymology 2. So named due to the belief that primates are the highest order of mammals or animals.

parole.significato: An intermediate sprint within a race, usually offering a prize and/or points.
parole.testo: From French prime (“reward, prize, bonus”).

parole.significato: The chief member of the cabinet and head of the government, especially in a parliamentary democracy; often the leader o…
parole.testo: Calque of French premier ministre.

parole.significato: The state of being the firstborn of the children of the same parents.
parole.testo: From French, from Late Latin primogenitura, from Latin primus (“first”) + genitura (“birth”) (from genitus, past participle of gignere).

parole.significato: A fictional heroic prince in various fairy-tales.
parole.testo: Calque of French Roi Charmant (“Charming King”).

parole.significato: The husband of a queen or an empress, who is not a king or an emperor in his own right, or is accorded this title in a…
parole.testo: Calque of French prince consort.

parole.significato: A style customarily (but not automatically) awarded by a British monarch to his or her eldest daughter.

parole.significato: Being or relating to a princesse dress.

parole.significato: A lady's long, close-fitting dress made with waist and skirt in one.

parole.significato: Prepared with spring vegetables.

parole.significato: An engagement of the blades that attempts to control the opponent's weapon.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a prism; having the form of a prism; containing one or more prisms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French prismatique. Equivalent to prism + -atic.

parole.significato: A combatant or soldier who is captured by an enemy power during or immediately after an armed conflict.

parole.significato: Synonym of prize.

parole.significato: A menu in which the entire meal is offered at a single fixed price.

parole.significato: A particular method for performing a task.

parole.significato: A small, hollow case of choux pastry with a filling.

parole.significato: A secret pocket in a magician's coat, used in vanishing tricks etc.

parole.significato: A set of structured activities; a plan of action.

Doublet of programm

parole.significato: Synonym of proletarian.

parole.significato: The process by which an organism produces others of its kind; breeding, propagation, procreation, reproduction.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French prolifération.

parole.significato: Fertile; producing offspring or fruit in abundance, applied to plants producing fruit, animals producing young, etc.

parole.significato: The state of being prominent: widely known or eminent.

parole.significato: Standing out, or projecting; jutting; protuberant.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being promiscuous.

parole.significato: Strongly marked; decided, or distinguished, in manners, attire, or appearance.

parole.significato: A person who disseminates propaganda.

parole.significato: An aliphatic hydrocarbon, C₃H₈, a constituent of natural gas.
parole.testo: From clipping of propionic acid + -ane, from French propionique, from Ancient Greek πρό (pró) + πίων (píōn, “fat”). Analyzable as prop- + -ane, borrowing or calque of German Propan.

parole.significato: Propensity.
parole.testo: From French propension, and its source, Latin prōpēnsiō, from the participle stem of prōpendeō.

parole.significato: The frequently specialised or reduced leaf produced at the first node of a new shoot.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to propionic acid or its derivatives; propanoic
parole.testo: From French propionique.

parole.significato: A theological student who performs religious functions and is a candidate for the ministry.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French proposant.

parole.significato: Of or relating to property or ownership.
parole.testo: From French propriétaire, from Latin proprietārius. By surface analysis, propriety + -ary. Compare with the Latin proprietas (“property”) and proprius (“ownership”).

parole.significato: A writer of French prose.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French prosateur.

parole.significato: A gastropod with gills in front of the heart, formerly thought to belong to a single group, Prosobranchia.

parole.significato: A document, distributed to prospective members, investors, buyers, or participants, which describes an institution (suc…
parole.testo: From French prospectus (“a prospectus”), borrowed from Latin prospectus. Doublet of prospect and prospekt.

parole.significato: dejection; depression
parole.testo: French. See prostration.

parole.significato: A system or policy of protecting the domestic producers of a product from foreign competition by imposing tariffs, quot…

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to protectionism, or an advocate thereof.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French protectionniste, equivalent to protection + -ist.

parole.testo: From proto- + -ein. Suggested by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in a letter to Gerardus Johannes Mulder, from French protéine and German Protein, both coined based on Ancient Greek πρωτεῖος (prōteîos, “primary”), from πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”).

parole.significato: A form of granite containing silvery flakes of talc or similar minerals.
parole.testo: From French protogine, coined in 1806 on the basis of Ancient Greek πρωτόγονος (prōtógonos, “first-created”), with an added suffix -ine, which the author used for certain minerals.

parole.testo: From French prototype or Late Latin prototypon, from Ancient Greek πρωτότυπος (prōtótupos, “original; prototype”), from πρωτο- (prōto-, “first”) (from πρῶτος (prôtos, “first; earliest”)) + τῠ́πος (tŭ́pos, “blow, pressing; sort, type”) (from τύπτω (túptō, “to beat, strike”), from Proto-Indo-European

parole.significato: The act of protruding.
parole.testo: From French protrusion.

parole.significato: A bulge, knob, swelling, spine, or anything that protrudes.
parole.testo: From French protubérance, from Latin prōtubērantia (“bulge; protuberance”), from prō + tūber (“swelling; protuberance”) + -antia (“-ance”).

parole.significato: A person who is guided and supported by an older and more experienced person (a protector or mentor).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French protégé, past participle of protéger (“to protect”).

parole.significato: A female protégé.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French protégée.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or reminiscent of Marcel Proust (1871–1922), French novelist, or his works.
parole.testo: From French Proust + -ian.

parole.significato: Place or source of origin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French provenance (“origin”), from Middle French provenant, present participle of provenir (“come forth, arise”), from Latin provenio (“to come forth”).

parole.significato: The quality of being provincial; having provincial tastes, mentality, manners.
parole.testo: From French provincialisme, equivalent to provincial + -ism.

parole.significato: To lay a stock or branch of a vine in the ground for propagation.
parole.testo: From French provigner, from provin (“a set, layer of a plant”), Old French provain, from Latin propago, propaginis, akin to propagare (“to propagate”). See propagate and prune.

parole.significato: One who engages in provocative behavior.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French provocateur. Doublet of provocator.

parole.significato: A female provocateur.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Gallicism, derived from provocateur + -euse, as the French female equivalent of provocateur is provocatrice.

parole.significato: A female provocateur.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French provocatrice.

parole.significato: An honorable, upstanding man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French prud'homme. Compare prude.

parole.significato: A person who is or tries to be excessively proper, especially one who is easily offended by matters of a sexual nature.
parole.testo: From French prude, from Old French prude, prode, feminine of prou, prod, prud (“good, excellent, brave”), from Latin prōde. Related to proud but unrelated to prudent.

parole.significato: The condition of being prudish; prudishness
parole.testo: First attested in 1709. prude + -ery and from French pruderie.

parole.significato: A kind of small and very acid French plum, especially when stoned and dried, from Prunus spinosa.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French prunelle.

parole.significato: Someone (especially a woman) who affects refinement and delicacy; a fastidious or pretentious woman.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French précieuse.

parole.significato: A summary or brief: a concise or abridged statement or view.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French précis (“summary”), from a substantive use of its adjectival sense "precise". Doublet of precise.

parole.significato: Ready-to-wear.
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1957 in Punch. See cite below. Reborrowed from French prêt-à-porter (1951), itself a calque of English ready-to-wear.

parole.significato: The act or practice of writing psalms.
parole.testo: Compare French psalmographie.

parole.significato: A fictitious name (more literally, a false name), as those used by writers and movie stars.

parole.significato: The branch of medicine that focuses on mental and behavioral health by subjectively diagnosing, treating, or preventing…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French psychiatrie. First attested in 1846.

parole.significato: That brings on a dreamlike mental state; hallucinogenic.
parole.testo: From psycho- + dys- + -leptic, probably after French psychodysleptique.

parole.significato: A psychologist.
parole.testo: From psycho- + -logue, a calque of French psychologue.

parole.significato: The study of the human mind.

parole.testo: From French réprobation, or Latin reprobatio. By surface analysis, reprobate + -ion.

parole.significato: Rep.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French reps, ultimately from English ribs.

parole.significato: Someone who favors a republic as a form of government.
parole.testo: From republic + -an, partly after French républicain.

parole.significato: A large or dangerous shark, specifically, (zoology) a member of the family Carcharhinidae.
parole.testo: From French requin, altered by association with Etymology 1, above.

parole.significato: Any member of the taxonomic family Carcharhinidae (order Carcharhiniformes).
parole.testo: Perhaps from French requin (“shark”).

parole.significato: The great white shark (Carcharodon carcharias).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French requin (“shark”).

parole.significato: A fief held by an intermediary or subtenant
parole.testo: From French arrière-fief. See rear (“hinder”), and fief.

parole.significato: Diligent inquiry or examination to seek or revise facts, principles, theories, applications, etc. (that are currently a…
parole.testo: Early Modern French rechercher (“to examine closely”), from Old French recerchier (“to seek, to look for”), by surface analysis, re- + search.

parole.significato: Any of various plants of the genus Reseda having small, pale grayish green flowers, such as dyer's rocket (Reseda luteo…
parole.testo: From French réséda, from Latin resēda, said by Pliny the Elder (23–79 C.E.) to be from resēdāre (“to soothe”), from re- (“again”) + sēdāre (“to assuage, calm”)), an allusion to the healing properties of the plant.

parole.significato: A place where anything is kept in store.
parole.testo: From French réservoir (“collection place”) (fig.), réservoir (“storehouse”) (lit.). in turn from French réserver (“to reserve, keep”).

parole.significato: To exit, cancel, or draw back from a lease or contract.
parole.testo: From French résilier (“cancel, annul, invalidate”).

parole.significato: The act of cancelling, annulling or drawing back from (a contract).
parole.testo: From French résiliation, or resiliate + -ion.

parole.significato: A person who resists; especially a member of a resistance movement.
parole.testo: From French résistant; equivalent to resist + -ant.

parole.significato: Resounding, echoing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French résonnant or Latin resonantem.

parole.significato: Active power or movement; spring.
parole.testo: From French ressort.

parole.significato: Placed so as to face one another; face to face.
parole.testo: French, present participle of respecter.

parole.significato: A projection in an entablature.
parole.testo: From French ressaut.

parole.significato: An eating establishment in which diners are served food, usually by waiters at their tables but sometimes (as in a fast…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French restaurant, present participle of the verb restaurer, corresponding to Latin restaurans, restaurantis, present participle of restauro (“to restore”), from the name of the 'restorative' soup served in the first establishments.

parole.significato: The owner of a restaurant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French restaurateur.

parole.significato: A female restaurateur.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French restaurateuse or formed in English by application of French rules (see French -eur, -euse), as it is more common in English than in French, where the more common feminine form of restaurateur is restauratrice.

parole.significato: A female restaurateur.
parole.testo: From French restauratrice, female form of restaurateur.

parole.significato: A child sent by their parents to work for another household as a domestic servant.
parole.testo: Borrowed French reste-avec, from Haitian Creole restavèk, from French rester (“stay”) + French avec (“with”)

parole.significato: Restructuring.
parole.testo: Mistranslation by non-native speakers, based on their native languages’ equivalent terms. These include, but are not limited to, French restructuration, Portuguese reestruturação, and Spanish reestructuración. Likely independently reformed various times.

parole.significato: Synonym of result.
parole.testo: From French resultat (now résultat), from Medieval Latin resultātum.

parole.significato: A summary or synopsis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French résumé, past participle of résumer (“to summarize”), from Latin resūmere (“to take back”); compare resume.

parole.significato: A table or shelf behind an altar, on which are placed images or holy objects.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French retable, ultimately from Medieval Latin retrotabulum.

parole.significato: Serving to impede (slow down) the action of something
parole.testo: Borrowed from French retardant, equivalent to retard (“to slow down”) + -ant.

parole.significato: anachronistic, dated, especially in artistic style.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French retardataire.

parole.significato: A reticle; a grid in the eyepiece of an instrument.
parole.testo: From French réticule, from Latin rēticulum, diminutive of rēte (“net”). Doublet of reticle, reticulum, and Reticulum.

parole.significato: A kind of retrenchment, as in the body of a bastion, which may be disputed inch by inch after the defenses are dismantl…
parole.testo: From French retirade. Compare Spanish retirada (“retreat”). See retire.

parole.significato: An act of retiring; withdrawal.
parole.testo: From French retirement, from retirer (“withdraw, retire”); corresponding to retire + -ment.

parole.significato: A flask with a rounded base and a long neck that is bent down and tapered, used to heat a liquid for distillation.
parole.testo: From French retorte.

parole.significato: To improve something (especially a photograph), by adding or correcting details, or by removing flaws.
parole.testo: From French retoucher.

parole.significato: an instruction by a drawer of a bill of exchange that the bill may be returned without protest if it is dishonoured by…
parole.testo: From French retour (“return”) + sans (“without”) + protêt (“protest”).

parole.significato: To trace (a line, etc. in drawing) again.
parole.testo: From French retracer, from Middle French retracier.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to, the past, past times, or the way things were.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rétro, ultimately from Latin retro.

parole.significato: Extending in scope, effect, application or influence to a prior time or to prior conditions
parole.testo: First attested in 1610. From French rétroactif, equivalent to retro- + active.

parole.significato: Descriptive of an art movement, particularly in Slovenia, that looks back to the past, as opposed to avant-garde.
parole.testo: From avant-garde, with French avant (“before”) replaced with retro- (“pertaining to an earlier time”). Piecewise doublet of rearguard.

parole.significato: Located behind the pharynx.
parole.testo: Mid 19th century from retro- + pharyngeal, after French rétro-pharyngien.

parole.significato: Turned up, especially when describing the nose.
parole.testo: From French retroussé, past participle of retrousser (“to hitch up, hike up”), from re- (from Latin re- (“back, backwards; again”), from Proto-Italic *wre- (“again”)) + trousser (“to fold up, hitch up”).

parole.significato: To get back to the business at hand.
parole.testo: Humorous calque translation of French revenons à nos moutons, from “La Farce de maître Pierre Pathelin”

parole.significato: Revenge or retaliation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French revanche. Doublet of revenge.

parole.significato: The political policy of endeavouring to regain lost territory.
parole.testo: From the French revanche (“revenge”) + -ism, based on revanchisme. By surface analysis, revanche + -ism. Piecewise doublet of revengism.

parole.significato: A revanchist person; occasionally, anyone seeking vengeance.
parole.testo: From French revanchiste, from revanche (“revenge”) + -ist.

parole.significato: The sounding of a bugle or drum early in the morning to awaken soldiers.
parole.testo: From French réveillez, imperative form of réveiller (“to wake”).

parole.significato: Someone who returns from a long absence.
parole.testo: 19th century. From French revenant, the present participle of revenir (“to return”). Compare revenue.

parole.significato: The act of revendicating.
parole.testo: French revendication.

parole.significato: To regard someone or something with great awe or devotion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French révérer, ultimately from Latin revereor, from re- + vereor (“to fear”).

parole.significato: A state of dreaming while awake; a loose or irregular train of thought; musing or meditation; daydream.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rêverie.

parole.significato: A lapel of a garment, turned back to show the reverse side.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French revers (“lapel, reverse side”). Doublet of reverse.

parole.significato: Having reverted to a previous (more basic or more natural) state.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French revertent, from Latin revertor, equivalent to revert + -ent.

parole.significato: Able to be reverted.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman French revertible, from Late Latin revertibilis, from Latin revertere, from re- (“re-: again, back”) + vertere (“to turn”), + -ibilis (“-ible: able to”). Equivalent to revert + -ible.

parole.significato: To face (an embankment, etc.) with masonry, wood, or other material.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French revêtir (“to reclothe”).

parole.significato: A layer of stone, concrete, or other hard material supporting the side of an embankment.
parole.testo: From French revêtement, from Old French revestiment, from revestir (French revêtir), from Late Latin revestire (“to clothe again”), from Latin re- + vestire (“to clothe”).

parole.significato: The process of revising:
parole.testo: Borrowed from French révision, from Latin revīsiō.

parole.significato: To reanimate, bring back to life.
parole.testo: Partly from French revivifier and partly from Latin revīvificō, corresponding to re- + vivify.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a revolution in government; tending to, or promoting, revolution
parole.testo: Compare French révolutionnaire; equivalent to revolution + -ary.

parole.significato: A form of theatrical entertainment in which recent events, popular fads, etc., are parodied.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French revue (literally “review”). Doublet of review, which it replaced in these senses.

parole.significato: A fox.
parole.testo: From French renard.

parole.significato: Divination by reading a random passage from a poem.
parole.testo: From French rhapsodomancie, from Ancient Greek ῥαψῳδός (rhapsōidós) + -mancy.

parole.significato: A diamond simulant, strass.
parole.testo: From Rhine + stone; a calque of French caillou du Rhin (“Rhine pebble”).

parole.significato: Of, or aboriginal to, the Rhône valley.
parole.testo: An adaptation of the French rhodanien, Rhodanien with the suffix -ian.

parole.significato: A form of rum specifically distilled from fresh sugarcane juice.
parole.testo: From French rhum agricole (“agricultural rum”).

parole.significato: Mirthful, cheerful, smiling, light-hearted.
parole.testo: From French riant.

parole.significato: Cheerful, agreeable (chiefly of a place, landscape etc.); pleasing to look at.
parole.testo: From French riante, feminine of riant (“smiling, laughing”). Compare riant.

parole.significato: An engine of war used in the Middle Ages, consisting of a protected elevated staging on wheels, and armed in front with…

parole.significato: A method of firing a projectile so that it skips along a surface.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ricochet, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Paul Ricœur (1913–2005), French philosopher best known for combining phenomenological description wit…

parole.significato: A fortification or barrier such as a small earthen mound or ridge, a file of troops, etc.

parole.significato: A small woman's handbag; a reticule.
parole.testo: Apparently from French ridicule (“reticule”), probably a punning alteration of réticule after ridicule (“ridicule”).

parole.significato: In roulette, an announcement made by the croupier while the wheel is spinning and no more bets can be placed.

parole.significato: A quickstep dance for two people.
parole.testo: Anglicized from French rigaudon. Ultimate origin unknown; perhaps related to Hebrew ריקודים or Arabic رقص.

parole.significato: A small stream.

parole.significato: A deeply ploughed agricultural soil type.
parole.testo: From French rigole (“drainage ditch”) + -sol.

parole.significato: A dish of meat cooked in fat then shredded and served in a ramekin.
parole.testo: From French rillette.

parole.significato: a crevasse at the upper end of a mountain glacier.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rimaye.

parole.significato: A form of rhyme with identical sounds, as in "pear" and "pair".
parole.testo: From French.

parole.significato: A thrust given in return after parrying a lunge.

parole.significato: A thrust given in return after parrying an attack.
parole.testo: From French riposte, taken from Italian risposta, a derivative of the verb rispondere (“to respond”).

parole.significato: Used when referring to a woman: feminine of risqué
parole.testo: Borrowed from French risquée.

parole.significato: A ball of meat, some variants covered in pastry, which has been fried or barbecued.

parole.significato: Synonym of rite of passage.

parole.significato: A ceremony or series of ceremonies, often very ritualized, to celebrate a passage or transition from one stage of a per…
parole.testo: From rite + of + passage, a calque of French rite de passage. The French term was coined by French ethnographer and folklorist Arnold van Gennep (1873–1957) and popularized in his work Les rites de passage (1909).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to rivers or their surrounding environments.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French riverain.

parole.significato: A necklace of diamonds or other precious stones, especially one of several strings.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rivière. Doublet of river and riviera.

parole.significato: A rolling paper.
parole.testo: From the Rizla+ brand of rolling papers, coined in 1886 from French riz (“rice”) and Lacroix, referring to the use of rice paper and the inventor's family name.

parole.significato: dressing gown
parole.testo: Borrowed from French robe de chambre.

parole.significato: A low-cut dress for women.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French robe décolletée.

parole.significato: A high-necked dress.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French robe montante.

parole.significato: A type of flowy, hanging, voluminous dress worn in the 18th century.

parole.significato: A sack-back

parole.significato: A tap; a faucet.

parole.significato: Artificial rockwork made of rough stones and cement, as for gardens.

parole.significato: The sand leek, Allium scorodoprasum

parole.significato: A quenelle (in the sense of food moulded into an elliptical shape) made using one spoon rather than two.

parole.significato: A style of baroque architecture and decorative art, from 18th-century France, having elaborate ornamentation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rococo.

parole.significato: A vain or blustering boaster; a braggart.

parole.significato: Seeking information or evidence, especially from a foreign court
parole.testo: Borrowed 1750 from French rogatoire, from Medieval Latin rogātōrius (“interrogatory”), from rogō (“to ask, enquire”). By surface analysis, Latin rog- + -ate + -ory.

parole.significato: Any of the later French kings of the Merovingian dynasty, considered to have played a merely ceremonial role.
parole.testo: From French roi fainéant (“lazy king”).

parole.significato: To render turbid by stirring up the dregs or sediment of.
parole.testo: Origin uncertain. Possibly from French or Middle French rouiller (“to rust, make muddy”), from Old French rouil (“mud, rust”), from Vulgar Latin *robicula, from Latin robigo (“rust, blight”)

parole.significato: A character or part played by a performer or actor.
parole.testo: From French rôle, from Middle French rolle, from Old French role, from Medieval Latin rotulus. Doublet of roll and rotulus.

parole.significato: A long-leaved variety of lettuce, Lactuca sativa var. longifolia.
parole.testo: A partial calque of French laitue romaine (“Roman lettuce”), from its supposed association with Rome.

parole.significato: A piece of fiction, especially a novel, describing real-life people or events.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French roman à clef (literally “novel with a key”).

parole.significato: A “thesis novel”: a novel that is didactic rather than entertaining, often taking the form of social commentary.

parole.testo: Borrowed from French roman à tiroirs (literally “novel with/made of drawers”).

parole.significato: A yellow hexoctahedral calcium antimonate mineral with the chemical formula (Ca,Fe,Mn,Na)₂(Sb,Ti)₂O₆(O,OH,F).

parole.significato: Broken, as an ordinary; cut off, or broken at the top, as a chevron, a bend, etc.

parole.significato: The movement of a leg in a semicircular motion, either on the ground (par terre) or in the air (en l'air).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rond de jambe (literally “circle of the leg”).

parole.significato: A French bureaucrat or functionary; an office worker.

parole.significato: A kind of script in which the tails of the letters are curly, giving the characters a rounded look.

parole.significato: Sculpture in the round.

parole.significato: A small circular object.

parole.significato: A graceful curvature or round object; a ring; a sphere.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rondeur (“roundness; round object”), from rond (“round”) + -eur (suffix forming agent nouns from verbs).

parole.significato: An instrument with a sharp-edged, scoop-shaped tip, for gouging out bone.
parole.testo: From French rongeur, from ronger (“to gnaw”).

parole.significato: A mangy or scabby creature.
parole.testo: From French rogne (“scab, mange”).

parole.significato: A lined and trimmed cloak that reaches to the knees, often with bright-coloured lining and trimmed with fur.
parole.testo: From French roquelaure, from the name of Antoine Gaston de Roquelaure.

parole.significato: A herb of the mustard family (Eruca sativa), with pungently flavored leaves often eaten in salads.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French roquette. Cognate with rocket, see that entry for other cognates.

parole.significato: An English person (as viewed by the French).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rosbif, from English roast beef. Doublet of roast beef.

parole.significato: A kind of sweet pink onion from Brittany in France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Roscoff, with the pronunciation influenced by Breton Rosko.

parole.significato: A regional contestant in the annual Rose of Tralee contest.

parole.significato: Hibiscus sabdariffa, an edible flower in the hibiscus family used to make hibiscus tea.
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps an alteration or misapprehension of French oseille denoting this plant, specific use of oseille sorrel; perhaps compare also sorrel.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Edmond Rostand (1868–1918), French poet and dramatist.
parole.testo: From French Rostand + -ian.

parole.significato: To cook on a rotisserie.

parole.significato: A ruff worn during the beginning of the 17th century; a cope.

parole.significato: Plebeian rank in France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French roture. Doublet of rupture.

parole.significato: A branding iron.
parole.testo: From French [Term?].

parole.significato: Annatto, achiote (Bixa orellana)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French roucou.

parole.significato: A wheel-like amulet of the ancient Gauls, intended to symbolize the sun.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rouelle.

parole.significato: A heavyweight breed of domesticated duck, of French origin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Rouen, from Latin Rotomagus. Replaced Middle English Rone, from Anglo-Norman Ron.

parole.significato: The behaviour of a roué; debauchery.

parole.significato: A flutter wheel.

parole.testo: Borrowed from French rouge, from Latin rubeus. Compare rare Middle English rouge, rouȝ (“red”); later borrowed again, as it is not attested until c. 1750. The game senses are of unknown origin according to the Oxford English Dictionary.

parole.significato: A solitaire card game played with two decks of playing cards.
parole.testo: From French rouge et noir (literally “red and black”).

parole.significato: A porcine infectuous disease.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rouget.

parole.significato: A type of sauce from Provence, France, often served with fish dishes, consisting of egg yolk and olive oil with breadcr…

parole.significato: An elaborate embellishment of several notes sung to one syllable.

parole.significato: A cyclist who performs well on flat and undulating roads.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rouleur (“one who causes something to roll, roller; something which rolls; cyclist who performs well on flat and undulating roads, rouleur”), from rouler (“to roll”) + -eur (suffix forming masculine nouns from verbs). parole.significato: The handle by which the bed of a hand press, holding the form of type, etc., is run in under the platen and out again.
parole.testo: Compare French ronce (“bramble, brier, thorn”), ranche (“a round, step, rack”), or English round.

parole.significato: Any of a number of species of fruit bat, of the genus Rousettus.

parole.significato: Any of certain fruit bats:
