parole.testo: Borrowed from French truffade, from Occitan trufada.

parole.significato: A plot of land cultivated to produce truffles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French truffière, from truffe (“truffle”) + -ière.

parole.significato: Having a delicately crackled surface.
parole.testo: From French, derived from truite (“trout”).

parole.significato: A set of three special trump cards used in some Tarock games, having a higher value than the other trumps.
parole.testo: From French tous les trois (“all three”).

parole.significato: The pillar or center post supporting the lintel in the middle of a doorway or window opening, especially in a church.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French trumeau.

parole.significato: A wall mirror set in a decorative frame that often features a painted or carved panel under or above the mirror.
parole.testo: From French trumeau (“pillar between large windows or other openings; wood panel or mirror covering such pillar; mirror placed above a fireplace”).

parole.significato: The suit, in a game of cards, that outranks all others.
parole.testo: Possibly from French triomphe (“triumph”) or Old French triumphe. If so, it is a doublet of triumph and thriambus. Compare German Trumpf.

parole.significato: Synonym of Jew's harp.
parole.testo: Ellipsis of Jew's-trump, which may be from French jeu-trompe (literally “toy trumpet”).

parole.significato: One of the short stubby bearings on either side of a cannon; a pintle.
parole.testo: From French trognon (“core, stump”).

parole.significato: Very, to superior degree.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French très. Attested in English from the 19th century. Doublet of trans.

parole.significato: In style; fashionable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French très chic (“very stylish”).

parole.significato: unbecoming
parole.testo: From French très gauche (“very awkward”).

parole.significato: A large brass musical instrument, usually in the bass range, played through a vibration of the lips upon the mouthpiece…
parole.testo: Borrowed in the 19th century from French tuba (“tuba”), German Tuba (“tuba”), originally Baß-Tuba (literally “bass tuba”), or Italian tuba (“tuba”), from Latin tuba (“tube, trumpet, military trumpet”). The Latin term is of obscure ultimate origin, but is possibly connected to tībia (“shinbone, reed-

parole.significato: A short tubular opening at the top of a retort, or at the top or side of a bottle; a tubulation.
parole.testo: Compare French tubulure, from tubulé, past tense verbal use of tube. Equivalent to tubule + -ure

parole.significato: Germanic; Teutonic.
parole.testo: French tudesque

parole.significato: A light porous rock, now especially a rock composed of compacted volcanic ash varying in size from fine sand to coarse…
parole.testo: From French tuffe, tuf, from Italian tufo, from Latin tōfus. Doublet of tufa.

parole.significato: A type of thin, papery cookie, often bent into fancy shapes and added as garnish to dishes or desserts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French tuile (“tile”). Doublet of tile and tuille.

parole.significato: A large lake trout, Salvelinus namaycush, found mainly in Canada and northern areas of the US.
parole.testo: From Canadian French touladi, from an Eastern Algonquian language. (The fish is sometimes said to take its name from the Touladi River where some spawn, but the river more likely takes its name from the fish.)

parole.significato: A kind of silk lace or light netting, used for clothing, veils, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French tulle, named after French Tulle (a town), named after Latin Tūtēla (a Roman deity), from Latin tūtēla (whence English tutelary), from Latin tueor (whence tutor, tutorial).

parole.significato: To cause to swell.
parole.testo: From French tuméfier, from Latin tumefaciō, ultimately from tumeō, from Proto-Indo-European *tum-éh₁- (“to be swelling”), stative stem of *tum- (“to swell”).

parole.significato: A swelling due to the presence of fluid.
parole.testo: First attested 1725, from French tumescence, from Latin tumescēns (“swelling”), present participle of tumēscō (“to begin to swell”), from tumeō (“to swell”) + -ēscō (incohative suffix) (English -esce, in this form -escence), stem from Proto-Indo-European *tum-éh₁- (“to be swelling”), stative stem of

parole.significato: A whirlwind or vortex.
parole.testo: French tourbillon, from Latin turbo (“a whirl”).

parole.significato: Any of various rotary machines that use the kinetic energy of a continuous stream of fluid (a liquid or a gas) to turn…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French turbine, from Latin turbō, turbinem (“tornado, whirlwind; crowd”).

parole.significato: A broad, deep serving dish used for serving soup or stew.
parole.testo: From earlier terrene (thus pronunciations with /tj/, /t͡ʃ/ are spelling pronunciations), borrowed from French terrine. Doublet of terrine.

parole.significato: A native Algerian infantrymans in the French army during the Crimean War.
parole.testo: French Turco. Apparently, the soldiers were nicknamed thus as they dressed like Turks.

parole.significato: A member of a religious sect in mediaeval France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Turlupin.

parole.significato: A heliotrope; so named because its flowers are supposed to turn toward the sun.
parole.testo: French tournesol

parole.significato: crude zinc
parole.testo: From French toutenague, from Portuguese tutenaga, tutanaga, from Tamil துத்தநாகம் (tuttanākam, “raw zinc”). Doublet of tutty.

parole.significato: A four-sided pyramid- or obelisk-like trellis designed to help train climbing plants.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French tuteur.

parole.significato: To address by the informal French pronoun tu (“you”).
parole.testo: From French tutoyer.

parole.significato: To address (someone) in French using the familiar second-person pronoun tu; to thou.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French tutoyer.

parole.significato: A powdered form of impure zinc oxide used for polishing.
parole.testo: From French tutie; compare Spanish tutía, atutía, from Latin tutia, from Arabic تُوتِيَاء (tūtiyāʔ), from Classical Persian توتیا (tūtyā), from Sanskrit तुत्था (tutthā).

parole.significato: A ballet skirt made of layered stiff but light netting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French tutu, from cucu (“bum, bottom”), playful reduplication of cul (“arse”).

parole.significato: A nozzle or similar fixture through which the blast is delivered to the interior of a blast furnace, or to the fire of…
parole.testo: From French tuyère, from Middle French tuyere, from Old French toiere (“pipe-hole”), from tuyau, tueil, tudel (“pipe”), from Frankish *thūta (“pipe”), from Proto-Germanic *þeutǭ (“pipe, channel, flow”), from *þeutaną (“to howl, roar, resound”), from Proto-Indo-European *tu-, *tutu- (“bird-cry, shrie

parole.significato: The Quebec Sales Tax
parole.testo: From French TVQ.

parole.significato: A surgeon's case of instruments.
parole.testo: From French étuis pl. Compare tweezers.

parole.significato: Lack of dexterity in either hand; being ambilevous.
parole.testo: Calque of French avoir deux mains gauches.

parole.significato: One of a pair of specialised sound-producing structures located below each side of the anterior abdominal region of var…
parole.testo: Variant of timbale, from French timbale.

parole.significato: A person who is interested in helping blind people.
parole.testo: From French typhlophile, equivalent to typhlo- + -phile.

parole.significato: The art or practice of setting and arranging type; typesetting.
parole.testo: From French typographie from Medieval Latin typographia from Ancient Greek τυπογράφος (tupográphos, “certified copy”) + -ίᾱ (-íā). By surface analysis, type + -o- + -graphy.

parole.significato: The killing of a tyrant.
parole.testo: From French tyrannicide, from Middle French tyrannicide, from Latin tyrannicīda. Equivalent to tyrant + -cide.

parole.significato: Someone who kills a tyrant.
parole.testo: From French tyrannicide, from Middle French tyrannicide, from Latin tyrannicīdium. Equivalent to tyrant + -cide.

parole.significato: A traditional folk dance of Tyrol.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French tyrolienne.

parole.significato: Of a postage stamp, printed upside down relative to the following stamp of the same row or column.
parole.testo: From French tête-bêche (literally “head-to-foot”).

parole.significato: a bridgehead.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French tête de pont (“head of a bridge”).

parole.significato: A face-to-face meeting, or private conversation between two people, usually in an intimate setting; a head-to-head.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French tête-à-tête (“head-to-head”).

parole.significato: Reminiscent of Ubu Roi, an early absurdist play; absurdly grotesque.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ubuesque.

parole.significato: An idealized or fictional conception of a particular period of time, especially in the past.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French uchronie, formed after utopie (“utopia”), from Ancient Greek οὐ (ou, “not”) + Ancient Greek χρόνος (khrónos, “time”) + -ia.

parole.significato: A lancer, a soldier armed with a lance in a former light cavalry unit of the Polish, Prussian or German, Austrian, and…
parole.testo: From French uhlan, from German Uhlan, from Polish ułan, from Ottoman Turkish اوغلان (oğlan).

parole.significato: Ultimate; final.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ultime.

parole.significato: A Roman Catholic philosophy that emphasises the prerogatives and powers of the Pope.
parole.testo: From ultramontane + -ism, after French ultramontanisme.

parole.significato: Synonym of hammerkop (Scopus umbretta, a bird)
parole.testo: French ombrette.

parole.significato: A French literary movement based on ideas of collective consciousness and collective emotion.
parole.testo: From French unanimisme.

parole.significato: Of a piece of text, written and struck through; hence, figuratively in some sense both present and absent.
parole.testo: Perhaps a calque of French sous rature

parole.significato: Waving or wavy; applied to ordinaries, or division lines.
parole.testo: French ondé.

parole.significato: A person with only one leg.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French unijambiste.

parole.significato: Being the only one of its kind; unequaled, unparalleled or unmatched.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French unique, from Latin unicus.

parole.significato: The diachronic process of forming a new single word from a fixed expression of several words.
parole.testo: Probably from French univerbation, from uni- (“uni-”) + Latin verbum (“word”) + French -ation (“-ation”).

parole.significato: Having one brood or generation in a year
parole.testo: From French univoltin. By surface analysis, uni- + -voltine.

parole.significato: Living or situated remote from the seacoast.
parole.testo: Possibly a calque of French Pays d'en Haut, a designation from 1610 referring to the area of New France west of Montreal. By surface analysis, up + country.

parole.significato: Urdu-speaking.
parole.testo: From Urdu + -phone or French ourdouphone.

parole.significato: A white crystalline organic compound, ethyl-carbamate, NH₂COOC₂H₅, used in the synthesis of other organic compounds.
parole.testo: From French uréthane, coined (1833) by Jean Baptiste Dumas. Etymonline proposes an apparent decomposition as urée + éther + -ane.

parole.significato: Pertaining to, contained in, or obtained from urine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French urique. By surface analysis, urine + -ic.

parole.significato: One who has the use of anything held in trust for another.
parole.testo: French usager.

parole.significato: A West Indian sugar factory.
parole.testo: From French usine. Doublet of officina and oficina.

parole.significato: To commit usury.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French usure (“usury”, noun). The change to a verb in English may be influenced by back-formation from usury. Piecewise doublet of etymology 2.

parole.significato: To cause to degenerate through usage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French usure (“wear from usage”). Piecewise doublet of etymology 1.

parole.significato: The act of using something.
parole.testo: From French utilisation or from utilise + -ation.

parole.significato: To make use of; to use.
parole.testo: From French utiliser, from Italian utilizzare, from utile (“useful”), from Latin ūtilis, from ūtī (“use”). Attested c. 1810.

parole.significato: US, Canada, and Oxford British English standard spelling of utilisation.
parole.testo: From French utilisation or from utilize + -ation.

parole.significato: US, Canada, and Oxford British English standard spelling of utilise.
parole.testo: From French utiliser, from Italian utilizzare, from utile (“useful”), from Latin ūtilis, from ūtī (“use”).

parole.significato: One who murders one's wife.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French uxoricide or Latin uxor + English -icide.

parole.significato: The murdering of one's own wife.
parole.testo: From French uxoricide or Latin uxōricīdium.

parole.significato: All or nothing, all in, for broke; riskily putting everything on the line to either win it all or lose it all.
parole.testo: From French (je) va (la) banque, a call used in the 18th century in games like Rouge et Noir and Faro to announce that one was betting as much money as the bank had, to either win or lose that amount.

parole.significato: A substance given to stimulate a body's production of antibodies and provide immunity against a disease without causing…
parole.testo: The noun is probably partly: * derived from vaccine (adjective) (see etymology 1); and * borrowed from French vaccine (“cowpox (short for variole vaccine); vaccination against smallpox using material from cowpox”), vaccin (“cowpox material used for smallpox vaccination”), both noun uses of vaccin (a

parole.significato: A keeper of stock or cattle; a herdsman.
parole.testo: From French vacher (“cowherd”). Doublet of vaquero.

parole.significato: A cake-shaped dessert made of a meringue shell filled with ice cream and topped with whipped cream.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vacherin glacé (literally “frozen vacherin”).

parole.significato: A dairy, a vaccary.
parole.testo: From French vacherie, from vache (“a cow”), Latin vacca. Compare vaccary. By surface analysis, French vache + -ery.

parole.significato: A piece of strong steel wire with the ends curved and pointed, used on toe or quarter cracks to bind the edges together…
parole.testo: From French vachette.

parole.significato: A large membrane-bound vesicle in a cell's cytoplasm.
parole.testo: From French vacuole, from Medieval Latin vacuola, formed as a diminutive of Latin vacuus (“empty”).

parole.significato: A paste of burnt garlic and onion with herbs, from India; a type of masala.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vadouvan, from Tamil வடகம் (vaṭakam).

parole.significato: The state or characteristic of being a vagabond.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vagabondage.

parole.significato: The personal servant of a monarch.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French valet de chambre.

parole.significato: In France, a person who offered his services as a guide, messenger, etc. for hire, especially to strangers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French [Term?].

parole.significato: A pipette-like tube for drawing liquor from a cask through the bung-hole.
parole.testo: Compare French avaler (“to let down, drink up”). Compare avalanche.

parole.significato: A piece of hand luggage such as a suitcase or travelling bag.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French valise.

parole.significato: A mythological creature (usually humanoid and undead) said to feed on the blood or life energy of the living.
parole.testo: From French vampire, from German Vampir, via Hungarian from a Slavic word, probably Serbo-Croatian vàmpīr /ва̀мпӣр, from Proto-Slavic *ǫpyrь, further possibly from Proto-Turkic *ōpur (“glutton, witch, evil spirit”), or from native construction. Doublet of dhampir and oupire.

parole.significato: A round of iron on the shaft of a tilting lance, to stabilize and protect the hand.
parole.testo: From French avant (“fore”) and English plate.

parole.significato: Someone sent in advance; an avant-courier, precursor, or scout.
parole.testo: From French avant-courrier. See avant, van of an army, and courier, and compare avant-courier, vaunt-courier.

parole.significato: A precursor; one who comes before, or who leads a change.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French avant-courier.

parole.significato: Willful damage to or destruction of any property, such as graffiti or defacement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vandalisme, first used by Henri Grégoire to decry the pillage and destruction of art in the course of the French Revolution, in reference to the East Germanic tribe of the Vandals, which looted Rome in 455. By surface analysis, vandal + -ism.

parole.significato: An ichneumon, Atilax paludinosus (syn. Herpestes galera), native to Africa and Madagascar. It is reddish brown or dark…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vansire, from Malagasy vontsira.

parole.significato: evaporation
parole.testo: Compare French vaporation, Latin vaporatio.

parole.significato: The monitor lizard.
parole.testo: Derived from French varan. Doublet of worral.

parole.significato: The incinerated ash of certain coarse seaweeds, formerly used for the production of soda and iodine, among other compou…
parole.testo: French varech; of Teutonic origin. See wrack and compare vraic.

parole.significato: A military tunic.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vareuse.

parole.significato: An imperfection on the inside of the hind leg in horses, different from a curb, but at the same height, and often growi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French varisse, from Latin varis-, oblique stem of varis. Compare varix and French varice.

parole.significato: Of, from or pertaining to Warsaw.
parole.testo: From Latin Varsovia (“Warsaw”) + -an, or French Varsovien.

parole.significato: A polka-like Polish dance.
parole.testo: From French, literally "from Warsaw".

parole.significato: A type of frock worn in Spain between the 17th and 19th centuries.
parole.testo: From French vasquine. Compare Spanish basquiña.

parole.significato: A style of multi-act theatrical entertainment which originated from France and flourished in Europe and North America f…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vaudeville.

parole.significato: An inhabitant of the Swiss canton of Vaud.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vaudois.

parole.significato: The first part.
parole.testo: From French avant (“before, fore”). See avant, vanguard.

parole.significato: A false wall raised in front of the main wall as a fortification.
parole.testo: From French avant-mur. See vanguard and mure.

parole.significato: A good-for-nothing; a scoundrel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vaurien; used by Isaac D'Israeli for the name of the eponymous character of his 1797 novel Vaurien: or Sketches of the Times.

parole.significato: Vangueria madagascariensis, a flowering plant with a large orange edible fruit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vavangue, from Malagasy voavanga, from voa (“fruit”) + vanga (“spotted with color”).

parole.significato: The quality or tenure of the fee held by a vavasour.
parole.testo: French vavassorie.

parole.significato: A sentinel, usually on horseback, stationed on the outpost of an army, to watch an enemy and give notice of danger.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vedette.

parole.significato: A conveyance: a spacious device for carrying or transporting substances, objects, people or animals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French véhicule, from Latin vehiculum (“a carriage, conveyance”), from vehō, vehere (“to carry”).

parole.significato: A shaded night-lamp
parole.testo: From French.

parole.significato: veining; veins collectively
parole.testo: From vein + -age, or from French veinage.

parole.significato: An early two-wheeled conveyance upon which one rode astride a wooden frame propelled by means of pushing the feet again…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vélocipède, from Latin velox (“swift”) + pes (“foot”).

parole.significato: An indoor arena, having an oval banked track for bicycle racing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vélodrome, from vélo + -drome. By surface analysis, velo- + -drome.

parole.significato: A knit fabric similar to velvet, but usually somewhat coarser.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French velours (“velvet”).

parole.significato: A mother sauce in French cuisine, consisting of a light stock thickened with a blond roux.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French velouté (“velvety, smooth”).

parole.significato: An old French unit of liquid measure, approximately 7.617 litres.
parole.testo: From French velte.

parole.significato: For sale; available for purchase.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vénal, from Old French venel, from Latin vēnālis (“for sale”), from vēnum (“something for sale”); compare English vend.

parole.significato: The fact or state of being for sale, especially with reference to bribes or corruption.
parole.testo: From venal + -ity, from French vénalité or Latin vēnālitās, from vēnālis (“venal”), from vēnum; compare English vend.

parole.significato: Synonym of sell, (now especially) to sell through a vending machine.
parole.testo: 17th century, likely a backformation from earlier vendible, vendee, vendor inspired by the underlying French vendre, from Old French vendre, from Latin vendere, from vēnum dāre (“to give (something for) sale”).

parole.significato: The annual grape harvest, especially in France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vendange.

parole.significato: A saleswoman in a fashionable clothing store.
parole.testo: French vendeuse (“saleswoman”).

parole.significato: A huntsman, especially in France.
parole.testo: From French veneur.

parole.significato: Synonym of venom.
parole.testo: From French venin (“venom”), from Latin venēnum (“juice; venom”). Doublet of venene and venom.

parole.significato: An alley; a narrow street.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French venelle (“alley”).

parole.significato: To sell; to vend.
parole.testo: From French vente, from Latin vendere (“to sell”).

parole.significato: A pebble or little stone shaped and polished by wind-blown sand.
parole.testo: Blend of vent (“wind”) + artifact (“an object shaped or created by some process or agency”) from French vent from Latin ventus

parole.significato: Related to the abdomen or stomach.
parole.testo: From French ventral, from Latin ventrālis, from venter (“belly, abdomen”); by surface analysis, ventr- + -al.

parole.significato: At breakneck speed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ventre à terre.

parole.significato: A strike or blow.
parole.testo: Alteration of French venue. Doublet of venue.

parole.significato: A stage in the ripening process of grapes or olives. It is the relatively short period during which the firm, green ber…
parole.testo: From French véraison.

parole.significato: Overabundance of words.
parole.testo: From French verbiage. Compare verb meaning "word" in verbal and verbose.

parole.significato: A mottled green serpentine marble.
parole.testo: From French vert antique (“a kind of marble”), from verd, vert (“green”) + antique (“ancient”). Compare Italian verde antico.

parole.significato: A method of painting or other work which employs only varying shades of green, or work executed with this method.
parole.testo: Compare French vert (“green”), as well as English grisaille or brunaille, from French.

parole.significato: An official in charge of a royal forest; in modern times, still extant in the New Forest and the Forest of Dean
parole.testo: From French verdier, from Late Latin viridarius, from Latin viridis (“green”).

parole.significato: A green aniline dye.
parole.testo: From French verd, vert (“green”). Dye was originally a commercial name.

parole.significato: verdigris
parole.testo: French vert-de-terre, literally "green of earth".

parole.significato: Charged with leaves, fruits, flowers, etc.; said of a border.
parole.testo: French verdoyer (“to become green”). See verdant.

parole.significato: A small pale (vertical band down the middle of a shield).
parole.testo: From French.

parole.significato: silver frost
parole.testo: Borrowed from French verglas.

parole.significato: Synonym of verifier.
parole.testo: From French vérificateur. By surface analysis, verificate + -or.

parole.significato: A type of backslang used in French, in which the order of the syllables or sounds of words is changed.
parole.testo: From French verlan, itself a verlan of à l'envers (“upside down or back to front”).

parole.significato: A brownish-red variety of almandine garnet.
parole.testo: Obsolete trade name, from French vermeille (“bright red, vermilion”).

parole.significato: A dry, or sweet apéritif wine flavored with aromatic herbs, and often used in mixed drinks.
parole.testo: From French vermout, vermouth, from German Wermut (“wormwood”). Doublet of wormwood.

parole.significato: A secondary scale with finer graduations than the primary scale of a measuring device; the vernier measures between gra…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vernier. From Pierre Vernier, the inventor.

parole.significato: A private viewing of an art exhibition before it opens to the public.
parole.testo: From French vernissage, derived from the earlier habit of the artists to varnish their paintings the day before the opening of an exhibition.

parole.significato: The glass harp
parole.testo: From French verrillon (“glass harp”).

parole.significato: Any savory or sweet food served in a small glass, typically in France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French verrine.

parole.significato: A type of light poetry suited to the amusement of polite upper-class society.
parole.testo: From the French vers de société.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the city of Versailles, Yvelines department, Île-de-France, France or the famous palace located…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French versaillais, from Versailles + -ais. Doublet of Versaillese.

parole.significato: Experienced, practiced.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French versant, present participle (used as a noun) of verser, from Latin versō, frequentative of vertō (“to turn”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Russian green
parole.testo: French vert russe (literally “Russian green”)

parole.significato: A joint of the back.
parole.testo: From French vertebre, from Latin vertebra.

parole.significato: Verticalness; the state or condition of being vertical.
parole.testo: From vertical + -ity; compare French verticalité.

parole.significato: To furnish with a vestibule or vestibules.

parole.significato: A mark left on the earth by a foot.
parole.testo: From French vestige, from Latin vestīgium (“footstep, footprint, track, the sole of the foot, a trace, mark”). Doublet of vestigium.

parole.significato: Able to live on its own (as for a newborn).

parole.significato: Pulsing with energy or activity.

parole.significato: A thick, creamy soup made from potato, leeks, onions, and chicken stock, and normally served cold.

parole.significato: Victimization.

parole.significato: The study of the victims of crime, and especially of the reasons some people are more prone to be victims.

parole.significato: A baked product made in a similar manner to bread, but with ingredients giving it a sweeter, heavier quality closer to…

parole.significato: Old-fashioned, outmoded.

parole.significato: Old money; wealthy persons whose fortunes are inherited, and who are therefore perceived to have refinement and good br…

parole.significato: Watchful, especially for danger or disorder; alert; wary.
parole.testo: From French vigilant or its source, Latin vigilans, present participle of vigilare (“stay awake”), from vigil (“awake”). Doublet of vigilante, from Spanish. Displaced Old English wacor.

parole.significato: A person who grows vines for wine production, a winegrower

parole.significato: A running ornament consisting of leaves and tendrils, used in Gothic architecture.

parole.significato: A soft dress material, a mix of wool and cotton.
parole.testo: From French vigogne.

parole.significato: A type of poem, consisting of five tercets and one quatrain, with only two rhymes.
parole.testo: From the French villanelle, from Italian villanella, from villano (“peasant”), from Latin vīllānus (“farmhand”), from vīlla (“estate”). The origin references the pastoral themes originally associated with this form.

parole.significato: A Vietnamese village.
parole.testo: From French ville. Doublet of vill and villa.

parole.significato: Mulled wine.
parole.testo: From French vin (“wine”) + chaud (“hot”).

parole.significato: An unusual white wine made in the Jura region of France from late harvest Savagnin grapes, a local white variety.

parole.significato: A cheap claret, used as a table wine in France.

parole.significato: The addition of alcohol to wine to allow it to stand transportation.

parole.significato: A pot or jar in which vinegar is made.

parole.significato: The card game pontoon.

parole.significato: A subdivision of a parish, corresponding to a cueillette in the parish of Saint Ouen.

parole.significato: A law enforcement officer subordinate to a centenier and responsible for a vingtaine.

parole.significato: A type of white wine-producing grape originally grown in the Rhône valley.

parole.significato: An emetocathartic alkaloid, of uncertain composition, obtained from violets.

parole.significato: A kind of organ stop producing a string-like sound.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French violon (“violin”).

parole.significato: The transfer of a surplus from one account to cover a deficit in another.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French virement.

parole.significato: An arrow or bolt for a crossbow having feathers or brass placed at an angle with the shaft to make it spin in flight.
parole.testo: From French vireton. See vire.

parole.significato: Synonym of slash ⟨/⟩.
parole.testo: An anglicization of French virgule, from Latin virgula.

parole.significato: A variety of winter pear.
parole.testo: From French virgouleuse, from Virgoulée, variant form of Villegoureix, a village in the Limousin province of France. Compare vergaloo.

parole.significato: A single individual particle of a virus (the viral equivalent of a cell).
parole.testo: From French virion. By surface analysis, virus + -on.

parole.significato: A ring surrounding a bugle or hunting horn.
parole.testo: From French virole (“ferrule”). See ferrule.

parole.significato: A computer technology that simulates a real or imagined environment so that the user can interact with it as if physica…

parole.significato: In relation to; compared with.

parole.significato: A permit to enter and leave a country, normally issued by the authorities of the country to be visited.

parole.significato: A make-up artist.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French visagiste.

parole.significato: One who visits; a guest; a visitor.
parole.testo: From French visitant, present participle of visiter.

parole.significato: A light cape or short cloak made of silk or lace, formerly worn by women in summer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French visite. See visit.

parole.significato: An American mink (Neogale vison).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vison (“mink”).

parole.significato: Related to or affecting the vision.
parole.testo: From Middle English visual, from French visuel, visual and directly from Late Latin vīsuālis (“of sight”), from vīsus (“sight, vision”) + -ālis (“adjective suffix”), from vidēre (“to see, perceive; look (at)”); see visage. By surface analysis, Latin vīsus + -ual.

parole.significato: visa.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French visé, past participle of viser (“to issue with a visa”).

parole.significato: A curtain of light translucent material intended to be secured directly to the woodwork of a French window or glazed do…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vitrage (literally “glass covering”), ultimately from Latin vitrum (“glass”).

parole.significato: A stained glass window.

parole.significato: An artist who uses stained glass as a medium.
parole.testo: French vitrail + -ist

parole.testo: Borrowed from French vitrine, from vitre (“pane of glass”), from Old French, from Latin vitrum (“glass”).

parole.significato: The act of vitriolizing someone; the act of committing an acid attack.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vitriolage. Analyzable as vitriol (“sulfuric acid”) + -age.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to vitriol; derived from or resembling vitriol.
parole.testo: From vitriol + -ic; or from French vitriolique (cognate with Italian vetriolico, Portuguese vitriolico, Spanish vitriólico).

parole.significato: Vituperative.
parole.testo: From French vitupéreux, from Late Latin vituperosus, from Latin vituperāre (“to blame, censure”), from vitium (“fault, defect”) + parāre (“to furnish, provide, contrive”).

parole.significato: A sutler accompanying a continental European army, especially the French army.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vivandier.

parole.significato: A female vivandier.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vivandière.

parole.significato: In mort, bridge, and similar games, the partner of dummy.

parole.significato: Used to express appreciation of diversity, especially between the sexes; sometimes referring to cultural diversity, and…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French, literally “long live the difference”, from vive (“long live”) + la (“the”) + différence (“difference, diversity”). Although correct and unremarkable French, it is not a stock phrase in French as it is in English.

parole.significato: provisions; victuals
parole.testo: From French vivres, plural of vivre (“to live”).

parole.significato: Someone who lives well.

parole.significato: Reproduction via embryos that develop from the outset without interruption (as opposed to germinating from a seed).

parole.significato: The office, dignity, or authority of a vizier.
parole.testo: From French vizirat. Equivalent to vizier + -ate (forms nouns enoting rank or office, the concrete charge of it, a state ruled by people of such an office).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a vowel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vocalique, from vocal + -ique.

parole.significato: A vocal exercise performed by singing one or more vowels without actually forming any words.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French.

parole.significato: A practitioner of voodoo.
parole.testo: From French vaudouisant, from vaudoiser (“to practice voodoo”).

parole.significato: A light, translucent cotton fabric used for making curtains and dresses.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French voile (“veil”). Doublet of veil and velum.

parole.significato: Lo, there it is; ta-da; presto; behold!
parole.testo: Borrowed from French voilà.

parole.significato: A carriage; a vehicle, now chiefly in French contexts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French voiture, from Latin vectūra. Doublet of vecture and vettura.

parole.significato: A small, compact car.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French voiturette, first used in 1895 by Léon Bollée to describe his new motor tricycle.

parole.significato: One who lets horses and carriages to travellers.

parole.significato: An organ stop consisting of either one or two ranks of pipes slightly out of tune, so as to produce a beating effect wh…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French voix céleste (“heavenly voice”).

parole.significato: A heraldic symbol consisting of a pair of outstretched wings, often conjoined at their shoulders.

parole.significato: The study of volcanoes.
parole.testo: From French volcanologie, from volcan (“volcano”); and/or directly from volcano + -logy.

parole.significato: A shutter on a window.

parole.significato: A conscious choice or decision.
parole.testo: From French volition, from Medieval Latin volitiō (“will, volition”), from Latin volō (“to wish; to want; to mean or intend”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“to choose; to want”)) + -tiō (suffix forming nouns relating to some action or the result of an action) (ultimately from Proto-I

parole.significato: A steep, controlled dive, especially by an aircraft with the engine off.

parole.significato: A circular movement in which the horse goes round in a small circle.

parole.significato: A reversal of attitude, policy, or principle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French volte-face.

parole.significato: One of a picked company of skirmishers in each regiment of the French infantry during the Napoleonic Wars.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French voltigeur, from voltiger (“to vault”), Italian volteggiare. See volt (“a tread”).

parole.significato: One whose life is devoted to sensual appetites; a pleasure-seeker, a sensualist.
parole.testo: From French voluptuaire, or directly from its etymon Late Latin voluptuārius, from Latin voluptārius (“pleasure-seeker; agreeable, delightful, pleasant; sensual”), from voluptās (“delight, pleasure, satisfaction”) + -ārius (suffix forming adjectives from nouns). parole.significato: The characteristic spiral curve on an Ionic capital, widely copied in other styles and in neoclassical architecture.
parole.testo: From French volute, from Italian voluta, from Latin volūta, from the feminine of volūtus, perfect passive participle of volvō. Doublet of vault.

parole.significato: One of a series of wedge-shaped bricks or stones forming an arch or vault.

parole.significato: To address (someone) in French using the formal second-person pronoun vous.

parole.significato: A person who derives sexual pleasure from observing other people engaging in some intimate or sexual activity; one who…

parole.significato: A female voyeur; a woman who derives sexual pleasure from secretly observing other people.
parole.testo: From French voyeuse.

parole.significato: verisimilitude

parole.significato: A tailspin.

parole.significato: The ideology which supports Walloon autonomy or independence; Walloon nationalism.
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from French wallingantisme. By surface analysis, Wallingant + -ism.

parole.significato: A guariba: a South American monkey (sapajou).
parole.testo: Anglicization of French ouarine, a misreading of ouariue (i.e. ouarive), ultimately from the same source as guariba.

parole.significato: A deep blue variety of iolite, sometimes used as a gem.
parole.testo: Equivalent to French saphir d'eau.

parole.significato: A French tram driver.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French wattman, a pseudo-anglicism derived from watt + -man.

parole.significato: A small wave; a ripple.

parole.significato: A play belonging to a 19th-century neoclassical theatrical genre involving a tight plot and a climax close to the end.…

parole.significato: The lands in the vicinity of the Welsh-English border.
parole.testo: From French marche (“frontier area, border lands”), Old English mearc (“boundary”).

parole.significato: voila; ta-da, presto; lo and behold
parole.testo: French voilà pronunciation respelling

parole.significato: A schoolmaster.

parole.significato: An unconsummated marriage.
parole.testo: Calque of French mariage blanc. “White” is the traditional symbol of purity and therefore of virginity. It may also refer to the absence of hymenal blood on the couple’s sheets.

parole.significato: A peace agreement after a war, in which the parties do not impose onerous terms on one other.
parole.testo: Calque of French paix blanche.

parole.significato: A head of real or synthetic hair worn on the head to disguise baldness, for cultural or religious reasons, for fashion,…
parole.testo: Clipping of periwig, itself an alteration of French perruque. The meaning of "to reprimand" perhaps came from this being something a bigwig would do or perhaps from the expressions to flip one's wig, wigs on the green, or dash my wig!

parole.significato: Any late-maturing variety of true melon (Cucumis melo), such as honeydew melon (Inodorus Group), Cassaba melon (Cassaba…

parole.significato: Of, or from, the state of Wisconsin.

parole.significato: A marmoset, principally in family Callitrichidae.

parole.significato: in the very act; red-handed.
parole.testo: Corruption of "with the mainer", from French main (“hand”).

parole.significato: A woman's fur-lined cloak, mantle, or pelisse with large sleeves, worn during the early 19th century.
parole.testo: PIE word  *wĺ̥kʷos Borrowed from French witzchoura (obsolete), vitchoura (“witzchoura”), from Polish wilczura (“(archaic) wolfskin”), from wilczy (“wolf-like, lupine”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos (“wolf”)) + -ura (suffix forming feminine nouns).

parole.significato: Speech or writing that is overly abstract, vague, metaphorical or pretentious in order to avoid addressing salient issu…

parole.significato: The water-soluble part of the yellow carotenoid pigment present in the cell sap of some plants.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French xantheine, apparently an arbitrary respelling to distinguish it from the similarly spelled xanthine. Ultimately from Ancient Greek; see xanthine. By surface analysis, xanth- + -ein.

parole.significato: Any of a group of alkaloids that include caffeine, theophylline, and theobromine as well as the parent compound, a prec…
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, from French xanthine, reflecting New Latin combining forms: xanth- + -ine; ultimately from Ancient Greek ξανθός (xanthós, “yellow”), because xanthine is yellowish-white. By surface analysis, xanth- + -ine.

parole.significato: A small two-masted, and later three-masted, Mediterranean transport ship with an overhanging bow and stern.

parole.significato: A word used in utterances of a language but generally marked as foreign.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French xénisme, from Ancient Greek ξενισμός (xenismós, “strangeness, novelty”).

parole.significato: Knowledge of a language one has never learned.
parole.testo: From xeno- + -glossia, borrowed from French xénoglossie.

parole.significato: The art of making xylographs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French xylographie, corresponding to xylo- (“wood”) + -graphy (“writing”).

parole.significato: A collection of samples of various types of wood.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French xylothèque.

parole.significato: Especially in the Tour de France: the yellow shirt worn by the leader of a stage of a cycling race, which is then award…
parole.testo: Calque of French maillot jaune: maillot (“jersey, shirt; vest”) + jaune (“yellow”, adjective).

parole.significato: A member of a French protest movement which started in late 2018 against rising fuel prices and advocates for economic…

parole.significato: From the late-19th to the early-20th century, a member of a movement that campaigned for reform of the Ottoman Empire.

parole.significato: Synonym of mustard gas.

parole.significato: Château d'Yquem, a prestigious wine produced in Sauternes.

parole.significato: A term of derision used by Quebec separatists to refer to Federalist-voting French Quebecois housewives.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Yvette. The politics sense is a reference to the name of a docile young girl in a school textbook, and was popularized by separatist politician Lise Payette (1931–2018).

parole.significato: A genre of pop music of the early 1960s in Europe.
parole.testo: From French yéyé, from English yeah-yeah.

parole.significato: A militant open-air demonstration in the form of a defended squat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ZAD, short for zone à défendre (“zone to defend”).

parole.significato: A horse of a dark colour with no lighter spots.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French zain.

parole.significato: The unit of currency of Zaire from 1967 to 1998.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French zaïre. Named after the Zaire River, another name for the Congo River.

parole.significato: A lesbian.
parole.testo: From French des amies.

parole.significato: The marbled swamp eel (Synbranchus marmoratus).
parole.testo: Trinidadian alteration of French anguille (“eel”).

parole.significato: A Turkish policeman.
parole.testo: From French zaptieh, from Ottoman Turkish ضبطیه (zaptiye, “policeman”), from Arabic ضَبْطِيَّة (ḍabṭiyya, “policeman”).

parole.significato: A zelatrix (nun).
parole.testo: Probably from or influenced by French.

parole.significato: A motorcycle taxi found in Benin.
parole.testo: From French zémidjan, from Fon zěmìjàn.

parole.significato: The outer skin of a citrus fruit, used as a flavouring or garnish.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French zeste.

parole.significato: The edible pine nuts of the Aleppo pine, used to make a variety of dishes.
parole.testo: From French zgougou, from Arabic زقوقو.

parole.significato: A thick, soft woolen fabric with a long nap.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French zibeline (“sable”).

parole.significato: A line or path that proceeds by sharp turns in alternating directions.
parole.testo: Attested from 1712. Borrowed from French zigzag (attested from 1662), possibly from a Germanic source via Walloon ziczac (although German Zickzack is attested only from 1703). parole.significato: A form of zinc oxide powder used as an artist's pigment.
parole.testo: Partially within English and partially as a calque of French blanc de zinc after Edme-Jean Leclaire greatly improved its quality and industrialized its production in a suburb of Paris, France.

parole.significato: A good-for-nothing person.
parole.testo: Claimed by Swedish scholar Jan Ivarsson (quoted in Green's Dictionary of Slang) to derive from French zob (“dick, cock”), itself from Arabic زُبّ (zubb).

parole.significato: The condition of being, resembling, or acting like a zombie.
parole.testo: Possibly from French zombitude, or independently from zombie + -itude. Compare jerkitude, punkitude. Attested in English from the 20th century; see quotations below.

parole.significato: The worship of animals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French zoolâtrie, New Latin zoolatria, from zoo- + -latry.

parole.significato: Ictonyx striatus, a small, carnivorous, nocturnal African mammal resembling a skunk.
parole.testo: From French zorille, from Spanish zorrillo, from zorro (“fox”) + -illo.

parole.testo: From French, from Arabic زَوَاوِيّ (zawāwiyy), used to refer to a Kabyle soldier, especially of the Igawawen people.

parole.significato: A style of dance music originating in the French Antilles, combining Latin American, African and Western disco rhythms;…
parole.testo: From French secouer (“to shake up”), via creole.

parole.significato: The intimate pairing of homologous chromosomes during the synaptic stage of meiosis
parole.testo: From French zygotène, corresponding to zygo- (“union, zygosis”, from Ancient Greek ζυγόν (zugón, “junction, yoke”)) + -tene (“filament”, from ταινία (tainía, “band, fillet”)), equivalent to zygote + -tene. Coined by Victor Grégoire in 1907 and in English by Edmund B. Wilson in 1912.

parole.significato: A small dish of forcemeat, typically cooked in a mold and served with a rich sauce.
parole.testo: From French zéphire. So named because the dish was considered light like a zephyr breeze or cloth. Compare Russian зефи́р (zefír, “marshmallow”), another light food named for the breeze. Doublet of zefir, Zephyr, zephyr, and Zephyrus.

parole.significato: Down with.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French à bas (literally “to the bottom”).

parole.significato: Having a bouche on the dexter side.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French à bouche (“with mouth”).

parole.significato: Reluctantly, unwillingly, with disgust.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French à contrecœur, à contre-cœur, from Old French avoir a contrecuer, avoir contrecœur (“to dislike”), from à (“for, with”) + contre-cœur (“aversion, dislike”) (contre (“against”) + cœur (“heart”)); compare Old French estre contre coer a (“to be adverse to”).

parole.significato: To be played by two people.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French à deux.

parole.significato: In abundance, galore.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French à gogo.

parole.significato: Allowing selection from a fixed list of individually priced options shown on the menu.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French à la carte (“on the menu; according to the card”).

parole.significato: Served in a broth in which it was poached or cooked.
parole.testo: French à la nage (“swimming”, literally “in the (act of) swimming”).

parole.significato: Of a dinner service, having courses already cut and handed out to individual guests.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French à la russe (“in the Russian manner”).

parole.significato: To the greatest extent, to the utmost.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French à outrance. Compare to the outrance.

parole.significato: Apropos of nothing; without connection to anything; by the way, unrelatedly.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French à propos de bottes (literally “on the subject of boots”).

parole.significato: For or between three parties. Often used in reference to alliances.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French à trois.

parole.significato: Someone who is utterly devoted to another and willing to carry out difficult or disagreeable tasks for them; a simp.

parole.significato: A sketch.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ébauche, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“wood, thicket”).

parole.significato: A mass of debris or shingle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French éboulement.

parole.significato: An ebonist; a cabinetmaker who veneers furniture.
parole.testo: From French ébéniste.

parole.significato: A card game in which one can discard certain cards from one's hand and replace them with cards from the deck.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French écarté (“discarded”).

parole.significato: A movement performed in ballet involving a leap from both feet simultaneously.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French. Doublet of escapee.

parole.significato: A small, chocolate-covered, creme-filled pastry puff in a general oblong shape, typically larger than the miniature Fre…

parole.significato: A brilliant or successful effect; brilliance of success or effort; splendor; brilliant show; striking effect; glory; re…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French éclat, from éclater (“to burst out”). Akin to Old English slītan (“to split”). More at slice, slit. Doublet of slate and slat.

parole.significato: A figure drawn, painted or sculpted so as to show the muscles of the body without skin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French écorché (“flayed”).

parole.significato: A contra dance in a Scottish style, popular in France and Great Britain around the late eighteenth century.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French.

parole.significato: A silver coin formerly used in France, with varying values.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French écu. Doublet of scutum, escudo, scudo, and scute.

parole.significato: A two-handled bowl for soup or porridge.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French écuelle. Doublet of scuttle and scutella.

parole.significato: Spirit; zeal; ardor.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French élan.

parole.significato: The life force or vital principle posited in the philosophy of Henri Bergson; any mysterious or creative vital principl…
parole.testo: An unadapted borrowing from French élan vital (“life force”, literally “vital impetus or force”), coined by Henri Bergson in 1907.

parole.significato: A seditious tumult; an outbreak.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French.

parole.significato: A French person who has departed their native land, especially a royalist who left during the French Revolution.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French émigré.

parole.significato: A secret or unofficial decision-maker.

parole.significato: A graduate of the École nationale d'administration.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French énarque.

parole.significato: To scandalize, provoke the middle class.

parole.significato: Presenting one's shoulder to the audience.
parole.testo: French épaulé

parole.significato: A French grocer.
parole.testo: From French épicier. Doublet of spicer.

parole.significato: A traditional soft, pungent French cheese made from cows' milk.
parole.testo: From French Époisses, after the village where it is made.

parole.significato: A team.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French équipe.

parole.significato: Any of the distinctive forms that a cloud takes relating to the altitude of its base, either "low", "middle", or "high"…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French étage. Doublet of stage.

parole.significato: A public storehouse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French étape, from Middle French estappe, from Old French estaple (“warehouse; a place where merchants bring their wares to be sold”), from Middle Dutch stapel (“warehouse; market”), from Old Dutch stapul, from Frankish *stapul. parole.significato: a form of a language at any given time, seen synchronically
parole.testo: Borrowed from French état de langue (“state of language”).

parole.significato: The staff of an army, including all officers above the rank of colonel, all adjutants, inspectors, quartermasters, comm…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French, from état (“state”) + Latin major (“greater”).

parole.significato: The leading ballet dancer in a company
parole.testo: Borrowed from French étoile. Doublet of estoile, stella, and stelo; related to aster and star.

parole.significato: Thoughtlessness, carelessness; a thoughtless act.

parole.significato: A mountaineer's stirrup.

parole.significato: The surrealist technique of cutting away parts of images to develop a new image.

parole.testo: Borrowed from French étui.

parole.significato: bull's eye, oculus

parole.significato: A small, round figure; a decorative dot.
